en: Homage to the Buddha!

I shall compose this priceless anthology of the words of various lords of poets—words that are captivating, the supreme ornaments for the throats of the learned, and that cause the heads of the great poets to bow. (VidSrk 0.1)

May that Victor protect you—he before whom neither the Māras, the foremost of those led by Smara, nor the breasts of the wives of Māra, could cause agitation; for those Māras were the gait of the Sugatas, radiant with the tips of their upraised circular halos, with chests armored, full of vital heat, wounded, destroyers of the hearts of adversaries, and harsh; while the breasts of the Māra-wives had cast off their garments, displayed the weight of their physical forms, and were agitated. VidSrk_1.1 *(2)

May that Teacher, the preceptor of the three worlds, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence so difficult to cross, and who is a valiant hero bold in conquering the hosts of Māra—may he bring you joy; he upon whose ten toenails the three gods Brahmā, Īśa, and Kṛṣṇa bowed down, thereby clearly attaining the state of the "thirty" through their reflection. (VidSrk 1.2)
For Vasukalpa, both desire and anger were obstacles to his self-mastery; having slain the bodiless one (Kāma), what indeed was achieved by Tryambaka through his wrath?
May that leader of sages, the kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha), who pacifies a hundred enemies such as Manmatha through forbearance, grant you prosperity. VidSrk_1.3 *(4) //

May that Sugata, the sole bridge for crossing the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, bring about your prosperity— He who cannot be swept away by the continuous floods of water at the end of an eon, even by the pride of the irresistible strength of Māra’s retinue. (VidSrk 1.4)
May the Blessed One, the Teacher of Aparājitarakṣita, who has dispelled all darkness and is comparable to the sun, protect the entire world from the lower realms;
may that Lord of Sages, who shatters the walls of saṃsāra and is devoted to crushing the pride of Kandarpa—the thorn within the root of existence—grant his protection. (VidSrk 1.5)

May those rays from the tips of the toenails of Vasukalpa— whose compassion is like a cluster of blossoms on the nectar-tree, whose wife Wisdom possesses the beauty of a pearl necklace for his neck, and who sends forth spray from the surging flood of the river of tranquility— meet upon your heads as various garlands worthy of the consecration for sovereignty over the world, while trembling at the feet of him who grants the gift of fearlessness.

May the wish-fulfilling tree of the six super-knowledges grant you the fruit that is the seed of perfect enlightenment— a tree whose cool, firm meditation-basin is sprinkled with the water of ethical discipline, whose great height is the trunk of generosity, whose leaves are the shimmering radiance of vast wisdom, whose branches are irresistible vigor, which bears the blossoming flowers of patience, and which provides a beautiful shade.
We have indeed suppressed all modes of expressing our wonder regarding the conquest of the world by that single Cupid, the delight of Śrīdhara, through the side-glances of his beloved;
yet the Sugata did not even begin to move his eyebrows— those alone being sufficient to conquer him along with his army— and thus the mere mention of his virtues serves only to leave us speechless.

Even for the Teacher Kumudākaramati— whose great manly prowess was the abode of the fruit of his desire to uplift the multitude of beings who were the consumers of the sins accumulated through countless births and immeasurable cycles in every single life—

some praise his excellence by saying he conquered even Smara; yet what can we say of him, when Smara himself was instantly reduced to ashes by a mere spark from the fire of Umā’s lover’s sidelong glance?
May that vow of Vallaṇa, the conqueror of Māra, protect you—a vow which rendered his host of streams fruitless, and wherein he displayed great valor in opening his mouth to devour Māra’s head;
for when the demon-warrior saw the reflection of his own gaping maw mingled with the wondrous crest-jewels [of the Buddha], his very courage was cast down. (VidSrk 1.10)
Of the illustrious Pārśvavarman, [the son] of Suvaṭa.

May this handful of flowers, offered to the Jina, bestow prosperity upon you— flowers whose unprecedented beauty was fashioned by the thick pollen-dust clinging to them as they swayed in the playful movement of his own feet moving restlessly in sport, and which were made to blossom wide by the mutual kissing of swarms of bees greedy for honey as they embraced one another.

May that Teacher— who delights in having conquered his enemies, whose teeth possess a luster that faints within the rays emitted from the path of his quivering red lips as they are released by fear, and who holds mastery over all regions— grant you happiness and auspiciousness, like the intense glow of twilight when the great majesty of the night of ignorance is rising to its conclusion. (VidSrk 1.12)
Of Trilocana, the bearer of the three eyes.

May the Jina protect you—he who was praised by Rati with tears, trembling, and horripilation: by her whose passion was intensely aroused because his form was more beautiful than even Kandarpa’s; by her whose heart was agitated with fear because he had brought even an excellent woman to old age; and by her bowed low with the weight of her faith because his heart was impenetrable even by the arrows of Māra.

May the Śākya Sage protect you—he whose method of worship consists of the clusters of eyes shimmering on the bodies of the golden-thighed [nāgas] prostrate near his lotus feet, appearing like clearly blooming blue lotuses; and whose unprecedented monastic robes are made manifest by the sprout-like rays of light arising from the jeweled crowns of the multitude of gods who bow in homage. VidSrk_1.14 *(15) //
"Of Vasukalpa,
who is this one [you], O Flower-armed One, in the act of destroying my meditative absorption? Even if all the gods were armed with flowers, what of it?"—
may that Teacher of yours, the conqueror of Māra in the ten directions, who surely reduced them here to the state of having flowers as weapons, grant you his weapon.
[Chapter] 2: The Conduct of the Sugata, followed by the Conduct of Lokeśvara.
Neither the lotus nor the moon possesses a face as stainless as yours, owing to the weight of its dense beauty and fragrance, nor does it possess a rain of layered veils of pure, radiant moonlight.

May he protect you—he who possesses a joy that is wondrous and beyond all bounds, which dispels the sleep of the intoxicated bees and brings delight to the cakora birds, and who holds the lotus in his hand.

Victorious is the Lord of the World, whose face possesses the splendor of a mass of white rays, and whose gaze is moistened by innate, heavy compassion; he who has quenched the thirst of the entire multitude of pretas with a flowing flood of nectar from the lotus-hand of Buddha Ākaragupta, which is held in the gesture of granting boons. VidSrk_2.2 *(18) //

May Lokeśvara protect you—he who, on the glorious Mount Potalaka, resounds with the deep echoes of his profound exposition; who is encircled by the splendor of his own dense mass of light; and who resembles a mass of snowflakes caught in the waves of the Milk Ocean churned by Mount Mandara, whose form is firm and whose speed is exceedingly intense. (VidSrk 2.3)

From the nectar-lake of your heart, made lush by the rain of Jñānaśrīmitra’s compassion, a stream has issued forth; becoming gradually slender yet beautiful through its flow of mercy, it has become fivefold as it enters the slightly parted lips of those afflicted by thirst via the channels of their mouths—what else could this be but the fruit of his arm? (VidSrk 2.4)
The movement toward the end of the two-fold sweetness.

I pay homage to the Lord Khasarpaṇa, who, like the three-eyed Śiva, bears immeasurable light; who, like a poet, is praised by a multitude of gods and sages; who, like the springtime, is filled with compassion; and who, like the moon, is the protector of the sky. (VidSrk 2.5)

If this smallness of the belly of the Supreme Person were not innate, how could there be such heaviness? If it were not so, how could his heart be indolent toward its own purpose, and how could his mind be intent on performing what is beneficial for others? (VidSrk 2.6)
"His face is not the moon; this whiteness is not the brilliant moonlight; his eyes have the luster of water, yet the moon has no pair of spots with intense radiance.
Having inferred this, the lotus approached the presence of the Moon, laughing fearlessly. May that face of the Lord of the World be for your auspicious day! (VidSrk 2.7)
May he—the Amitābha, who, like the sun within a mass of matted locks surrounded by dark clouds, gazes upon a cluster of red Aśoka blossoms;
he whose body is as if fashioned from the radiance of the moon—shatter your weariness and bestow upon you a wave of the nectar of the bliss of tranquility. (VidSrk 2.8)
Thus ends the section on Lokeśvara within the Buddhākara.
Next is the section on Mañjughoṣa. Third.

May Mañjuśrī be remembered—he who is garlanded by swarms of bees falling upon his rays that flash with the fragrance of his limbs; who possesses the beauty of blooming blue lotuses strung together on a shimmering golden thread; who is bristling with the garlands of light-rays radiating upward from the tips of his toenails; and who appears as if worshipped by showers of flower-clusters released by the gods. (VidSrk 3.1)
Adorned with a shimmering golden ornament.

May the Youthful Lord (Kumāra), whose nature is Bhairava, protect the world as he dances—a mass like the conflagration at the end of an aeon with sparks of fire flashing from his body and arms raised with weapons; who creates the illusion of swarms of flies on the buffalo’s head as it is offered upon the tips of his infinite horns; whose multitude of feet shine as if covered by the leaves dropped by the gods out of terror, and who eclipses the sun with the flood of his stars. VidSrk_3.2 *(26)

May that youth, the upholder of the lineage of the Sugata, protect you for a long time—he who was gazed upon in various ways by the celestial damsels: with a shout when wielding his sword, with anxiety when holding a book, with playful grace as a child, and with longing in his most enchanting beauty. (VidSrk 3.3)

May that Mañjuvajra be vigilant for your welfare and happiness— he who, with the crimson saffron-colored water of splendor poured from the golden jars of the feet of Puruṣottama— whose sprout-like fingers are charming— consecrates one who pays homage into the sovereignty of Dharma. VidSrk_3.4 *(28)

"Even the names of these [Buddhas], whose feet have conquered their enemies and whose splendor is created by the beauty of Mañjuśrī’s lovely faces, have not been heard by us; where indeed are the likes of the moon and other luminaries? Yet this blue lotus moves with audacity near me!"—may this pair of eyes of yours, red at the corners as if out of anger, protect you. (VidSrk 3.5)
% NB Ingalls conjectures *himāṃśuprakṛtayaḥ* for *b*.
[This is] the work of Śāntākaragupta.
Colophon: Thus ends the *Mañjughoṣavrajyā*.

Then follows the section on Maheśvara. Victorious is that God who wields the trident as his weapon and is encompassed by the three *guṇas*; he whose art fashioned the three worlds, whose preceptor composed the triple Veda, upon whose head the imperishable Triple City became like a garland, and who bears three blazing eyes as if to survey the three realms. (VidSrk 4.1)
Of the teacher Vasukalpa.

Victorious is the state of exhaustion at the limit of aiming by the Foe of Cities (Śiva), as he discharges his weapon from a bow drawn by the string of the preeminent serpent—now bowed and now raised—with the hope of capturing the Ancient Puruṣa who has become speech; while the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) rushes forward and then retreats, exhausted by the sparks of the flashing fire.

May the moon protect you— that sprout of jewels in the head-ornament of Maheśvara, bitten by the leader of the serpent host who is distracted by the longing to drink the essence of nectar, and who thus wanders [in fear].

That which was held for the purpose of filling the mold is now being torn away by the flames from the tufts of hair on the forehead and eyes of Śiva, after having been squeezed in a pair of tongs. (VidSrk 4.3)
"O digit of the moon, may there be welfare for Murāri; O river of the gods, may there be auspiciousness; O row of skulls, may there be prosperity; O serpent-king’s vine, may there be well-being;

O mass of rogue [snakes], may there be health!"—may that Tandava dance, at which these gathered together thus addressed one another when the actor of the cosmic dissolution's fury had come to rest, lead to your glory. (VidSrk 4.4)
"O Goddess, behold this state of these lotuses, who were once friends comparable to your face; as the sky slowly turns crimson, they have come to this.
May the customary twilight worship of Śambhu protect you—worship during which Pārvatī was deceived by him as he offered his joined palms under the pretext of imitating the closing lotuses.
"O Pārvatī, why are you so harsh? This lack of affection is innate to those born of stone; how could a man made of ashes ever possess affection?
"Your anger toward me is fruitless; what fruit could there be from a beloved who is a pillar (Sthāṇu)? May Śambhu, thus rendered speechless by Girijā, protect you for a long time. (VidSrk 4.6)

From the manifestation of your form, O Destroyer of Tripura, I inferred that in previous births I had likely never bowed before you anywhere. Now, bowing in this birth, I am bodiless; yet even in the future, I shall not be free from limitation. O Great Lord, both these offenses must be forgiven.
How can the greatness of the great ocean be described, before whom even Mount Maināka—terrified by the blow of Indra’s thunderbolt—sank into the mass of waters like a mere toy boat?
Yet even he found peace within the hollow walls of a hut formed by the tips of moss-creepers rising from the backs of pāṭhīna fish rolling in the deep waters.
% NB = 1208 below/ /var{@viluṭhatpāṭhīna@/lem /emend, @viluṭhan pāṭhīna@ /edKG}

Salutations to that Śambhu, upon whose expansive jeweled hood this earth—sealed by seven such oceans and surrounded on all sides by as many sky-scraping mountains and vast, wide continents—found its refuge; and because of that shelter, even Śeṣa, appearing like a submerged spot of darkness, became a mere ornament upon his body.

May these rows of Śiva’s heads, entwined with the trunks of serpents, protect you—heads whose ghostly state has been dispelled by the nectar-essence flowing from the moon as it melts, scorched by the flames of poison issuing from hoods that quiver due to the pressure of the tight knots on their throats; and which repeatedly gaze with wide-open, tawny eyes, out of a thirst for blood, upon the radiance of [Śiva’s] own brown eye. (Vallana 4.10)
Of that very [serpent],
[the ornament] known as the *phaṇāpīḍa* (or *phaṇapīṭha*).

May the southern face of Śambhu destroy your sin—that face which has tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair like a mountain peak enveloped in a forest fire; which, with its three fierce, tawny eyes, resembles a dark cloud pierced by three suns; and whose very deep palate and root of the underworld are revealed by the moon-like radiance of its fangs, striking fear into the three well-formed faces. (VidSrk 4.11)
[Emend: *rakṣovibhīṣaṇasya* [Ingalls, *hantvadhaṃ* {edKG}] The terrifying demon Rākṣasa.

May the loud laughter of Śambhu as he dances bestow blessings upon you—laughter whose thunderous sound is as deep as a row of clouds, which obstructs the spreading darkness swallowed by the moonlight of the crescent moon blossoming with the brilliance of his unrestrained teeth. VidSrk_4.12 (41)

May the head of Dhūrjaṭi protect you—its Gaṅgā flowing forth, its crescent moon rising, the hollows of its rows of falling skulls resounding with the swelling *bhaṃ* sounds driven by the force of the fierce winds swirling within;
its mass of thick, tawny, and formidable matted locks loosened as they slip from exhaustion under the weight of the intensity of his dense *tāṇḍava* dance. VidSrk_4.13 *(42)*
Accompanied by ten reflections of his own image reflected in the mirror of Gaurī’s nails, Śambhu, bowing at Gaurī’s feet, triumphs as the eleventh himself. (VidSrk 4.14)

May the matted locks of the Lord of Beings protect you—locks in which the waters of the Mandākinī fall, mingled with the fragments of skulls used as crest-ornaments; whose luster is blended with the light from the sockets of his eye on the forehead that resembles lightning; and where the moon appears charmingly indistinct amidst the tips of non-tender ketakī flowers, while the mass of hair is bound with garlands of serpent-coil bracelets.
Victorious is that flood of Gaṅgā’s waters belonging to Bhavabhūti, resting upon the lofty crest of Śambhu,
wherein the digit of the moon sinks and emerges again like a sapharī fish.
May that moon protect you—curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk, which rests upon the head of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), tawny with fire;
it shines like a sprout, white as crystal, emerging from the skull-bowl that is daily moistened by the flowing waters of the Mandākinī.

May that Śiva protect you, and Girijā, and that moon of play whose body was filled with the rays of his teeth, as the daughter of the mountain, her face beaming with laughter, took the fallen crescent of the moon and the bracelet broken in a lovers' quarrel, joined them together into a circle, and said, "Look at this! VidSrk_4.18 *(47) //
Homage to Śambhu, who is as beautiful as a moon-fan kissing his lofty head, and who is the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds. (VidŚrk 4.19) [48]
Repelled when he clung to her hand, violently struck even as he seized the hem of her garment, cast off when grasping her hair, and ignored with agitation when falling at her feet;

rejected even as he embraced her by the young women of Tripura whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears—may that fire of Śambhu’s arrow, like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, remove your misfortune. (VidSrk 4.20, Bāṇa)

May the gale-force winds protect you—winds that belong to Bhīma, who is addicted to the grand spectacle of his twilight *tāṇḍava* dance, and whose circle of staff-like arms whirls with fierce spinning;
for when these winds rise up with speed, the mountains suddenly flee from the battle arrays, and Indra must once again brandish his thunderbolt. (VidSrk 4.21)

May the fire vomited from the corner of the eye of the Three-eyed One—the fire whose splendor blazes forth instantly, which first flickers at the hair, crackles intensely upon the skin, grows faint in the flesh, emits hissing sounds as it flows through the blood, produces clattering noises in the bones, and flares up with fierce beauty in the marrow-like parts of the body—may that fire cast away your misfortune. (VidSrk 4.22)

May that Dhūrjaṭi protect you—he by whom, during the performance of his full-moon evening *tāṇḍava* dance, the golden mountain Hemādri, together with the moon, was made to tremble by the movements of his rhythmic hand-gestures;
and who, through his exceedingly wondrous amazement, bears the splendor of a head with beautiful luster, its locks and earrings swaying, as it is shaken by the Earth herself.

Deep in the hollow skull, thin within the interstices of his matted locks, and surging against the cluster of jewels on the hoods of the serpents in his crest; soft at the edge of the crescent moon as it trembles with the force of its motion—may this roar of the Gaṅgā upon the head of Hara purify you for a long, long time. (VidSrk 4.24)
May there be peace for you from the garland of skulls belonging to the Lord of the Worlds, whose writing—composed of not very well-known syllables—is read word by word here and there by the Gaṇas:

"He shall create the universe; he shall protect the earth; he shall rule over the waters; he shall be taught by the serpents; he shall take delight among those full of passion; he shall destroy the world; and he shall enjoy the heavens."
He protects;
[Ingalls conjectures *vakṣati* or *rakṣyati* for *rakṣati*]. Note: Ingalls conjectures *vakṣati* or *rakṣyati* for *rakṣati*.
And in verse c, read *aśiṣyate* for *śiṣyate*; and in verse d, read *atsyati* for *syati*.
[This is the view] of Bhojadeva.

May the mass of matted locks of Śambhu protect you—locks that are tawny like the rays of the young sun; which, like a flame, rises upward from the mature heat of his asceticism; which possesses the beauty of an anthill inhabited by serpents in the form of the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā; and which, like the twilight, dwells together with the moon whose body is as tender as a fresh lotus stalk.

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the afflictions of the world and the slayer of Tripura, who—though your head rises upward with speed because the surface of the earth sinks under the weight of your feet—are praised by the assembly of the eldest gods rejoicing at the unshaken state of the heavenly realm; and who, though the Daughter of the Mountain flees in terror, does not abandon her because she is pursued by the ever-expanding right half of your body.

May the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Bāṇa protect you—his knees bound by the double-knotted coils of his arms as he embraced his couch, all his senses stilled through the internal restraint of breath and the cessation of thought; beholding the Self within the self alone, with the faculties withdrawn, through the vision of reality, and fixed in the *brahman* at the point of dissolution formed by his gaze upon the void. (VidSrk 4.28)
*var{śūnyekṣaṇa (emended by Ingalls;
śūṇyakṣaṇa edKG)*}

May the dance of the one who wears the crescent moon on his crest protect you—a dance in which a great circle of fire is formed by the hosts of Rudras, suns, and stars whirling about due to the force of the wind from his incessantly revolving arms;

a dance in which mountains fall, rise, and stumble; where the earth sinks, the fire creeps, and all the peaks tremble; where the lofty crown of his head quivers, the rays of the moon flash, the luster of his eyes streams forth, and the cascades of the Ganges gush out. (VidSrk 4.29)
"Mother, mother! What is this that Father has hidden in his cupped hands? Child, it gives off a sweet fragrance; do not go, take it yourself!

When Guha was thus sent by his mother, he pulled apart Śambhu’s joined palms at twilight, breaking his meditative absorption with a sudden burst of laughter. May that [laughter] protect you. (VidSrk 4.30)
"O fair-browed one, hold your creeper-like arms thus; take this stance; do not bend too far forward; curve the tips of your feet;
look at me for a moment!"—may those clapping rhythms (tālikāḥ) of Śambhu protect you, as he dances with his own face as a drum sounding like a rain-cloud, striking the beat of the dance's tempo.

Beholding the fire—flickering among the sprout-like ends of their upper garments, steady in the strands of their braided hair, slow in the seams of their bodices, and blazing like a flame upon the slopes of their breasts—the Lord, his eyes moist with compassion, triumphs as he lets his bow slip from his hand before the women of the harem of Tripura. (VidSrk 4.32)

When Śambhu kisses the lotus-face of the Mountain’s Daughter, the moon enters the lap of the peacock’s plumage-thicket, the lord of serpents descends from his shoulder with his hood gracefully curved,
and the bull, feigning deceit, scratches his eye with the tip of his hoof. (VidSrk 4.33)

May the cloud that is Śiva’s head bring you prosperity—clouds which, like the rainy season, are agitated by the flow of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) gushing forth with various velocities; which are terrifying due to the fire from the eye on his forehead flickering with rapid movement; and which emit sounds released by the impact of the wind rushing through the hollows of the rows of skulls. (VidSrk 4.34)
May he protect the universe even today, upon whose head the new moon does not wax, as if out of shame at being eclipsed by the face of Gaurī. (VidSrk 4.35)

May Hara protect you— he who was looked upon by Pārvatī with shame as "the naked one" (referring to Dharmapāla), with a charming smile as "the hater of the Mind-born" (Kāma), with wonder as "this one has uneven eyes," with terror as "the skull-bearer," with jealousy as "he who has taken the Ganges as his crest-ornament," and with fear as "the one whose bracelets are serpents."

May the anxious concern of both Hara and Guha for one another’s protection preserve you— concern arising when the serpent Vinayadeva was provoked by the peacock and the peacock, in turn, became distressed as it circled the body of that serpent.
[This is] the work of Jayārḍhavardhana, son of Bhayaja.
The splendor of vermilion on their foreheads, golden ornaments at the sides of their ears, the red tint of betel in their mouths, the smearing of saffron upon their jar-like breasts,

and the beauty of crimson silk upon the regions of their hips belonging to the wives of the demon lords— may the fire born from the discharge of the arrow of the Destroyer of Tripura consume all your misfortunes.

May Hara protect you— he who was embarrassed and ashamed by the clamor of the celestial nymphs, terrified by the fear that the circle of the heavens was being submerged by the fierce waves born from the seven oceans, as they surged up from the wind of the hissing of the serpent-king’s hoods, which were agitated by the force of his mass of matted locks whirling in the current of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā. VidSrk_4.39 *(68) //
May Śiva,

the destroyer of cities, protect you— he who is the object of the smiling side-glances of the Daughter of the Mountain; he from whose presence the serpent-king, his girdle, retreats in terror before the emerald crest-jewel of the Lord of the Thirty-three as it bows down, while he covers himself with his slipping upper garment and deerskin.

May that Śaṅkara protect you—he who, though skilled in the curious politics of kings, bears the moon, the daughter of Śrīśaila, and the celestial river; he who, when Dharmāśoka had swallowed a potent dose of Kālakūṭa poison and the God of Love had been forcibly reduced to the state of a slender eye on his radiant forehead by the forest fire at the end of the aeon, remained adorned with power. VidSrk_4.41 (70)
By Kavirāja.
Thus ends the section on Maheśvara;
next follows the section on his group.

"The Goddess has given birth to a son! Dance, O Gaṇas! Why do you stand still?"—when Bhṛṅgiriṭi was thus addressed by Cāmuṇḍā with joyful, outstretched arms and unasked-for words, may the sound produced by the rattling skeletons of their mutually clashing bone-cages protect you—a sound that surpasses the deep resonance of the beaten celestial drums.
May the pair of breasts of the Mountain’s Daughter protect you— breasts that resemble the frontal lobes of Indra’s elephant,
and which are smeared with the ash-paste from the pressure of Śaṅkara’s firm embrace around her neck. (VidSrk 5.2)

I praise your playful sport, which displayed manifest power before the assembly of Nīlakaṇṭha; it caused the earth to reel with the agitation of forceful trampling and crushing, made the world of Brahmā tremble as the shell of the cosmic tortoise bent under the pressure, shattered the stability of the cosmic egg, and cast the seven oceans into the cavities of your cheeks—which rival the subterranean realms—as you laughed.
"O guardians of the quarters, move aside! O clouds, leave the sky! O earth, go to the underworld! O mountains, enter the surface of the ground!
O Brahmā, raise your abode far away! For as I, the god Śambhu, dance, there is a great crowding here"—may this dismissal by Nandin protect you all.
"How can you have such exhaustion, O beloved? O Lord, why does this trembling come from the fire of your eyes? O Moon-faced One, may Bhava protect you from the fear of the king of serpents!
O Goddess, how is this horripilation caused by the spray of the waters of the Ganges? May Gaurī, thus intent on concealing her emotions toward her husband, protect you for a long time. (VidSrk 5.5)

May the assembly of Śambhu during his descent into dance purify you—this assembly where Ambikā lowers the fresh lotus-garland from Lakṣmīdhara’s neck because it hangs too long; where Nandin arranges his matted locks after setting aside a crescent moon; where Kāla fastens his skin, and Kālarātri brings a skull into his hand. Each member of the retinue is thus occupied with a separate task.
"Śatānanda, release Śṛṅgin;
Bhṛṅgin, let go! And you, Gajavaktra, abandon the base of your tail! Mandānanda, enough of this; Nandin, you are weak; Mahākāla, cease your clutching at my neck!

Having spoken thus, may the Bull bring you joy as he is led to the feet of Pārvatī, watching with his eyes the Three-eyed Lord, whose neck is turned and whose *kambala* scarf is fluttering, looking quite embarrassed.
O Bhāgīrathī, salutations to you, who are doubled in depth upon the head of Hara, which is crowded by the half of Gaurī being divided [between them]. (VidSrk 5.8)

This Bhāgīrathī, who flows from the ocean toward the abode of the lotus-born god [Brahmā] to serve as the ornament of the head of the blessed Bharga [Śiva], carries people here to the world of Brahmā with extreme speed; she does so even against the current, swiftly transporting those who have abandoned their bodies despite being moving upstream.
