they beautify the moon with a moonlight that has cast off its mantle of frost; and these very days wax strong and repeatedly intensify the god of love.
Having ended his long journey by the heart-gladdening and affectionate songs of the cuckoos, the southern breeze returns, announcing that Spring has arrived;
with its bracelets of humming, restless bees, it immediately bestows the jasmine-smiles of the forest-avenue brides as full-offering gifts.

When the darkness of the lord of the earth, the season of spring, had begun to spread— marked by playful flocks of cuckoos, swarms of bees hovering about, and *kiṃśuka* trees that have turned to glowing coals in the courtyards of the houses— the *campaka* trees held up, all around, a glistening row of lamp-flames in the form of their flower buds for him as he wandered.

These kunda flowers have shed their blossoms for the amusement of the mind; these trees are sluggish in the production of new blooms; and these cuckoos no longer weave words in their minds nor scatter them as song.
Yet, the rays of the sun cut through the lingering chill and do not assume that heat which brings on exhaustion.
The *vicakila* jasmine now attains a likeness with six-month-old pearls; the *aśoka* is honored with petals as red as the marks of teeth-bites from a woman of Bāhlīka;
this *kiṃśuka* flower, its tip brushed over by bees, slightly droops; and with its madder-red buds, the *pāṭali* tree bears a truly unique script.
Flowers appear within the internal knots of creepers, sprouts or shoots emerge from their midst, and the fifth note is mastered within the throats of female cuckoos merely by the power of desire;
moreover, if the god of love were to master his bow—which has long been abandoned—even in two or three days, he would conquer the three worlds. (VidSrk 8.15)

These days of King Śīlāditya’s son Rājaśekhara are cool, as if broken by the fragments of wintry nights; the days expand and, like *kiṃśuka* trees, they bear within them a sprout of fire for the torment of the quarters.

Moreover, in the regions of shadow and sunlight where their own support has gathered vastness, this world, its delight diminished today, finds no pleasure whatsoever according to its own will. (VidSrk 8.16)

These trees, made beautiful by ear-ornaments of blossoming clusters, swaying and danced by the moving breeze, their splendor of leaves and trunks shimmering with the dust of pollen cast forth by flowers;
with songs rising from the cries of intoxicated cuckoos in the deep-toned fifth note—dance as if they were a festival of Love restored to life. (VidSrk 8.17)
How much more so, then, the victorious weapon of the mango creeper belonging to the wielder of the bow of Smara—
especially when smeared with the poisonous paste of the abundant bees that have alighted upon it? (VidSrk 8.18) [Of Śubhāṅga]
Hail from the glorious Malaya mountain! The illustrious Spring Breeze, the friend of the God of Love, inquires after the welfare of lovers in their pleasure-houses and says this further:
"I have arrived at the forest, making the flocks of bees and cuckoos joyful; therefore, you must remain here together with your beloved mistresses."
In the midst of the forest, these cuckoos captivate the heart, their throat-sounds intensified by the excessive devouring of the dense buds of fresh mango trees;

they appear like the sparks from the charcoal embers of the bodiless God of Love, made terrifying by the mass of flames from the fire of the eye of the Lord Bhūteśa, appearing under the guise of their eyes. (VidSrk 8.20)
The filament within the *kiṃśuka* bud shines, rivaling a digit of the moon;
it appears like the bow of the Creator, covered by a red quiver and sealed with lac. (Vidūṣaka’s Verses on Flowers 8.21, Vallana)

The ponds have their surfaces bristling with the knots of lotus leaf-sprouts; the bees, clustering upon the buds of mango trees, remain in a state of utter stillness. Even the slightest fatigue from traveling the road now serves as a lesson for the wind to rise up and scatter dust, bringing misfortune to those who would otherwise enjoy the journey.

The southern breeze, wafting a sweet fragrance, approaches shaking those trees which, with their fresh, reddish shoots, provide a festival for the eyes of Abhinanda. (Ingalls conjectures *sampravasatām* for *sāmpratamayām* in pāda c.)
As soon as he is embraced by him according to the prescribed rite, this world goes mad with a mind agitated by the intent for unrestrained play. (VidSrk 8.23)
A certain splendor, surpassing even the buds, has gathered upon the aśoka tree; the mango tree assumes its noble form according to the rites appropriate for the season.

Moreover, the breeze—skilled in opening the prologue to the victory of the Bodiless One (Kāma)—creeps along at will, a companion to the playful grace of the young sandalwood creeper on the slopes of Mount Āṣāḍha.
I believe that fire has taken refuge within the *kiṃśuka* trees under the guise of dew-drops; indeed, it turns the forest dark with its smoke known as buds.
Otherwise, how could it emit a row of deep red flames under the pretext of flowers for the sake of tormenting the wives of travelers?
From Pautāyani [to] Vyāma.

May the complete attire of women, a total mobilization for the sake of the young men’s pleasure, bring delight: a variegated string of *kurubaka* flowers upon the hips, lovely mango blossoms and red *aśoka* flowers upon the ears, *mādhavī* vines upon the breasts, and locks of hair dyed tawny by the pollen of *bakula* trees covering every limb—this is the universal adornment of the female folk.
In this month of Sāvarṇi, whose magnificent beauty is gathered from fresh sprouts as red as copper and which bears the signs of the onset of youth in the form of emerging swarms of bees,
women drink in the face of the one allied with the Flower-Bowed God with glances that are full of affection, smiles, and excellence. (VidSrk 8.27)
Today, the buds of the mucakunda trees, filled to the brim with bees whose mouths are like the snares of a hunter and whose lovely wings appear black as if smeared with poison,
shine like the quivers of the God of Love.
The trees shed sap for the sake of Śubhāṅga; Madana hurls his five arrows;
and the cuckoo, its throat no longer choked, pours forth sweetness. (VidSrk 8.29)
Like the days of the illustrious Dharmākara, which were formerly shrunken by the dullness produced by irresistible frost,
the days now gradually resume their expansion as the cold ceases. (VidSrk 8.30)
Upon the Śrīdharaṇīdhara mountain,

there appeared new buds of lotuses, green at their bases and pale red at their tips; their petals were so tightly closed that their joints were difficult to discern, and they possessed the luster of young parrots.

The heat now brings forth beads of perspiration upon the cheeks of the Dravidian women— beads that have been rubbed with turmeric and made pungent by fresh nail-marks, and which are set in motion as they rest their budding eyes upon the swaying sprouts of their trembling ears.
For the Lord of Yoga, the night passes immediately after the day has been cut short and heated; thereafter, she too, becoming exceedingly diminished, attains his perfect grace.

One [Vedic authority] declares that in this world the nature of man lies in his desire for women, while another clearly proclaims that the woman's disposition is to abide in accordance with the man. (VidSrk 8.33)
Now, the bud of the *plakṣa* tree, skillful at parting its inner petals, loosens its bond like the beak of a parrot;
thereafter, alas, it emerges on all sides with a clearly beautiful hue, capable of rivaling the loveliness of women’s lips.
The humming of bees rises up with the sweet warbling of the bowstring of Love; the clusters of blossoming *kaṅkelli* flowers emerge, as treacherous as poison-tipped arrows.
O travelers, now the mango tree here spreads its impurity with vehemence—like a messenger of Death, its sprouts quivering amidst a web of buds.

Here is this glorious young mango tree, now densely budding; its breeze is anointed with the fragrance unfolding from the flow of sap in sprouts that have been broken by the weight of bees eager for mutual play—alas, it bestows madness! VidSrk_8.36 *(187) //
When the mango tree has sprouted, put forth foliage, formed buds, and blossomed, so too has passion sprouted, put forth foliage, formed buds, and blossomed within my heart.
The full-blown *navamālikā* jasmine, delighting the sense of smell, intoxicates; the dark, newly formed cluster on the *kiṃśuka* tree has indeed become greyish.
Intoxicated bees gather white clusters of honey, while perspiration, accompanied by droplets, finds its place upon the full and firm breasts of women.
Here, Bhavabhūti’s friends now secretly break open the first buds of the mango blossoms to protect those suffering in separation. (Vidśrk 8.39)
By Rājaśekhara. Thus ends the section on Spring; [now begins] the section on Summer. 9.
Separation has been caused even by beloved people; the night-blooming lilies have blossomed; even a friend has acted harshly; longing has been prolonged by passion;
heavy infatuation has been acquired by the dull-witted, and the mine of faults is being resorted to—alas, is this the Kali age? No, no, it is not that; the arrival of the summer season has come.
The embrace of those fawn-eyed women— who have just bathed, whose bodies are still moist with sandalwood paste, and who wear hair adorned with slightly blossoming jasmine buds—
gradually causes the God of Love to sprout once more, even though his power had been withered by the scorching heat of the summer sun.
The day of the auspicious Arjuna has become exceedingly hot, and the night is likewise excessively thin;
both are separated by their opposing natures, like a husband and wife filled with mutual resentment. (VidSrk 9.3)

O traveler, how do you survive as you journey through the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the heat of the fierce sun makes all hopes for shade vanish, when the creepers are scorched, when the deer are ever intent on killing, when the trees are withered, when the bees are sluggish, and when the jasmine is destroyed at will; when the streams are drying up, when the dust of the earth is heated, and when the waters themselves seem to be flames? (VidSrk 9.4)
Bāṇa’s day, heavy with the heat of its onset, exhausts the wife of the crow; it ripens the mango tree and the neem tree alike.
Now, at the end of the night, the day—noisy with the smoke from the looms—dispels the sleep born of delight in the wind made still by the frost.
With the columns of smoke— dense, thin, spreading, extensive, severed, curved, and rising— that possess the luster of Kāśmīra saffron,

the wind, as if moving along, draws patterns upon the faces of the women of the quarters with the fragrant breezes of aloe-wood, like a wandering artist using the flames of a forest fire. (Vidyākara’s Subhāṣitaratnakośa 9.6)

The trees standing along the roadside generate longing in travelers; their vicinity is filled with herds of fawns attracted by the songs of water-girls who delight in the sweet caresses of swinging cradles, and they possess gentle breezes capable of dispersing the spray of sweat-drops from the crowds of wayfarers. (VidSrk 9.7)

The day is being carried away by birds whose shoulders are somewhat relaxed by the interior of their flapping wings, whose heat from their sides subsides as the space within their eyelashed and downward-turned wing-covers closes, and who, having abandoned the forceful upward thrusts caused by the impact of rapid winds, find support through the dense compression of their nests gained by the contraction of their shanks.
Today that royal swan will affectionately spread her two wings over the head of the child—who, though he dwells upon a smiling lotus—is as fortunate as one sheltered by a white parasol.
And even the young parrot, afflicted by thirst, will drink from the pearl necklace clinging to the full breasts of the fair-limbed girl, mistaking it for a pool of water while dwelling in her lap.
At the onset of summer on earth, the sky bears a mass of dust, shaped like a cloth parasol, stirred by the wind to ward off the heat;
meanwhile, these bees, their minds suspicious that it might be a forest fire among the *mandāra* trees, do not hasten to drink the nectar.

At its root, it was absorbed in water; for a moment, it rested upon sandalwood paste; it left light traces on lotus stalks, pearl necklaces, and the like, and even upon the moon; it paused for a while in the shade of a grove of succulent plantain trees; but now, it dwells in the supreme coolness of an embrace around the neck of my beloved. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 9.11)

With the corners of his eyes reddened at the edges, the buffalo—occupied by the cavernous depths of his eyelids—is slowly moistened at the joints of his eyes by drops of water that resemble mossy creepers trickling from the tips of both horns raised in fear of the small insects; thus, immersed happily in the water, he sleeps due to his extreme exhaustion.

The trunk of the elephant reveals its heat by sprinkling spray upon its temples; the forest on the banks of the ponds bears the marks of mud from the rubbing of buffaloes' bodies against them; and the palms are parched with exhaustion as the sun scorches the world with its rays; meanwhile, the deer, enemies of the lions, spend their time in the hollow mountain caves, weary from the heat.
The dust on the path of travelers has grown thick enough to burn their nails; a buffalo churns the water remaining only in the belly of a puddle, distressing the fish within.
The gaze of the female hyena runs toward the *dhātakī* grove out of thirst for blood, while the birds in their nests among the reeds and *śamī* trees hold their throats panting.
For Bāṇa, these days are delightful:

their waters are pleasant for bathing, the forest breezes are fragrant from contact with *pāṭali* flowers, sleep is easily found in deep shade, and they are beautiful in their ripening. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 9.15)

At midday on the roads, where roadside wells have ceased their function, travelers stir with their arms the water that is scalding at the surface yet intensely cold at the bottom; they drink from these reservoirs whose waves are strewn with fragments of young *śaivala* moss torn away, and which are turbid from the agitation caused by buffaloes plunging in after being released from the plow—Kālidāsa’s [verse]. (VidSrk 9.16)
Avoiding heavy objects because it abounds in earth, the fire of the Lord of Yoga embraces the cow-dung from the forest, the anthills, and the loose grass thick with flames;
wandering through the forest, it greedily devours the moist eggs and embryos of scattered birds, mistaking them for clarified butter. (VidSrk 9.17)

In time, that lake became one where the *śarāri* birds had fled far away, where the *baka* cranes were distressed, where the *kāraṇḍava* ducks had departed, and where the *kaṅka* herons were languishing; it was devoid of *cakravāka* ruddy geese, with no *madgu* cormorants gathering, and its *plava* ducks had gone; the *krauñca* curlews were afflicted, the *dhārtarāṣṭra* geese were gone, the *koyaṣṭi* lapwings had fallen away, the *ṭiṭṭibha* sandpipers were absent, the *sārasa* cranes were sinking, and the *kurara* ospreys were no longer attached to it. VidSrk_9.18 *(208)* //1//
Emerging from that very water, the crest of *saptalā* flowers rests upon their braided hair; the *pāṭala* garland sprinkles coolness upon their breasts;
the delicate-tipped *śirīṣa* flower settles gracefully upon their ears; thus, upon the limbs of women, his own tokens distribute his ascetic heat here and there.

The coolness, gathered together as if out of fear of the day’s heat, takes refuge upon the surface of the *śirīṣa* stalks, which possess a honey-like quality and possess flower-filaments as tender and green as parrot feathers. (VidSrk 9.20)
The hearts of the fawns are stolen away by the flutes which are cool to the ear; the wine, when mixed with cold water, becomes worthy of honor;
and the breasts of the fawn-eyed women become like snow; for the great favor of the Lord of Love resides above the month of Śuci. (VidSrk 9.21)
Wet garments, bracelets for play made of lotus shoots, ear-ornaments of *śirīṣa* flowers, necklaces fashioned from *vicakila* blossoms,

and bodies moistened with sandalwood paste— these, for the fawn-eyed women in the heat, constitute a rite for conquering death at the hands of the Lover of Rati, requiring neither ritual manual nor incantation.

The splendor of summer prevails, delightful at the close of day; it signals the desire for love during the final watches of the night, makes coconut water somewhat thick, and even brings to ripeness the royal plantains. (VidSrk 9.23)
O King Śekhara, even as the ocean’s water-machines and palaces tremble, the heat of this season breaks apart the deep embrace of Śrī and Nārāyaṇa as they sleep;
moreover, the cruel rays of the sun, like parched cakes, sear the moon—which has lost its beauty save for its skeletal frame—upon the heated surface of the sky’s cauldron. (VidSrk 9.24)
Of Nārāyaṇa Lachchi. [Colophon: Thus ends the section on Summer; next follows the section on the Rainy Season.
The water of the mountain streams, its dwelling nestled among the reed-blossoms of the groves, now shows buds of jasmine blooming along its banks;
and here, upon the mountain ridges that laugh with opening *kuṭaja* flowers, the clouds form a canopy for the dance of the peacocks on the slopes.

To the north, a fresh rain-cloud, dark as a mature *tāpiñja* fruit ripening above a bower of *jambu* trees blackened by the weight of their fruit, takes refuge on the mountain peak, its slender ripples dashing against the riverbank.
The quarters of the sky, darkened by banks of clouds, become like the slopes of mountains where the kadamba trees possess the lush beauty of a dense mass of blossoms loosened by yawning;

the marshy banks of river currents bear rising jasmine creepers and *ketaka* flowers; and the state of the forests is one smiling with the fragrance of emerging *śilīndhra* and *lodhra* blossoms. (VidSrk 10.3)

Now these days have arrived, carrying the splendor of the transition between the departure of the summer heat and the onset of the rains; days when the rows of clouds are glossy like fragments of sapphire, tossed and shaken by the eastern gale that blows scented with the fragrance of full-blown *arjuna* flowers; days fragrant from the earth being sprinkled by showers, bearing the beauty of the meeting of the end of the heat and the beginning of the water.

Beholding these [clouds], the doe hastens away, mistaking them for young locusts out of a desire to eat sprouts of grass; the hen protects the buds of the *chatrī* plant for a long time, thinking they are her eggs; and the peacock, frantic with the longing to swallow a venomous serpent, shakes his head and runs from afar toward the edge of the forest, mistaking the rows of swarms of black insects for a snake. (Bhavabhūti) 10.5 (219)

How were those nights passed by those away from home—nights when gentle winds blew at the onset of the monsoon, when the sky was overspread with clouds, when the quarters of the horizon were glimpsed for a moment during flashes of lightning, and when the moon, stars, and planets lay dormant;
nights when the air bore the fragrance of wine produced by kadamba trees drenched by rain, and when the sound of frogs spread far and wide as they leaped about without interruption?
The riverbanks— where the lords of yoga have slept on reed-tops with snakes dozing there, where waterfowl cry out, where herds of deer have formed their dung-heaps,
and where the waters overflow; banks now covered by the swaying *ulapa* grass bent down by swarms of ants and filled with wild cocks— today make even my restless mind yearn for them.
Having called his beloved who was lingering somewhere with sweet warbling notes, and having repeatedly gazed toward the various quarters of the sky, he then leaves the stage-like earth on foot;
now, this joyful peacock dances, fanning a canopy made of rows of feathers amidst the deep sounds of the clouds, which are as sweet as the resonance of a large drum.
The clouds, heavy with yellow water, pour forth rain in unbroken streams; sleep comes upon the eyes that are closed by the sound of those showers.

When the people in every house have their eyes sealed by sleep and become as silent as mute, the nights resound with a tumultuous clamor from the loud croaking of frogs, free from all other distractions.

In the watchtowers where the spray is kept out by bamboo blinds, the fortunate men drink the lotus-like mouths of their brides, while the warbling of the *dātyūha* cranes in their cages is awakened and mingled with the sound of falling rain.

The mountain ranges are free from forest fires; the woods, once burnt, have sprouted anew; the ten directions are bristling with the sprouts of clouds; the sky is rid of the dust of the earth; and what is more, the Kadamba trees have acquired a luster thick with the swelling buds of the *kalika* flower. In how many moments are the knots of the peacocks' vow of silence shattered? (VidSrk 10.11)

In the field where the bellies of the young frogs croak slightly as they are filled with fresh water, and where the vīraṇa grass on the edges of the banks is as pale as a cluster of snail shells, children with sticks in their hands—smeared with streaks of mud—run about impetuously in every direction, shouting "cubhru! cubhru!", eager to catch the fish that leap up.
With the space between them suffused by the radiance of sapphire jewels flashing on all sides, this cloud is like a blue silk parasol for Indra who has descended to the mortal world. (VidŚrk 10.13)
With masses of darkness streaked by fireflies, with clearly flashing lightning, with the swelling of great clouds inferred by smooth rumbling, and with conchs blaring;

with the preceding winds scented by the opening of *ketaka* flowers and rain falling—these nights, I cannot believe that they will be endured by people separated from their lovers. (VidSrk 10.14 [228])
While this [rain] is intensified by the trumpeting of elephants in rut, which is worn out by intoxication, and while the mind is granted a state of numbness as the roar of the downpour intensifies;
placing itself upon the lap of the quarters and making them resound with the thundering of clouds, I think even the sky—its eyes of moon and sun sealed—is falling asleep. (VidSrk 10.15)

In the rainy season, during the night, the fortunate ones— whose eyes are slightly heavy with sleep, who have climbed onto the firm roofs of their houses where the sound of waterfalls pours incessantly from deep clouds,
and whose chests are pressed by the weight of their lovers' breasts— lie asleep amidst clusters of leaves and listen as they are embraced with both arms by their beloveds.
(VidSrk 10.16) [The sky] is free from the agitation of dust, and the light of the stars is obscured by thick layers of clouds.
This rainy season, burdened by the weight of its long clouds, is like an elderly woman with heavy breasts.
Enveloped within by the flickering flames of the submarine fire of the ocean, these clouds—obscured and turbid from thirst—clearly drank the waters out of delusion.
Otherwise, how could the clouds now possess the luster of half-smoldering charcoal, as if burning under the guise of the wreaths of Indra’s rainbows flashing across their heights?

By making the path slippery and obscuring her feet with a reprimand of thick water droplets, and by wiping away the decorative marks from the surface of her cheeks, the cloud offered an immediate atonement for its offense by repeatedly pointing out the way to the unchaste woman’s lover’s house with flashes of lightning. (VidSrk 10.19)
Now that the rain has ceased, why do these nights, thick with deep darkness, stir up in the minds of travelers' wives a suspicion of being streaks from the fire of love?
These flickering rows of fireflies fall all around like the dust of lightning-flashes violently ground to powder by the collision of masses of dark clouds.

Making the sky seem as if it could be grasped by hand, making the quarters of the horizon appear as if they were dwarfs, shattering the clouds in an instant with their roars, and raising a tumultuous sound with their downpours—where indeed is there dry land not submerged? At night, the clouds rain down, surveying the entire earth with the flashing glances of their eyes, the unrestrained streaks of lightning. (VidSrk 10.21)
With their plumage shaken by upturned tails, uttering whistling sounds through their gyrations, and with their beaks open and feet repeatedly lifted in the cadence of the rhythm;
beholding the dark cloud-banks that rival the color of their own necks, the peacocks dance with their tail-feathers fanning near their raised necks. (VidSrk 10.22)

Now, the ground beneath the trees is encircled by the bark of bamboo shoots, whose leaf-tips resemble the ears of young goats dark with quivering hair; these bamboos are friends to the mountain forests, rivers, and villages, having become companions to the unrestrained secret trysts of the Śabara couples.

With their eyes closed, resting their heads on their flanks, and having gradually submerged themselves as desired, these birds—afflicted by the heat—now find relief in the fresh water; repeatedly touching their shoulders, backs, chests, and the surface of their wings with their feet, they remain with their knees drawn up, while droplets of spray rise upward with the force of the sudden flapping of their wings.
Even the marrow is smeared [with sorrow] when the cloud rains for one who has not performed merit—[a sorrow like] the deep embrace of a young elephant calf eager for its exit-play.

The cries [of grief] are equal to the thundering; the tears from the eyes, to the unceasing streams of water; and the fires of sorrow born from that separation, to the flickering flashes of lightning.
Within me is the face of my beloved, and within you is the moon; our condition is exactly the same. O friend cloud, why then are you constantly intent on burning me?
"Do these [streams] spring up from the earth toward heaven, or do they descend from heaven to the surface of the earth?
Are they moving or still?"—pondering thus, the women touch the streams with the tips of their fingers.
(VidSrk 10.27) With his body confined within a crystal cage formed by the weight of the streams—the pure, flowing water clinging to the underside of the royal parasol—[the elephant]...
The traveler was led away by the command of Kāma, who had become enraged by his transgression of her own teachings, as if he were being led to his beloved. (VidSrk 10.28)
Today water will fall everywhere upon the earth; today its heat shall be extinguished; today the countryside, eager for the harvest, will strive in the fields.
O cloud, at your rising, the peacocks—sportive and languid in every direction, their crests covered by the parasols of their flickering tails and plumage—will dance.
For the blue-throated one (Śiva) sings, Gaurī dances with eyes as flickering as lightning,
and thereafter this great cloud, Mahākāla, beats the drum.
Upon their locks of hair there is the luster of powdered incense, and on the planes of their cheeks the appearance of drops of perspiration.
Having achieved his purpose, he gazes upon the drops of water from the clouds that delight the young women.
(10.31) "O restless one, you cannot remain [here] because the rain has not fallen at the time of the clouds;
you are longing. "No, no, my friend! The path is indeed slippery. (10.32)
The fresh ketakī flower, entwined by a young black serpent,
shines like the fallen tusk of an elephant adorned with an iron ring. Today, upon the stalks of the ketakīs, the leaves become increasingly smaller toward the top.

The needles [of the Ketakī flowers], with hair-like filaments as soft as the wool of a young ram's tail, pierce me. This is the Kāla-Kāpālika (the Black Skull-Bearer) who has arrived, striking terror into the wives of travelers; his body is entirely covered in dust from the rubbing of *ketakī* blossoms, his hair is dark clouds bound with the corpses of rows of cranes tossing within them, and he carries as a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) the fragment of a beautiful bow adorned with a fluttering banner of lightning.

O traveler, how can you sustain your life while dwelling in such a monsoon season—as the quarters turn dark with clouds, the rainbow appears, the lightning flashes in play, day and night are obscured, the peacock rejoices in the thundering, the playful anger of the peahens fades, the streams are full, the thirst of the *cātaka* birds is quenched, and the moonlight is utterly bewildered? VidSrk_10.36 *(250)*

Having exhausted the nights, forcibly seized the waters of the rivers, scorched the entire earth, and consumed every forest thicket—where has the hot-rayed sun gone now? Thus intent on searching for him, the clouds seem to move in every direction, illuminating them with the light of lightning-lamps.
The nights— filled with masses of darkness terrifying from the piercing flashes of lightning, with the heavens crowded by the obstruction of incessant dark clouds and deprived of light,
with trees near their edges inferred only by fireflies, and dominated by the humming of swarms of insects intoxicated by the floodwaters— cultivate a profound depth.
Due to Abhinanda’s joy,
the expanses of these forests— where the beautiful moon-like plumage of peacocks is made radiant with delight— have become like young trees in full bloom;
for they are touched by serpents whose half-bodies emerge from their hollows to drink the wind from the clouds, appearing like the tips of bamboo shoots sprouting from the mountainsides.

These riverbanks of the Anūpa region produce a longing in the heart— banks where conch shells resound upon the reeds growing along the marshy edges, where the waters are turbid from clusters of crabs tearing through the mud, and where the ground is pitted with hollows and the soft earth is strewn with upturned earthworms. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 10.40)
Upon these marshy grounds, where the fresh downpour from the Lord of Yoga has fallen, the small shells— white as cowries— are bright with the tracks of darting minnows; there,
crabs scurry about with their pincers busily engaged as if to count them, while the ponds, manifesting their splendor, seem to be selling their very hearts.
The righteous Parjanya now bathes the great Liṅga of the Vindhya mountain with pure waters released from hundreds of jars of sapphire-like clouds.
Now, in the cauldron of the sky, the great cat that is the cloud drinks the milk of moonlight with its tongue of flickering lightning-tendrils;
these two verses belong to Yogeśvara.
With her half-emerged womb-cavity, soft and copper-colored like the palm of a plantain tree,
she drinks the torrential rain of the summer heat with her cupped hands, as if afflicted by a fever.
(VidSrk 10.44) Of that very [woman]...
With rows of water-pouring clouds hanging down to the earth like ascending creepers, the sky appears like a banyan tree, shining with leaves as dark as rain-clouds. (VidSrk 10.45)
The orb of her hips was tawny with Nīpa flowers fashioned into a girdle; her shoulders were touched by a Kandalī bud resting upon her ear;
and the region of her breasts had a pale luster from necklaces of Yūthikā flowers—such was the natural adornment, lovely in itself, that was dear to beautiful women. (VidSrk 10.46)
When the black collyrium has been washed away by the spray of raindrops, when the fine dark garment upon the jar-like breasts has become one with their eyes,

and when her naturally slender form is revealed— blessed is the fortunate man who, having achieved his purpose, stands ready to arrange another costume for those women who were masters of the gloomy days.
The moon is as if non-existent anywhere, and the sun is as if gone abroad; the circle of planets and stars in the sky is as if erased after being drawn.
Day or night—both have their distinction lost amidst these clouds arrayed in dense formations. What is this most terrible resolve that has been undertaken?
/var{vilupta@/lem /msK (cf. Browne 2001, 21), pralupta@ / edKG (unmetrical)}: either *vilupta* (as in msK, cf. Browne 2001, 21) or *pralupta* (as in edKG, though unmetrical).
Speech was uttered only so long, hope for life was placed within the mind only so long,

and the feet of travelers were set upon the path only so long as these foothills of the Vindhya range had not been seen— hills encircled by clusters of blossoming dhārākadamba flowers and agitated by fresh clouds possessing the dark luster of sloughed serpents.

At their will, on the banks of rivers near mountains and close to the nesting grounds of herds of female buffaloes, the cranes plunge into rows of young grass, their gaze fixed on devouring fresh locusts;
meanwhile, in a corner of a field, a flock of pigeons somehow manages to swallow grains of *kodrava*—frightened by the obstacle of scarecrows made of *vīrut* creepers and straw placed within them.
When this cloud has gathered, the lord of birds practices a few *kakāra* notes, emitting double the number of *repha*s at the end;
then that gallinule, with its broad neck moving, proceeds with a gradually rising, clear, slow, and sweet cry, bowing down in due order. (VidSrk 10.51)
Thus ends the journey during the rainy season (10).
Next, the journey during autumn (11):
Autumn, bearing the bow of Indra upon her pale cloud-breast, resembling the marks of fresh nail-scratches;
While making the spotted moon appear radiant, she increased the heat of the sun even further.
"Though I possess a moon-like face, the splendor of a cloudless sky, and sprout-like lips as lovely as the bandhūka flower, shame on me!
For, alas, my breasts have sagged. Thus, as it were, this autumn bears a great heat.
These are the days of autumn, hospitable to swans as guests, serving as life-restoring herbs for the lotuses whose lifespans have been consumed by time, and bringing old age to the clouds;
during these days, the rivers captivate the mind, variegated by the arrival of wagtails and their distant banks rippled ever so slightly as the waters recede.
With their smoky-grey wings and pale bellies fluttering on all sides, the *khañjana* birds scatter the approaching autumn like women scattering parched grain with haste;
and the moon-faced night, smiling, places upon the courtyard of the sky the auspicious jar of the moon, white from its libation of moonlight and accompanied by the sprout of its spot.
Rows of white-winged swans cast the shadow of white clouds upon the sky and the water; through their hundreds of reflections, they create the illusion of white lotuses.
If it were not for the autumn, which moistens the mind with the sound of jeweled anklets sweet, rapid, and resonant, and with waves that murmur like voices, where else would there be such longing?

The gardens, their trees made to bristle with joy by the dense blossoms of the *śephālī* flowers that cling closely to the earth, delight the dwellers at night; these quarters are flooded with the fragrance of blooming water-lilies shaken by the breeze, while the cries of joyful curlews rise up in a sudden burst of song.
On the ground strewn with circles of night-blooming lilies, as the youths— aware of the falling pollen— loudly mutter some secret mantra of Smara,
this deep and honey-intoxicated clamor of the masters that are the bees swells forth, now that the stubborn seizure of pride has been overcome.
Looking downward with its head turned and tilted to both sides, moving slowly in smooth circular paths through the sky by the steadiness of its wings, the hawk—
expert in seizing prey— after a long time, swooping down with extreme speed from the side, suddenly strikes with its moving talons upon the head of its victim.

With its tail held high, its feet moving with a rhythmic grace, and its wings drooping and quivering, the *khañjarīṭa* bird— its beak made slightly vocal by the sweet, intoxicated warbling from its throat—
dances for a while near its beloved, whose eyes are fixed on it with longing and steadied by a stream of tears of joy.

These riverbanks of autumn delight the mind: where the tips of the beaks of flocks of herons, bent low as they are occupied in searching for schools of fish submerged within the water, possess a white luster; where wagtails wander about; where the surrounding areas are covered by rows of cooing *kādambara* birds; and where lines of intoxicated *kurara* cranes warble sweetly. VidSrk_11.10 *(275)*.
The sun shines fiercely like a low-born man newly wealthy; the ruru deer sheds its horn like an ungrateful friend;
water becomes clear like a sage’s contemplation of the Dharma; and the mud turns crimson like a poor man driven by lust. (VidSrk 11.11)
Scorching, uttering cries like those of swans in rut, wearing a garment white as the moon,
and bearing breasts that are pale and full— a certain maiden shines like an autumn day, resembling a woman separated from her lover.
With their intentions gradually stilled, their sandy banks formed by fragments of white moonlight, and strewn before them with flocks of cranes warbling sweetly;
filled at night with the variegated forms of blooming star-lilies, the ten directions flow forth from the sky like long rivers. (VidSrk 11.13)

With their hindquarters broadened by thighs swollen and spread wide, the herd of white cows wanders through the outskirts of the villages— lands green with newly sprouted crops— during nights that smile with the radiant glow of the moon, while the heavy, deep-sounding bells, clustered upon the dangling, thick blankets, ring out.

Upon its back, which has the luster of a conch shell fragment, the white water-lily (*kumuda*) of the pond blooms, marked with lines on its petals as red as lac, while its outer leaves are tawny and green like *gorocanā* pigment. VidSrk_11.15 *(280)*.

The forest rivers, with waters as dark blue as glass, inspire terror; their currents are rendered treacherous by dense, thick reeds, yet they are accessible once one has crossed over them; the sand on their banks is churned by the bellies of crocodiles that have emerged and retreated; and their mud-filled depths reveal fresh, moist impressions marked by the distinct tracks of tigers.
The tracks of carts, whose essence is the crushed pulp of sugarcane rinds, bear banners of thick dust; a flock of parrots settles upon the heads of *śūka-śāli* rice, bowed down by the ripening grain.
From the fields, rows of minnows enter the nearby irrigation channels; the clear mud on the riverbanks brings comfort to the sun-baked cowherd. (Vidūṣaka’s Verses 11.17, attributed to Abhinanda)

The sprouts, though marked by mud, possess a luster as if they have been freshly bathed and anointed; the marshy banks, with tufts of *kāśa* grass driven by the wind, resemble flocks of sheep. The rivers, with *khañjana* birds hastening to settle on their newly formed banks, appear as if their eyes were smeared with collyrium. Upon the surface of the sky, which possesses the hue of Kṛṣṇa’s body, the swans bear the beauty of conch shells. (VidSrk 11.18) Amidst the cries of the swans, there arises another kind of hoarse sound from those who are warbling, produced by the friction of their parched throats.
Now, in the lotus ponds, the tips of the knots at the ends of the lotus roots have emerged, rivaling the sprouting tusks of young, tender female elephants.
Now, the boundaries of the fields belonging to Śrī Kamalāyudha have been prepared with platforms by their owners to ward off the boars that are eager for mouthfuls of ripening rice;
the trees have had dense nests built in their branches by pigeons seeking a home, and the anthills have their interiors dug out by the sharp claws [of the boars]. (VidSrk 11.20)

The curious maidens are well able to fashion playful crest-ornaments from Indra’s cotton-wool— soft as a digit of the moon and tossed by the wind— which, like the saliva of Śatānanda’s celestial elephants, serves as a smile for the quarters of the sky and creates the illusion of foam from the green horses of the sun’s chariot weary from their journey. (VidSrk 11.21)
Between her breasts, a lotus stalk bears the luster of a necklace upon the fair-limbed girl; near her ear, blue water-lilies serve as the ear-ornaments for Acyuta;
and at the parting of her hair, the glow of red gems is matched by Bandhujīva flowers. Thus, the seasonal attire of the rice-guardian maiden imparts a supreme beauty.

Today, these rivers bring joy: their branches are revealed by the departure of the honey-bees, their banks are occupied by wandering wagtails, and they are adorned with royal swans sporting with force; their waters smile with saphara fish darting about in fear of being seized by the beaks of wandering ruddy geese. VidSrk_11.23 *(288) //

The banks of the forest rivers, where the forests are now only partially submerged and flickering, where the successions of waves have dried into sandbanks, and where the remaining water in the depths leaves behind mud marked with the tracks of swans— these banks captivate the mind. (VidSrk 11.24)

The forest groves on the riverbanks, where the hollows of trees are drained of water by the crushing of snakes and where dead moss and sprouts hang from the branches, recede into the distance as they proclaim the greatness of the former current.
The days have ripened, fragrant with the scent of the ripened kharjūra fruit, belonging to one of auspicious limbs;
they possess a heat difficult for the twice-born to endure, who were satiated by the invitation to the first ancestral rite.
The receipt of funeral offerings from the wealthy by the Lord of Yoga, and the slippery path leading to his dwelling—
these two things disturb the minds of the twice-born residing in the royal camp. (VidSrk 11.27)
Of Vāgura. Thus ends the journey during the autumn. 11. Next, the journey during the winter. 12.
This is that season, the friend of the glory of the kunda flower and the kinsman of the north wind, which is the messenger of death for the wealth of the lotus ponds;
where women, distressed by a dullness feigning sleep even when their lovers' embraces are firm, welcome the tight embrace of their beloveds under the pretext of slumber.

Whose mind is not now filled with longing by the clusters of betel-nut trees—trees made beautiful by fruits that are dark at the tip with attached tilaka-marks, pale-red in the middle like ripe paṭola gourds, slightly brown at the base, and on their stalks as dark as the feathers of a parrot or a peacock, yet thick and sturdy? (VidSrk 12.2)
At the bases of the petals, the pollen of the filaments—once fallen and now motionless—no longer carries away even as the wind blows, for it has lost its brilliance that rivaled yellow orpiment.
In the bud of the night-lily, the bees, their luster dimmed at dawn, lick the nectar mixed with dew, finding it increasingly tasteless.

The morning breeze blows freely through the lotus ponds, fragrant with blooming priyaṅgu flowers and scattering hidden sparks of fire under the guise of frosty spray; it is capable of making the bristling hairs on the cheeks of the florist’s young wives firm, as they thrill with the intense joy of witnessing the abundance of kunda blossoms.
The peasants take pride in their straw while being praised by hundreds of travelers; the thick mist from the chewing of the cows’ cud brings comfort to the pregnant cattle.

At dawn, when the first rays of the sun have reached his back, the great bull lies in the outskirts of the village boundary, his eyelashes moist with frost and covered with a paste of mustard flowers.
The forests of *damanaka* belonging to the Lord of Yoga, now entirely pale with their stalks, have their leaf-patterns carved out by the leaves and possess both pungent and sweet fragrances.

In a small grass hut at the corner of a barley field, upon a bed of fresh straw and with a pillow, a pair of plowmen sleeps soundly; nearby, the frost—marked by lines formed by the great heat from their jar-like breasts—passes them by.

Having observed a pair of rabbits fleeing from the edge of the field, these common folk, having called out to others with great excitement and raised a clamor, have abandoned their desire to reap the rice; now, with sickles, ropes, and clubs held in their hands by both the old and the young, they run hither and thither.
Having placed her tattered garment behind her back, she sits between her thighs—which are marked by the scars of burns from fire—resting her hands upon the embers of the *kukūla* fire;

covering her sides, numbed with trembling, with both elbows, her skin bristling with horripilation, this old woman does not leave the interior of the house today, neither in the morning nor in the evening. (VidSrk 12.9)
For the Vaiśya:
May the fire of dried cow-dung, consisting mostly of smoke, frequently vomiting its brilliance due to excessive agitation, and being constantly tended by his wife, be served.
At the end of the day, it shines as it is enjoyed by the women of the cowherd settlements, who have cast aside their playful garments from the region of their breasts with a toss of their arms.

Now, at the end of the day, these villages—intent on their labors, with the outskirts of their threshing floors sprouting with ripened rice, and girdled by circles of smoke from fires of cow-dung fuel that are dear to the frost—are enchanting. (VidSrk 12.11)
At the base of Abhinanda’s tree, the jujube fruits are somewhat greenish, yellow on the sides,
and red at the tips; they are sweet and fragrant now, as their ripening has not yet reached its full depth.

"May you be blessed! It is only fitting that your fame is sung by hundreds of travelers; it is appropriate that your form is unsurpassed, O man of merit, for by your generosity you have surpassed Karṇa. Having gazed upon him for a long time with such a wretched eye, a traveler who had come from afar—content with a single handful of chaff—is praised, while the plowman merely basks in pride.
Of the Lord of Yoga. Thus ends the section on Winter (Hemantavrajyā). 12. Next follows the section on the Cold Season (Śiśiravrajyā). 13.

Even when occupied with the worship of the *kunda* flower or their own adornment, nor even during the preparation of festive offerings, women do not show such devoted attention as they do at the inaugural consecration of the *Kundacaturthikā* festival; for by the soft warbling of their flutes, they delight the minds of the youths who have summoned the God of Love. (VidSrk 13.1)

In the forest of *damanaka* shrubs, smoke-grey from the fires of dried cow-dung, the falling snow is difficult to perceive; yet, clinging to the hair, it displays a charming grace like a silken garment. It now obscures the appearance of the sun and bestows a whiteness over all the limbs of the travelers. (VidSrk 13.2)
Pūṣan, the traveler of the sky, has set out from the eastern mountain at dawn, his body encircled by a collar of dense mists that can be pierced only by a needle;
I think that even though he has embraced the fire all night long, he is unable to quickly hasten his feet, which remain bound by coldness.

At dawn, the channels of the mountain torrents—though far above and wide open—are perceived as if full of water; they cause the traveler’s pace to slow for a moment, as they emit streams of vapor from their slender waters, appearing like rivers filled with water that tremble before the gaze of one looking across the shore.

In the company of their beloveds, who are like stones bathed in frost, the jests of those long away from home—playful acts involving the emission of water—fade away even during the midst of lovemaking;
for they have become objects of the eyes of lovers whose splendors, now devoid of loveliness, are as if bereft of fortune through the waning of the moon’s light.

As the beloved of the lotuses approaches, his luster growing faint, the water— surrounded by swans with worn, coarse, and soiled wings who stand day and night inside and outside as if they were affectionate kinsmen keeping watch— releases tears, as it were, earned from the destruction of the lotuses.
For the fortunate, whose bodies are filled with manifold joys and delights from embracing dark-limbed women whose mouths are full of fresh betel, the arrival of the cold season is delightful;
but for us, whose knees are seized by trembling as we sit covered by torn and patched rags spread across our laps, the heart simply sinks.
The monkeys tremble violently; the cattle, goats, and sheep, cold and emaciated, grow faint; and the dog, though thrust for even a moment into the hollow of the hearth, does not leave it.
Furthermore, this wretched person, afflicted by the calamity of suffering from the cold, desires—like a tortoise—to withdraw his own limbs into his very body.
Now the houses of the plowmen are worthy of Lakṣmīdhara’s praise; they are filled with the fragrance of new rice-pots, rejoicing at the first cutting of the ears of grain,
while the young women, their bracelets jingling as they raise their vine-like arms, seize, toss up, whirl, and smoothly let fall the pestles.
The ripening, parched sesame seeds are able to excite the pigeons; the mustard plants attain a blackness upon their flowers being crushed by the fruit;
the wind, scattering the hemp and carrying particles of frost, approaches bringing shivers; and the sacred fire is attended by travelers who have engaged in heated disputes over dry wood.

The children of the Lord of Yoga have achieved their purpose: they dangle among the sprouts that are heavy with clusters of fruit; they pluck the *kolī* fruits right from below because of their loveliness;

and the stalks of *puṇḍra* sugarcane, held by their hands as if by a machine, spit out their juice as the knots of new shoots become visible through the opening of the leaf-sheaths loosened by ripening.
The moon bears a resemblance to the face of a woman distressed by her husband; the radiance of the sun is now dull, like the command of one whose wealth has vanished;
the fire of dried cow-dung is sweet with the anger of a newlywed bride, while the icy wind is cruel with its embrace of unrighteous people.
As the fire— its glow gradually obscured by the repeated striking of sticks upon the straw, which has been heated like parched grain by the frosty wind—
is being kindled, a certain pungent odor is scattered from corner to corner of the threshing floors, rising with smoke and the sharp crackling sounds of mustard seed husks bursting open.
In the forest of the Lord of Yoga,
where most things have perished and which is frequented by the withered creepers of the great dissolution, the seeds of the *kṛṣṇala*— red as the eyes of an intoxicated cuckoo—
are revealed from the bursting pods of the *śamī* trees due to their ripeness; they manifest the clear companionship of the surrounding vines.
The fruit-bearing trees shine with young shoots as smooth and pale as parrots and as long as a young woman’s hand, their luster enhanced by the winter season;
their lovely clusters, greenish-brown with pollen-filled buds, burst forth limb by limb, attracting bees with their sharp fragrance. (VidSrk 13.15)
Śatānanda’s complexion, once dark as barley-grass, has faded from the parched beans; the outskirts of the village have grounds grey with lentils, and the *yamānī* forest is in bloom.

The *śatapuṣpikā* plants are rich with flowers, the *siddhārthaka* seeds are laden with fruit, the *vāstuka* greens are succulent, and the *kustumbinī* vines are covered in clusters of blossoms. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 13.16)
Before Śubhāṅga’s eyes, the jujube fruit in the forest first becomes mostly pale; then, marked by a brownish tint, its body next becomes suffused with a reddish quality due to the excess of ripening;
and finally, as it begins to dry, becoming uneven with its own protruding ridges and devoid of fragrance, it attains a state of tastelessness.
Thus ends the section on the Cold Season (13).
Next is the section on Love (14):
This is that Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is renowned throughout the three worlds, who now, distressed by separation, bears a woman within his own body out of longing for a lover.
"By him, indeed, we have been conquered!"—thus saying, Love triumphs, laughing as he strikes his beloved’s hand with his own. (VidSrk 14.1)

May those side-glances of women protect you—the arrows of the five-arrowed god who conquers the three worlds, possessing great power; discharged from the bow of his eyebrows drawn by his dark-blue banner, they steal the beauty of swarms of bees upon blue lotuses; they are swift black antelopes with sharp and cruel points that pierce the hearts of men; their feathers are long-cornered eyes, and they are perilous with the venom of smiles, while their lashes are thick and fine.

Victorious is the Mind-born, whose commands are honored by all living beings, whose craftsmanship consists of vast and wondrous fancies, and who—through his flower-arrows that do not even touch them—simultaneously strikes the three worlds with those same flowers at once. (VidSrk 14.3)
Even the Lord of the Universe, whose left side is eternally occupied by his consort, is his enemy; the Moon, the sole drinking-cup for the nectar of heaven, is his friend;
the flowers that kiss the minds of the worlds are his arrows that pierce the vitals; and Pleasure and Delight are his wives—where, indeed, is the majesty of Kāma not supermundane?
Victorious is Ananga, the supreme friend of the Moon, the beloved of Rohiṇī, who bestows the initiation into the sport of love upon women, the family preceptors of strength;
he triumphs as the director of the drama of amorous play, and even with his flower-arrows, he is the conqueror of the God of Gods. (VidSrk 14.5)
I revere the god Anaṅga alone, King Śekhara, who—under the guise of the lotus-petals of women’s eyes—with his long and elegant noose, has tightly bound the three worlds;

by whom even that Lord Kapālī, his body marked with ashes, was forcibly initiated into the playful vow of bowing at the feet of the daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), who was enraged by love. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 14.6)
Victorious is that bee born of the imagination of Lalitoka, who kisses the hundred-petaled lotus of Rati’s face;
he whose dwelling is the glance from the corner of the eyes of a passionate woman. (VidSrk 14.7)
Oh, the skill with the bow of the great-souled Manmatha! By Dāmodaragupta:
Having left the body unharmed, he pierces the mind within. (VidSrk 14.8) [330]
The bow is a garland, the bowstring a swarm of humming bees, and the target is the heart of a woman; these five arrows are sound and the rest.
May that Kāma—who possesses such power to conquer the three worlds while remaining bodiless, and who dwells in the side-glances of his beloved—grant you all your desires.
Victorious is that flower-bowed god, the deity of the graceful amorous play of women unrestrained by the intoxication of passion;
for the sake of his conquest of the three worlds, he possesses as his unprecedented equipment the garland, the moon, and the honeyed nectar—embodiments of the erotic sentiment itself.
No teacher is to be sought from anyone; the beloved image is the object of worship; the offerings are gazing, embracing, and kissing;
the self is the sacrificial gift—let us pay homage to this divine initiation of the god whose banner is the makara, which conquers the essence of all other vows. (VidSrk 14.11)
Of Vallaṇa. Thus ends the section on the intoxication of passion (madana-vrajyā), [chapter] 14.
Next is the section on the transition of youth (vayaḥ-sandhi-vrajyā), [chapter] 15.
There is a certain playfulness of the eyebrows, an unprecedented transformation of the eyes, and the fullness of the breasts is still indistinct at this time of the onset of youth.
Now, for this young girl, does it resound as nectar, or as honey, or as manifest bliss itself—this sweet fifth note?
The time for Vīryamitra’s [practice] has arrived.

The breaking of high locks of hair, the practice of arranging the mass of braided tresses, the grooming of the teeth, the fastening of the waist-knot, the training in the graceful play of the brows, the sidelong movements of the eyes, and the transfer of clever expressions into speech—this indescribable sequence of amorous play in women fades away moment by moment as childhood declines. (VidSrk 15.2)
Which limb here does youth not adorn with excellence? Nevertheless, there is a certain clever boldness in the pair of eyes;
for it receives from the object of sight every shift of emotion, and it reveals to the observer’s mind the state of the person being beheld. (VidSrk 15.3)

These two budding breasts of hers belong to Rājaśekhara; they possess the beauty of a pair of palm-leaf cymbals smeared with saffron, belonging to the dancer of fresh youth—slightly expanding in their movement at the center, yet having attained their own boundaries at the edges. (VidSrk 15.4) [337]

At the onset of the city of youth, this lovely line of hair shines upon the plains of the women’s hearts like the dolphin-bannered standard of the flower-arrowed god. These two [verses] are by Laḍahacandra.
This pair of her budding breasts, marked by the seal of their uplifted nipples and with the boundary between them clearly defined within,
is like a pair of fresh bronze cymbals smeared with saffron, used for the staged drama of a young woman’s burgeoning youth. (VidSrk 15.7)
Her hip seeks a comparison with a smooth jeweled pedestal; her cheek, pale as a honey-bud, rivals its beauty;
and as she enters into youth, her body, emerging fully from the waters of her thick, saffron-like loveliness, reigns supreme.
The chest bears two budding breasts; the lower lip, possessing the luster of the *madhūka* flower, seems to smear its beauty slightly across the surface of her cheeks;
youth approaches this fawn-eyed girl; and what is more, her body now exists with a charm as lovely as if it were anointed with the nectar-paste of emerging loveliness.

Desist from going outside the house; let your restlessness be far away. Those playful antics of childhood still persist even now. O daughter, your short tunic is bursting in an instant, pressed down by your swelling hips.
A reply both affectionate and artful, speech that is both spoken and kept secret, a face turned away even when entreated with effort, and a mind poised between compliance and refusal—
victorious is this certain other sweet flavor, charming in its duality, belonging to the deer-eyed girl dwelling in the interval between childhood and youth.
Lakṣmīdhara’s hip still yearns for its own splendor and has not yet attained fullness on all sides; nor has his chest, though graced by the division of breasts, reached its expansion;
and the playful seal of her eyes flickers and has not yet become stable—thus, her youth, having first descended, triumphs. (VidSrk 15.12)
Her mind is curious about the game of dice and the stories of Śārī; she always delights in learning witty sayings; her circle of companions acts as her teachers in the art of holding a mirror;

she takes pleasure in imitating the conduct of mature women; yet, due to her childhood, she feels a slight bashfulness as her youth begins to rise—such is this indescribable sequence of play in the fawn-eyed maiden.
Her gaze is the ornament of childhood, yet at every moment boldness is being practiced; likewise, her chest retains its former shape, yet it seeks a new beauty for her breasts.

Although she does not yet possess heaviness, the region of her hips has increased in circumference; thus, the slender maiden’s body—conquered by the God of Love and drinkable solely by the eyes—is triumphant.

With the hem of her bodice drawn up to her neck, a smile merely hinted upon her face by the sealing gesture of her fingers over her breasts, languid in her play with dolls, with sidelong glances and the transfer of clever, double-meaning speech— this indescribable sequence of her dalliance changes moment by moment as her childhood fades away.

As youth slowly creeps over her, the slender-limbed girl undergoes a transformation beyond compare: her chest is marked by breasts whose roots are now clearly defined; her eyes, with their affectionate side-glances, have become experts in the slight dance of the brow;

her creeper-like eyebrows are skilled in nectar-sweet smiles and clever speech; her heart is filled with the blossoming of love; and her limbs are enveloped in a radiant beauty. Such is her new state as she matures.
O friend, time and again, in many ways, I have drunk in the sound of male cuckoos winding through the channels of my ears in the grove of mango trees;
yet today, though that sound is once more dear to my hearing, why does my whole body tremble, why does fever arise in my heart, and why this agitation in my eyes—out of nowhere?
The eyes of the deer-eyed girl are slightly upturned, with a rare flicker of the outer corners; her chest is languid with the budding breasts that are about to expand;
and a few graceful curves have descended upon her hips. As she sheds her childhood, the body of this fair-complexioned one possesses an indescribable loveliness. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 15.18)

The hips possess the weight of fullness; the waist is bound by three folds; the heart experiences rising modesty while its long-standing restlessness remains present; the chest has breasts budding forth; and the eyes have acquired a slight arching grace. Thus, the body of the slender maiden spreads its splendor as childhood gradually slips away. (VidSrk 15.19)
Perceiving that he was still considered a child even today, the young women exerted themselves for a long time to adorn him with their own ornaments;

yet he, licking his desire while maintaining an air of reluctance, was embraced by the beauty of the transition between ages—he who, when looked at face-to-face after being absent from their gaze, would look up with shimmering pupils and, upon being seen, become bashful and break into a smile.
Vallaṇa’s neutrality toward all things; his shaking of the head when questioned; the sequence of his inner and outer mental states entirely surrendered to his beloved;

and furthermore, his delight in the art of creating the subtle play of a sidelong glance—oh, how every limb of this young woman is sealed with the dalliance of Love during the confusion of youth! (VidSrk 15.21)
Released from her feet, the quick-moving gait has taken refuge in her eyes; her hips abandon their fullness while her waist adopts slenderness;

This pair of breasts, which seemed as if held before her by Gobhaṭa and then pushed back by others, with its horripilation quivering as if it had been granted relief from its former constraint;

Afterwards, attaining an equal height, they clearly transformed into the shape of a pair of golden jars. Where can we find such a marvel? Tell us! (Vidagdhamukhamandana 16.5)
These two—the face of that charming girl, which is like a deer-marked leaf with musk-paste smeared by the moonlight of her smile, and the playful grace of the moon—steal away my heart.

Where is the beauty of the moon, and where is the surpassing luster of her lower lip? Where is the young girl, and where are those darting side-glances of hers that steal away all self-restraint? *Viddhaśālabhañjikā* 16.6 (389)

As the Lord of Rati enters the newly constructed mansion of his youthful body, fashioned by the artisan of youth,
her breasts— limbs with sprouts of loveliness— serve as two auspicious jars.

Those beautiful-eyed women who restore with their very glance the mind that has been consumed by the gaze of Virūpākṣa—may they be victorious over my son. (VidSrk 16.12)

If you wish to truly imitate the face of the long-eyed one, with its trembling locks and darting glances, [then take these].

If her thighs are as firm as a rain-cloud, if this lower lip is so skillfully fashioned, if her pair of breasts is so dense, and if her lotus-face is so triumphant—

Whatever has been acquired with great difficulty by the gods within the ocean, all of that is perceived in the faces of beautiful women:

This is not the blue lotus eye of Acalasiṃha, nor is this a water-lily; this is not his face, nor is this the Bandhūka flower, for his lower lip possesses its luster.
Even I was first deluded in this matter, O bee; what have you done? Cease your efforts, cease from them! You weary yourself in vain.
"O slender one, there is a desire for both your face—the weapon of the Mind-born [Cupid] to conquer, and the vessel for the eyes' repose—to imitate one another.
Because of this generated rivalry, as if from an aroused anger, this cool-rayed moon now robs the lotuses of their bloom.
Surely the face of your beloved was not within the range of your vision— that mind-born creator who fashioned such a masterpiece of beauty.

O slender-limbed one, that incomparable pair of yours, which is likened to the age of Vikramāditya, is a non-yuga (an ageless era) among your limbs; this moon here is but a drop of wax upon the honey of the beauty of your face.
Bewildered by the hope that "is there anything beyond the reach of practice?", the intoxicated cuckoo proclaims the mere accents of your speech.

If that face belongs to Kālidāsa, then the talk of the moon is silenced; alas, if that luster is gold, then the beauty of the *kuvalaya* lilies is lost; if that smile is nectar, what else is there?
