"Rājaśekhara is unable to create a likeness of that long-eyed beloved’s face"—
as if thinking thus, the cool-rayed moon repeatedly creates its own reflection and then shatters it again.
Since this moon rises when weighed against your face,
O lady with the downcast countenance, its lightness is clearly revealed by that very fact.
As if performing austerities out of a desire to conquer the moon of your face,
this moon has become emaciated and taken refuge on the banks of the river flowing from the matted locks of Śambhu.
O slender one, these two breasts of yours engage in a fierce conflict,
like two kings whose alliances have been broken as they invade each other's territories.
Generally, the ground of the slope of her breasts is a granter of abundant fruit,
upon which the plowshare of the fingernail is applied after first placing the hand.
The expansive circle of these breasts alone is beautiful,
for even kings, upon approaching them, tremble and pay tribute.
Acyuta holds Lakṣmī upon his chest, which is adorned with the cluster of the Kaustubha gem; Śaṃkara himself carries Gaurī as half of his own body;
yet I suspect that the Lord Brahmā, born from the lotus, even today practices long austerities, for he has not yet reached maturity and seeks a beloved who is devoted to him with her entire being.
Thus ends the section on the description of young women (Chapter 16).
Now follows the section on passion (Chapter 17):
Having placed her left hand upon the surface of my hip, she stood facing me with her waist gracefully swaying, her breasts turned away from me and her chin touching her shoulder.
Two or three glances, sent with affection, which release the fever of love and are thick with pearl necklaces containing sapphire gems shimmering within, [are cast]. (VidSrk 17.1)
The mere glances of your eyes, which reach to your ears and steal the luster of the blue water-lily, captivate my heart; why this agitation?
O charming girl, you have merely shown the roots of your arms—marked by the nail-scratches left behind—and covered in dust, under the pretext of binding your hair that was falsely released.
First shimmering like a star, then as if fixed in a painting, then gradually as if natural and playfully half-closed at the corner of her eye;
thereafter slightly blossomed, and following that, emaciated by waves of thick tears—may the gaze of that deer-eyed woman fall upon me. (VidSrk 17.3)

The playful dancing of Vīryamitra’s eyebrows, the movement of his face, and the glances of that deer-eyed woman—cast toward us for a long time with intent and curiosity—were indeed like friends born of the same womb as the long garlands of blue lotuses interspersed with ketaka petals; they were the very arrows of Love, smeared with nectar. (VidSrk 17.4)
Having been seen by Rājaśekhara, she casts her gaze downward; when addressed, she makes no reply; on the bed, she remains turned away; when embraced by force, she trembles;

as her friends depart from the bedchamber, she desires only to go out as well. Though she has gone, my new bride, through her very perversity, brings me today exceeding joy. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 17.5)
Victorious is that loving glance of the fair-browed one, cast with upturned lashes as she rests her lotus-face—bowed down by the weight of her modesty—upon her knee;
and since this region of her cheek, marked by a trace of the beauty of her smile, comes within the range of the eyes of the world, it is a creation unprecedented even to heaven.

O fool, you have been deceived by that startled look of hers which was never seen before— her gaze wide and bright with wonder as she suddenly let go of the swan she had mistaken for a lotus, its body half-submerged as it playfully nibbled at a lotus stalk like Pradyumna.
This expansive bosom of the dark-complexioned maiden, encircled by a garland of pearl-like rays, is a friend of the God of Love capable of eclipsing the splendor of the full moon;
it is beautiful with a smooth application of glowing saffron, its covering of thick, dark-blue silk having slipped away.
I think that, fearing one or the other—either her breasts or her hips—to be inferior, the Creator began to measure her waist with his hand;
otherwise, how could the impressions of his fingers, submerged there in its moisture of loveliness, appear under the guise of the three folds of her waist?

Let this faultless young woman, dark-complexioned and adorned with a single strand of pearls, be beheld—she who bears the friend of the flower-armed god (Kāma), wherein this tilaka-mark of musk nourishes the beauty of a spot, and wherein the morning sunlight of her loveliness, consisting of her smile, anoints the quarters of the sky; she who is graced by the darkness of youth. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 17.10 (474)
This body is a lake for the amusement of my mind: its lotus-face, its lotus-stalk arms, its water of the beloved’s loveliness, and its ripples of the folds of her waist.
The lordly elephant of my heart, having plunged into it and fallen into the mud of her love, does not emerge. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 17.11)

Having passed over her pair of thighs with difficulty and wandered for a long time upon the region of her hips, my gaze—now rendered motionless by the uneven folds of the three lines at her waist—has slowly ascended her lofty breasts as if parched with thirst; it now gazes repeatedly and longingly at her eyes, which are trickling with drops of water.
"Enough with union with my beloved, for it is exceedingly fickle, like a dream or an illusion, and bitter in its ultimate consequence"—
even if we contemplate this truth a hundred times over, the inner self does not forget the gazelle-eyed woman. (VidSrk 17.13)
Knowing her to be a neuter, the mind sent forth toward her delights in that very place; we have been undone by Pāṇini. (VidSrk 17.14)
This necklace rolls upon the circle of breasts of the deer-eyed women; even for pearls, such is their condition—what then can we say of us, the servants of Love?
"‘She is Dharmakīrti’s;

she is beautiful, she is young, she is slender-waisted, she is charming, she is lovely-faced’—thus does this inner soul of mine, afflicted by love and longing for his beloved who is now separated from him, mutter again and again like a mantra. (VidSrk 17.16)
That young woman possesses vigor while we are timid of mind; she is a woman while we are faint-hearted. She is burdened by heavy hips and unable to walk, yet we are likewise unable to go.
She bears a pair of full and elevated breasts, while we are weary; it is a marvel that we have become incompetent through faults that belong to others. (VidSrk 17.17)

By the side-long glances of that long-lashed-eyed woman— glances slow and languid with weariness, yet tender and motionless, their pupils smiling with an ever-increasing inner wonder— the helpless heart of Dharmakīrti has been stolen, cast down, drunk up, and utterly uprooted. (VidSrk 17.18)
As she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing that face which resembled a lotus with its stalk revolved,
the sidelong glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman— smeared as it were with both nectar and poison— is deeply embedded in my heart.
There is no clear discernment even regarding an object present before one; nor does there arise, even for a familiar thing, a memory that brings an end to the state of its non-existence.
There is no cessation of distress in the snowy lake or in the moon; the mind, void of resolution, wanders and sketches something indefinable. (VidSrk 17.20)
Beyond all definition and outside the scope of every word, that which has never before entered the path of experience in this life—
a certain internal transformation, dense with great delusion accumulated through the destruction of discernment— both numbs and causes torment.
We do not know what this is—that glance cast repeatedly by the deer-eyed woman as she departed, a gaze with wide, trembling pupils and eyebrows dancing at the edges;

for in one place a mass of sweat bathes her, in another a surge of tremors arises, and in yet another part of her limbs, the onset of Love’s pride is like a fire of chaff. (Bhavabhūti, Vidagdhamukhamandana 17.22)

O slender one, if this body of mine were sprinkled with nectar by your wondrous glances, would you not whiten my lower lip, which is already fairer than moonlight, and redden my eyes, which are already redder than the dawn? That [whiteness and redness] returns to being merely collyrium for my eyes—this is the confusion of my words; yet, thinking "the seizing of her hand is imminent," I have placed an elephant within the hollow of my own trunk.
How could there have been, in a single Manvantara, such a vast creation of my body through intense penance and that of this fair-browed woman? VidSrk_17.24 (488)
Surely the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāma) is the servant of that fair-browed woman,
since he acts upon the signals indicated by the movements of her eyes. (VidSrk 17.25)
At first motionless with wonder, then trembling with trepidation, then bowed down with shame, and for a moment expanding with the longing to see;
drawn back by a sense of innate nobility yet pushed forward by love—only with great difficulty did the fawn-eyed woman’s gaze finally reach her beloved.
The body moves forward, while the unsettled mind runs behind,
like the hem of a Chinese silk garment on a banner being carried against the wind. (VidSrk 17.27) — by Kālidāsa.
O young girl, whose mind does this lower lip of yours—not unlike coral in its hue—fail to agitate with thirst, like a desert path? (VidSrk 17.28)
On this slender woman, these two breasts appear as if high, and her navel as if deep; even on a flat wall, her folds are seen to be unevenly raised.
Softness appears in her limbs, and her naturally affectionate nature is evident; for as soon as she gazes at the moon of my face with love, she seems to speak with a smile.

She wanders at will through the courtyard of her own house, yet she dissolves upon seeing me; she looks at fortunate men with her full gaze, but she regards me with only half an eye. When I have departed, she converses with others, but again assumes silence; I have been led far away by that beloved woman, even beyond the reach of ordinary people.
He is indeed the foremost among those who enjoy the fruits of their good deeds, he is most fortunate, for behind him follows that fawn-eyed woman with her jar-like breasts resting upon his back;

as she strikes a louse on his head—which has been placed there on the path by the crushing of her thick fingernails—with a "ṭasiti" sound accompanied by the syllable "hūṃ. *Vidagdhaśālabhañjikā 17.31* (495)
It lassos the body, excessively bewilders the mind, spreads a burning heat,
and repeatedly induces delusion— such is her glance, a poison more treacherous than any other.
Exhausted by the labors of love, [he rests] upon the pair of his beloved’s breasts, which are as large as the frontal globes of an elephant in rut and moist with saffron.
Placing his chest within the cage of her arms, the fortunate man passes his nights with sleep obtained for but a moment.
Fie on the poetry of that dull-witted bad poet who equates a woman’s face with the moon!
Where in the moon are there the playful movements of the arching brow, the glances full of charm, or the expressions of anger, favor, and laughter? (VidSrk 17.34)

The longing for liberation persists only so long as the curved, collyrium-blue ray—the eye-tooth of deer-eyed women—does not bite into the hearts of those whose minds are shattered by the agitation of old age, death, separation from kinsmen, and sorrow. (VidSrk 17.35)
Whether they saw her or did not see her, they were all equally robbed:
for some her heart was stolen, while for others the fruit of their eyes was taken away. (VidSrk 17.36)
"She is but a child," "she has eyes like a deer's," "her face is a blooming lotus," "the buds of her breasts are gradually unfolding"—O heart, shame on you! You weary yourself in vain.
This is an illusion; even for a mirage, your desire to drink water is misplaced. Do not once again make this a locus for the delusion of love upon a path that must be abandoned.
In the presence of her beloved, silence was his speech; not looking was his very gaze;
and that which was the covering of his limbs by the trailing of her garment’s hem was his offering of his body. (VidSrk 17.38)
As if pinned down by horripilation, my gaze does not move from the surface of her cheek; my heart remains motionless, having fallen into the mire of the ocean of love.
My breaths seem to have gone forth to rescue these two, yet they have returned out of fear; alas, they remain performing this long journeying back and forth.
If this is a lotus, where is its radiance at night; if it is the moon, how could it exist by day?
Since your face possesses the characteristics of both, the Creator has displayed great skill in fashioning it.
While I was facing her, her gaze was concealed, her smile was provoked by some other pretext, and her conduct was restrained by decorum; thus, by her, passion was neither revealed nor suppressed.

Who is that fortunate one? Tell me, who is he who is the sole kinsman of Madana? Whose path do you honor with upturned neck, O fawn-eyed one—with those tremulous side-glances, possessing a luster as delightful as a garland of blooming *kunda* flowers interspersed with blue lotuses?
With her heavy breasts as Jupiter, her radiant moon-like face as the Sun,
and her two feet as Saturns, she shone like an assembly of planets.

O charming girl, tell me, who is that fortunate man whom you are gazing upon today with eyes that are languidly rolling, moist with love, averse to blinking for a moment, tremulous with shame, repeatedly half-closed, and as it were vomiting forth the secret intentions of the heart hidden within? (VidSrk 17.44)
Then, stretching her creeper-like arms sideways with fingers interlaced over the knot of her braid, the slender maiden turned away;
yet, revealing her shimmering left eye-corner, half-breast, and cheek, she cast glances whose beauty was mistaken for a garland of blue lotus petals. (VidSrk 17.45)
Gazed upon with a meaningful look by her beloved in the presence of her attendants, she, hastening to convey her own intention, comforted her lover;

then, uttering words pregnant with the *Vaidarbha* style, she affectionately drew near a child under the pretext of another task, kissing him, urging him on, embracing him, and even showing him mock jealousy.
She loosens her garment by turning away even while awake out of modesty, yet embraces him firmly with a mind overwhelmed by the delusion that it is a dream;

having offered her body for the pleasure of her beloved, she feigns sleep under the pretext of falling asleep—alas, the efforts of this slender-limbed woman are in vain toward one who does not understand her inner state!
When her beloved returned after crossing the impassability of the desert lands, the wife fixed her gaze—tremulous with tears of joy—upon his face;
she gave the young camel mouthfuls of *pīlu*, *śamī*, and *karīra* fruits, and then respectfully wiped with her own hem the dust clinging to the mass of his mane.
"Keśaṭa’s foot has been wounded by a sprout of darbha grass"—saying this, the slender girl stopped abruptly after taking only a few steps;
she turned her face back and began to disentangle the bark garment from the branches of the trees, even though it was not caught there. (VidSrk 17.49)
“*Śākuntala* 2.12, by Kālidāsa:

‘A salutation with joined palms was made from afar; it was not done again when he was accustomed to drinking water. My head was bowed in wonder at the sight of his form, not out of a desire to quench my thirst.’”
The traveler’s horripilation was manifested incessantly through joy, not from the cold; for, seeing the girl at the water-station, he performed the unbroken rite of pouring water.
O bee, you repeatedly touch Bāṇa’s tremulous glance with its flickering corners; moving close to her ear, you softly whisper secrets as if telling a confidential tale.
While she shakes her hand, you drink from her lower lip—the very essence of love. We are ruined by our search for the truth, O bee; you alone are truly successful!

“That affectionate glance she cast even toward another; that slow gait as if from dejection due to the weight of her unyielding limbs; and that jealous remark made by her friend, who was restrained with the plea ‘Do not go’—all of that, they say, was indeed directed toward me! Oh, how desire perceives its own likeness everywhere! (Śākuntalā 1.20) [Vidagdhamukhamandana 17.52] (516)

From *Śākuntala* 2.2 by Kālidāsa: "By making the moon, who had been put to shame by the beauty of her face, appear dull like a ball held in her hand, she bears a countenance flushed with a mixture of playful curiosity."

I have been made the recipient of those glances which rival the petals of the *ketaka* flower plucked by the tips of bees, and which are the sole companions of the long undulations of the outer corners of the eyes. VidSrk_17.53 *(517)*
O lady, cause your eyes to ripple; let the painted blue lotus fall away; reveal your lip so that the coral may turn white;
uncover your body so that gold may take on a dark hue; lift up your own face so that the sky becomes possessed of two moons. (Vidyākara 17.54)
One man of virtuous conduct is victorious; how much more so two who are well-united?
What wonder is it if the world has been conquered by the breasts of a slender-limbed woman?
O friend, the glances cast from the corner of the lotus-eyed one’s eye— which is as long as a water-channel, which at every moment acts as a rival to young fish leaping about,
and which pour out their entire essence toward me— are establishing a new state of non-duality between her eyes and the blue water-lily.

Creating descents of brilliant pearl necklaces upon the earth, scattering clusters of *ketaka* flowers in every direction, and fashioning milk-white moonlight in the sky, the glances of the fair-browed women wander about. (VidSrk 17.57)

Whatever the fair-browed women perceive with a glance that suddenly enters the channel of their sidelong glances, whatever they perform with both arms gracefully swaying in succession, and whatever they express through words whose very essence is the seal of cleverness— all that, I believe, is the elixir for the god of love, that ocean of aesthetic flavor, according to Rājaśekhara. (VidSrk 17.58) [*(522)]*

I remember her standing for a very long time on tiptoe, her chest uplifted by the gradual straightening of her neck, the entire wealth of the lines of her waist-creases trembling, holding her handmaid, and desiring to see me. (VidSrk 17.59)

The slender-limbed maiden bears near her ear a single, curling earring—yellowish-white from the application of saffron, its palm-leaf ornament fallen away by the force of her movement—which steals the heart like a thief and appears like the stalk of her lotus-eye coiled around it. (VidŚrk 17.60)
With the hem of her garment, with the prominent strands of her swaying pearl necklace, and with her braid of hair forcibly coiled into a circle,
the girl with the arched brows seems to fashion for a long time the three traditional parasols by means of the circles she creates as she playfully whirls around.

The ball-play of the fair-browed woman captivates the mind in an indescribable way: her graceful steps are accompanied by the resonant tinkling of heavy jeweled anklets; her girdle chimes with a *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound as it strikes against the shimmering clusters of pearls on her necklace; and this sport is made particularly vocal by the rhythmic clanging of her row of trembling bracelets.
That slender body with a complexion as sweet and innocent as milk; those eyes, long as the petals of a fresh *ketaka* flower;
and that very neck which mocks the conch shell—this very moon-faced woman is the weapon of Love.
Where can the thirsty drink the nectar-filled moonlight? Where is it possible to weave a garment from the fibers of lotus stalks?
Alas, how could the fragrance of bakula garlands ever be measured? How, then, can a dream manifest that lotus-eyed woman in person?
To Rājaśekhara, these [lips] are like nectar; of this there is no doubt. Even honey is not otherwise [so sweet]. Is even the mango fruit, though naturally sweet, ever as clear in its flavor?
Let a person who knows other tastes, remaining impartial, declare once more if anything else here could be sweeter than the lip of a beloved. (VidSrk 17.65)

The grove of blue water-lilies was rejected, fresh honey was disparaged, and alas, even nectar—supreme in its wealth of flavor—was deemed poison by her through those languidly sweet, playful side-glances; thus, under the guise of anxiety, she infused even the hearts of lovers with distress.

The ball-games of the deer-eyed women bring delight: their *colā* garments fluttering, their braids disheveled by the speed of their retreat; their right arms, raised in the toss, create a clamor as bracelets clash; their speech broken by panting, their trembling locks tossed up by the other hand, and their flower-garlands slipping loose.
"Did you arrive at the end of the watch, or at midday, or even later than that?

Or perhaps when the entire day had passed?"—with such childish talk, accompanied by tears and sobbing, she prevents the departure of her beloved who wishes to travel to a land reachable only after hundreds of days.
"May prosperity attend the *jhalajjhala* bird; may the fulfillment of desires grow within the flock of cuckoos; may there be the rise of the full moon;

may there be well-being for the blue lotus"—with these words, filling her tearful bride's speech at every step, the lover, having prepared his equipment for departure, was vehemently restrained by his friend standing nearby.
Even a word expressing the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) in a general sense, when addressed to me, becomes fixed upon a specific object;
for when it is said "some woman," my mind takes as its object that very same one with the small eyes. (VidSrk 17.70)
Then follows a series of the messenger’s words:
"The deer-eyed woman conceals her physical emaciation with her loveliness, and she sustains her life through constant meditation upon you; yet this remains new:
that the moon now vies with her face, whose cheeks have turned dark from sighs that rise up as they roll against the surface of her jar-like breasts. (VidSrk 18.1)
Agitated by love, she does not even look at her own face in a mirror when the moon is present; terrified even by the warbling of the cuckoo, she does not release her voice;

and it is a marvel that, though harboring hatred for the flower-armed god who inflicts unbearable torment, that young woman, O fortunate one, cultivates ever-increasing love for you at every step. (VidSrk 18.2)

While this moon—anointed with the luster of sandalwood paste—smeared the circle of the quarters with its beauty, O you who are composed of merit, these two [tears] of that fawn-eyed woman smeared her eyes;
her tears were on her hands, her face was on her breath, you were in the hollow of her throat, shame was in her heart, and your virtues alone were on her back and in her speech. (VidSrk 18.3)

O fortunate one, while you were far away during those nights as white as the moon of a Caṇḍāla, there appeared in her a lotus in the form of a face, a moonstone in the form of an eye, and the agitation of the flower-bowed god of love. (Vidvadbhañjikā 18.4)
The streams of her tears do not rob the lovely beauty of her moon-like face; her sighs do not mar the sweet luster of her bimba-fruit lower lip.
Yet, in her separation from you, some indescribable pallor on the cheeks of that slender woman—which corresponds to the loveliness of a ripened *lavalī* fruit—wastes away further day by day.
The heat of Dharmakīrti’s fever has spread to the water; his tears have formed into a thick mass of steam; his sighs have caused the wick of the lamp to dance; and his body is submerged in pallor.
But what more shall I say? Throughout the entire night, she remains by the window facing your path, her hand serving as a parasol to ward off the moonlight.
She wipes away the moon drawn with sandalwood paste with her bitten lower lip; she reviles the venerable God of Love by clenching her fingers into fists;
and she plucks the cluster of flowers, saying that Kāma’s arrows are indeed made of blossoms. O fortunate one, by you, that lovely-bodied woman has been driven to madness.
O Rājaśekhara,

when you are attained in a dream by that doe-eyed woman, her body— covered in a dense mass of horripilation— is bathed by a great flood of perspiration; then, as she wakes with the jangling sounds of bracelets snapping from being forcibly pulled, there follow incessant torrents of tears.

The state of her who was like Vasuki’s consort, brought about by the fire of love when you departed, cannot be described: as she rolled repeatedly upon a bed fashioned of leaves by her tearful companions,

the lotus petal— once smeared with the sandal-paste from that fair-limbed woman’s breasts, now dried and turned pale by her sighs blowing upon it— is still wandering in the sky under the guise of the moon.
She perceives the momentary destruction of Rudra and sees the entire world as having become empty;
she acts outside the bounds of traditional memory, like one who has attained the awakening of a Buddhist.

Seeking you, she wanders performing the vow prescribed by Smara: her forehead-line is smeared with sandalwood ash, she is sprinkled with tears, and she wears lotus stalks as a garment over her breasts. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 18.11 (545).
Where are those playful men, crooked as double-tongued serpents, who cruelly burn others with their bites, their hisses, and their glances?
O serpent-like woman, this certain coquettish grace of yours—which is like a snake that kills without fangs—slays with the terrifying heat of its mere memory.

Fearing that the coverlet on her bed— its surface stained by the saffron paste dissolved by perspiration and soiled by her embrace— was as if licked by the visible flames of the fire of love, that young woman, her internal fever powerfully aroused by the rays of the moon, longs for the comfort of sleep upon your lap, which is cooled by the mental recollection of you.

As her eyes are struck by smoke, she sheds a stream of tears capable of forming a torrent; her body releases sweat that, like the froth of a boiling liquid, has taken up the essence of sandalwood paste.
From the ashes produced by the burning of the fire of passion blazing within, a pallor emerges across her frame, as if exhaled by the force of her sighs.
On this very picture-board, your friend, for the sake of diverting her torment and distress, somehow managed to paint you;
she gazed at you with eyes clouded by tears, hurriedly honored you with mango sprouts, bowed her head before you, and then—under the pretext of love—concealed you from her companions. (VidSrk 18.15)
Having sprinkled her own body— the sacrificial oblation— upon this fire of separation from you with the waters of her tears, that beautiful woman of Ḍimboka,
desiring to destroy the suffering of separation in another birth, offers it as an oblation with the mantra-words uttered by the male cuckoo.
O fortunate one, although you are attainable through good deeds by Prabhākara, this beloved companion of yours does not come under the sway of those who lack merit.
Therefore, enough now with this persistence; be gracious. May the state of mutual affection, sweet with love, increase between you both for a long time.
The breaths of her speech are as unsteady as a swinging cradle; her eyes resemble waterfalls; and the surface of her cheeks is pale as a withering tagara flower.
What indeed can we say of the frailty of her limbs, before which even the crescent moon that rises on the first day of the lunar fortnight appears thin?

O cruel one, I shall describe to you the ground of that fawn-eyed woman’s torment: a fresh lotus petal placed upon her breast for the sake of cooling it first withers, then shrivels, thereafter turns to powder, and finally, becoming like glowing embers, she fans it away with her sighs as it burns her friend.

To her, the blue lotus is poison; moonlight is a forest fire; the breeze from the lily groves is like burning embers; her necklace is salt rubbed upon a wound; and sandalwood paste is indeed a painful cauterization.
O fortunate one, when you are slightly turned away, how is it that all these things simultaneously become the very opposite of what they are to her? Ah! How strange!

O fortunate one, having imagined you within her thoughts, Acalasiṃha’s beloved experiences a thrill of horripilation and embraces herself with a pair of arms that perform an empty embrace. Moreover, overcome by the pain of separation, she faints; yet after a long time, she returns to life through the syllables of your name-mantra recited at the root of her ear.

"Her breasts are so closely pressed together that they have deeply compressed the three folds of her waist; they are firm and high," [the lover thought as he] reached for their surface in distress. Yet, even though they clearly knew she was his "heart," those two did not protect themselves from the arrows of Love as they entered; or rather, where could one turn when facing such a situation? (Vidvadbhañjikā 18.22, by Vallaṇa)
How can I describe to you the torment of her, whose eyes are like those of a young fawn? For I have never seen the form of the Goddess of Marriage fallen into fire.
Surely that excellence of the Creator’s craft, which by its very nature is dear to the eyes of the world in the form of a woman, will now be frustrated by your deceit.
"O gambler, look at the day that was previously set as her limit as she counts it;
like this [finger] of hers, the nail-marks are worn away, while like you, the joints are harsh.
— Dharaṇīdhara.
*Colo iti dūtīvacanavrajyā*.
Then follows the section on sexual enjoyment (*sambhogavrajyā*):
Even though the garment has slipped from the surface of her hips due to the essence of mature passion, a second silken cloth is begun [to cover her] by the radiance of the gems in her girdle-string.
The lover gazed quickly and in vain; then the slender maiden blushed in vain; again he drew it away in vain; then she covered it in vain. (VidSrk 19.1)

When the act of love has reached its height and her beloved is occupied with the remaining tasks, what indeed is not heart-stirring for the woman who, pining in longing, repeatedly utters words slow with passion, each syllable full of meaning? (VidSrk 19.2)
When her lover, exhausted at the end of love-making, his eyes fixed upon her breasts and hips and agitated by the onset of passion, began to remove her silk garment— she,

casting her dear eyes for a moment on his hip, a moment on his hands, a moment on the tips of his breasts, and a moment into his eyes— for such a fawn-eyed woman, even the entire world is not worth a fraction of that moment.

Having performed various amorous dalliances through hundreds of such playful gestures and instructions on love, she now rests with her limbs relaxed, nestled in the lap of her lover; this is the abundant fruit of no small ascetic merit.

Does not this newlywed bride captivate the mind here—she who surpasses even mature women, whose lotus-face is bent low by the weight of modesty, whose eyes possess rows of shimmering lashes, whose body is the very abode of the splendors of the kingdom of love, whose passion for the God of Desire is ever-increasing, and who holds back her burgeoning anger? O you who are indifferent to my entreaties, it is resentment that has become dear to you, not I. (VidSrk 21.30)
"Shame, shame on you! O foul-faced one, by whom have you been made so? What bodily penance has not been performed here? Who has not been angry for two or three days? Who has not become human?
Are we not all such? Let even a single word of another be heard: surely fire arises even from sandalwood when it is excessively rubbed."
"Let Vallaṇa’s heart burst! Let Kāma do as he pleases to make my body thin; I truly have no further need for a lover with such fickle affection.
Having spoken these words impetuously out of a display of pride, that doe-eyed woman looked toward the path of her lover with apprehension.
On a single bed, they lay with their backs turned to one another, suffering in silence; though the conciliation remained in each other's hearts, both guarded their dignity.
Later, as their eyes mingled through the shifting of sidelong glances, the quarrel of pride was broken by a sudden, laughing embrace in which their necks were clasped.
O sprout of Love, cut away the shoot of anger with a playful glance; let me become a guest seeking refuge at your feet.
Look, be gracious: the orb of the moon, kissing the crest of the western mountain, is turning the color of the juice of the *lavalī* fruit.
"Aha! You possess a divine eye, for even that beloved of yours transfers her form—ungraspable by other eyes—to these young women.
Otherwise, how could you alone see her before you, while others see only beautiful figures made of her likeness?"
O beloved of my mind’s delight, abandon your silence; let my eyes drink in the streams of nectar as they open wide, and let the world become composed of blue lotuses.
Be gracious, for love utterly pacifies all restlessness; indeed, a servant is beyond reproach when he is innocent of offense.
O lotus-eyed one, if you have harbored anger toward me because of this childish prank, let that anger be dear to you; what else remains to be done?
Grant me the embrace previously offered by me, and grant me again and again the kisses bestowed by me.
"O friend Śatānanda, this rogue has been caught; he must not be released with a mere prostration.
Let this scoundrel experience for a long time the binding of your vine-like arms."
When Gonanda’s lover had become weary of their quarrels and ceased his persistent entreaties, when her pride was fading and the god of love was blooming, and as the time of night drew to a close,
she feigned sleep through a clever artifice and acted out a state of deep slumber; thus, her pride was not diminished, nor was her secret intimacy interrupted.
When her anger has somehow dissolved like a summer day and her favor has returned, followed by a gradual unfolding like the night—
then the moon-like face of the proud woman, having dispelled the mass of darkness that was separation with the rising moonlight of her smile, shines forth for the man of merit during the act of love.
Afflicted now by the malady of pride, I am unable to go to his presence; nor is there any clever friend who might lead me there by force.
Even that man, being proud, does not approach out of fear of appearing insignificant, O Mother; time passes away of its own accord, and life is fickle—thus my mind is worn down by anxiety.
"O friend, go quickly while he has not yet come within the range of my eyes and tell him that today his beloved has taken up a display of pride.
But once that lover, with his rogueish ways, is seen by me, my face will surely become filled with a broad smile that completely obstructs the flow of perspiration."
A wicked fist was struck here; she was clawed at the heart with nails, dragged by the sides, pulled violently by her braided hair, and bitten on the lip while she hissed "sīt.
Even though you were not present, I have now performed every deed that you would have done. Command me, O simple one—what more shall I do to your co-wife?
"O slender-limbed one, abandon your silence; look at me prostrate at your feet. Surely never before has your anger been such as this.
When the lord spoke thus, she, with eyes half-closed and cast askance, shed a profusion of tears but said nothing at all.

In the mind of the proud woman, it sprouted as a bud; in her flickering pair of eyes, it became a pair of leaves; in her words, which were mostly full of feigned indifference, it was likely put forth as a shoot; in each various gesture of anger, it blossomed as a flower; but when her beloved bowed at her feet, the tree of pride did not bear fruit, yet it did not remain barren at the end.
O proud lady, how small is Rājaśekhara’s offense of mistaking his family name; this transgression rolls at your feet for a long time—do not persist in your pride.
Cast away your anger, favor your beloved, and listen to what we say for your future welfare, dear friend: do not turn your fingernail into a river.
If this person has been found guilty by fate, he alone should be punished with the humiliations befitting a slave.
O fair-limbed one, why is this sandalwood leaf-design on the surface of your cheek being tormented by the channels of your tears?
"Having committed an offense, he has not even come; clearly my heart suspects something. Where shall I be? To whom shall I go in this forest of living beings? Who here will comfort me?

Having spoken thus, her face streaming with tears, the courtesan’s friend, despondent, entered the house. There, by that fortunate man, you were made his ultimate beloved and brought to tears as he listened to your lamentation.
From the eyelashes to the cheek, from the cheek to the slope of the breast, from the breasts to the waist, and from the waist to the newly blossomed lotus of the navel—
O Vallaṇa, we do not know what, where, or how much he has undertaken, that the drop of her eye-water wanders across every limb of hers.

"O Narasiṃha, scatter [the bees] from his eyes; let the blue lotus become dim in luster. O beloved, bestow the moonlight of your smile; let the lotus close its petals. Speak, O fair-faced one; let the peacocks remain silenced by shame. For a woman of pride, O proud lady, the humiliation of another cannot be endured through grounds of honor. (VidSrk 21.50)

"O friend, do you not see from his conduct—which is sweet with deceptive modesty—that this man is a rogue? For on your cheek, O naturally simple one, he bears this mark, stained with the deep red of lac-dye, which betrays a recent encounter. (VidSrk 21.51)

For two youths who have not yet attained the pleasure of play, whose intentions are blocked by excessive pride, who have suddenly become angry with one another in secret, and who long for each other’s first conciliation—their inner states, indicative of their underlying affection, rob them of sleep. (VidSrk 21.52)

These two [tears] have not been placed upon the ears of Sonnoka; such were the ways of your friend’s playful advances. This person has not been struck even by the tip of your big toe while prostrate at your feet.
O hard-hearted one, due to your addiction to the vow of false silence, this is merely a means to abandon your attendants, not the assumption of true pride.
The moon of her face does not grow dull, nor does crookedness take hold of her forehead; her lotus-eye does not redden, nor does her brow knit itself into a frown.
Yet this lower lip of my beloved proclaims the anger blooming within her, for it remains sealed with a firm seal even after a hundred questions.
Vaidyadhanya speaks such things as the occasion demands, she laughs, and she does not resist even in embracing or kissing;
yet today, some indescribable descent of aesthetic flavor (*rasāvatāra*) has been infused by a suppressed anger, hidden for fear of provoking her favor.
By embracing her husband with great fervor, she turned away his gaze that was fixed upon her breasts; by rebuking his face as it thirsted for her lower lip, she averted his kiss;
and by pressing firmly against his thighs and blocking his hand on her hips, this clever woman neither violated her love for her husband nor did she abandon her pride.
Those days when the lamp-flames flickered and were agitated by long-drawn sighs; those days when your gaze was heavy with anger at my prolonged wakefulness;
those days when conversations flowed sweetly with the clarity of singular trust—leave those other days behind, tread upon my feet: I am that same person, and you are another.
The onset of her embrace touches only her desire, yet her arms do not yield; her methods of compliance touch only her consciousness, yet not her speech.
At the hour when the night draws to its close, the mind of the spirited woman flows freely toward her lover, but her body has somehow turned back.

"O friend, today in the courtyard of the garden-house, in a dream, I raised this foot—red with lac and with its anklet tinkling—for the sake of performing the rite to satisfy the *aśoka* tree. While I was doing so, what shall I say? He, who is skilled in dalliance, suddenly emerged from the interior of the bower and, arriving unperceived, honored me at once by placing his head [at my feet]."
O friend, that Madhukūṭa is fortunate; it does not distress me that he has but slight affection for me, since every person enjoys the happiness brought about by destiny.
But this is the torment in my heart: that even though my beloved is indifferent, my wretched shameless mind somehow cannot turn away from him.
Even when her eyebrows are knit, her gaze looks up with even greater longing; even when her speech is restrained, this scorched face breaks into a smile;
even when her heart is made stern, her body takes on a thrill of horripilation—how, then, can there be a conclusion to my pride when that person is seen?

This beloved was turned away by his mistress—who had prostrated at his feet with oaths—as soon as he himself had taken only two or three steps from the bedchamber; yet, before he could go further, she ran back and, having made a salutation, held him fast by tying the knot of her lower garment with her joined palms. Oh, how strange is the course of love! *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 21.62 (696)

When the bond of love has departed, when the deep respect in my heart has dissolved, and when true affection has ceased as people pass one another on the road before them— then, O dear friend, as I reflect again and again upon those days that have gone by, I know not what reason there is for my heart not to shatter into a hundred pieces.
O fair-limbed one, your hips are broad and the greatness of your eyes is surely large;
now let the middle [of your waist], though possessing folds, become Māndhātṛ, and let the slope of your breasts be made [the world]. — By Dāmodara.

When her beloved was seen, her pride (māna) slightly closed like her eyes; when he came before her, it bent low like her face; when he stood outside and offered a touch, it bristled with horripilation like her body; when he spoke, it became slackened like the knot of her garment; and then, as he touched her feet, it departed from the fair-eyed woman like her sense of shame.
The journey of the proud woman is like a colic; thereafter follows the journey of the woman separated from her lover.
At that very moment, the tears shed upon the lotus stalks act as glowing embers, while the tears upon her pale cheeks act like a flowing stream of water.
Furthermore, while I was still applying the abundant juices of Malaya-tree resin to her hand, her hand became covered in dust by the friction of her sighing breath. (VidSrk 22.1)
Of the Infallible One.
"First you were conquered by the God [Śiva], who bears the crescent of the moon; immediately after by the Buddha of exalted intellect; and then by my beloved, that traveler.

Alas, having abandoned them, you strike down me—a young woman, emaciated and protectorless! Shame on you! Shame on your manliness! Shame on your rising power! Shame on your bow! Shame on your arrows! — Śrī Rājyapāla.

Because the words of her friends were not heeded in her ear, because the counsel of her kin was not respected, and because even as her beloved fell at her feet he was struck with a lotus from her ear—
therefore, the moon acts like a fierce fire, the application of sandalwood paste acts like sparks, the night acts like a hundred kalpas, and even a necklace of lotus fibers acts like a heavy burden.

Abstention from food, total withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects, the fixing of the eyes upon the tip of the nose, that which is one-pointedness of mind, this silence, and this entire universe appearing as a void—if you possess all these, tell me, friend: are you a yoginī, or are you a woman separated from her beloved?

"My child, these are not clouds; they are the elephants of the Lord of the Gods. These are not cranes; they are the earrings on their temples. These are not flashes of lightning; this is golden ornamentation upon the frontal globes of their heads. This is not water falling from the sky; it is ichor shaken by the wind of their breath. So why, O simple girl, do you vainly soil your face with tears of rain, thinking it is the monsoon?
"O friend, for a moment spread a couch with leaves fallen from the celestial trees—leaves dripping with drops of nectar—and make the moon your pillow."
If not, then like wood consumed by a fire whose fierce rows of flames expand through the sprinkling of the essence of affection, this fire of passion will not cease burning my limbs.
Since he has gone to the very state of the Sugata, he would bring about for me alone a state of being without support;
O friend, what else can be said? Your beloved is momentary, selfless, and utterly empty—he is indeed to be saluted.
The full surface of the cheeks of this large-eyed woman, wet with tears for her beloved who has passed away, and her lotus-face turned grey,
resemble moist fuel drenched with the juices dripping from a half-burnt throat and followed by particles of ash.
"This is a continuous downpour of lightning, this is a burning hailstone, and this is that thunder, and this is that swarm of frogs echoing with their cries"—
with such thoughts, the slender-bodied woman, fallen into the power of death, repeatedly fans the fire of passion spread through every limb by the heaving of her heavy sighs.
Wilted on both sides from contact with her full breasts and hips, yet remaining green in the center because it has not reached the middle of her body;
this bed of lotus leaves, its arrangement disordered by the tossing and turning of her slackened vine-like arms, speaks of the torment of the slender-limbed woman.

The intense passion of my mind, spreading and incessantly agitating, torments me like a smokeless fire fanned into a blaze; like a severe fever, it strikes every limb. Neither my father, nor my mother, nor you, O lady, are able to protect me from this. (VidŚrk 22.11)
The fever of her separation cannot be tested by the touch of palms even by those who are affectionate, for fear of being burned; it is a fire that cooks its own vessel.
While all efforts with sandalwood and medicinal herbs have been rendered powerless, these jewels of every necklace burst forth in a marvelous crackling like parched grain.

That your face is pale as a ripened palm leaf, that there is a storm of tears in your eyes, and that this cheek bears the imprint of five fingers from being rubbed by your hand—if all this exists yet no young man dwells in your heart, may Gaurī be angry; fie, fie on you, who conceal even your childhood friend from the world!

"O King Śekhara, he who has made his bracelets into armlets, whose mass of dangling curls is tucked behind his ear, and who stands before you on the path with palms joined in salutation—he asks after your welfare. Just as he had finished saying this much, the woman, her neck bent low in shame at the thought "It is he indeed," was pierced by all manner of aesthetic sentiments (rasas). (VidSrk 22.14)
O wretched moon, do not touch even the outline of her body, which is crackling with the great heat of separation from her beloved—even in play!
For here, your rays, as delicate as the stalks of young lotus fibers, suffer the pain of scorching as they roll upon it.

That great frailty in your body, that total lack of desire for anything, that nose fixed on its tip, those eyes, and that absolute silence—this state of yours tells me that your mind is dependent on one alone. Tell me, O fair-faced one, who is this one: is it Brahmā or is it your beloved?

This auspicious lady of Lakṣmīdhara’s—her limbs exceedingly emaciated, as beautiful as the core of a fresh plantain tree, like the form of the moon remaining as a mere crescent—is a festival for the eyes; yet, having fallen into this state, distressed by the fierce burning of the fire of love, she delights our mind and makes it tremble. (VidSrk_22.17) (716)

"O Sleep, may it be well with you; O Consciousness, are you at ease? O Friend, is it well with you, O Tranquility? Have you not all gone together with my beloved? Moreover, as he set out today for his union with his beloved, was our attendant—who is compassionate toward those in distress—not seen, having fainted and thus forgotten all pain? (VidŚrk 22.18)
Having first sat upon the center of the lotus, then gone to the space between the doors, and finally somehow emerged into the courtyard—yet her beloved was not seen—"O crow!
O royal swan! O parrot! O mynah! Tell me, what news? Thus the tear-choked words of the fawn-eyed woman prevail. (VidSrk 22.19)
Upon Citrāṅgada’s body, pale as a slightly crushed turmeric knot, there manifests this certain paleness born of separation;
for when it prevails, the limbs of the deer-eyed woman are fashioned together with her gold, as if silver were being rolled into it.
When Rājaśekhara’s beloved had departed, my heart departed; sleep went away along with consciousness.
O shameless life, have you not heard that the path is the same as that which the great man has taken?

Tears in the eyes instead of collyrium, the face resting in the palm instead of a play-lotus, paleness on the cheek instead of decorative leaf-designs, and sighs from the mouth instead of smiles— O charming girl, since your body is thus distressed by the union of separation, which man has been led by the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāma) to the state of grace? (Dharmakīrti, Vidagdhamukhamandana 22.22)

O goddess like a royal swan in a forest of passion-lotuses, why has this eye of yours lost its luster? Why are your cheeks devoid of the decorative patterns of cosmetics? Why are you so emaciated, so listless, and so stained with impurity?
This longing for Viṣṇu, the Enemy of Mura, comes upon me; my mind reckons his virtues and not his faults; sleep does not come;
the night slips away; my hope for union does not diminish; and my body grows thin, yet my passion does not. (VidSrk 22.24)
"O friend, I am this one made of iron, while that lover of mine is a cruel stone;
know that among attractors, liquefiers, and kissers, he is not even one of those—he is a magnetizer. (VidSrk 22.25)
This state of my body is but a boat upon the ocean of sound; there is no transgression of the limit you have set, nor are there grounds for reproach in your failure to act.
O friend, you need only ask Śiva: "Has he not come within your range? And has the mango tree not blossomed with buds stirred by the Malaya breezes? (VidSrk 22.26)

Vākūṭā lies awake, even in her dreams, longing for union with her beloved; sleep does not come to her. If she wishes to paint him in a picture, her co-wives break out in sweat. Or if this innocent girl begins to speak of his virtues, anger acts as a bolt upon her speech. Generally, that which is hoped for is accomplished through the turning power of auspicious days.
O Mother, the row of cranes—the single pearl-string upon the heart of the sky’s beauty, daughter of the Sun—please speak with great respect to that person:
"Having cast off this body, which has become as withered as a garland and is difficult to bear, I shall find happiness; I cannot endure the intense agony of separation. (VidSrk 22.28)

Having gazed along the path of her beloved as far as the range of her vision, the weary traveler’s wife—now that the roads had grown still at day’s end and darkness was creeping forth—placed one foot toward the whitewashed house; yet at that very moment, thinking "he has not arrived," she looked back again with her neck turned sharply and raised.

The sighs of Siddhoka have become rhythmic dances; his hand-palms are numb, the surface of his cheeks is parched, and his eyes are rippled with tears. His throat has matured into the sweet fifth note (*pañcama*), and the beauty that once brought forth the first-fruits of loveliness in his limbs has been reduced to mere talk by a paleness appropriate to his separation.
O Rājaśekhara, favor the female cakora birds by bestowing the moonlight of your smile; let the five-arrowed god of love remember his bow through the play of your eyebrows.
Delight the quarters with your lotus-eyes slightly blossoming; O charming girl, may these particular graces take their place in the hearts of the fortunate.
Why is Aparājitārakṣitā’s braid so disheveled? Why are her eyes devoid of collyrium? Why is there no musk-paste applied to her cheeks in the form of leaf-designs?
And why, O moon-faced one, does this entire array of ornaments, placed in the hands of your friends, grow weary from not being remembered by you?
"Time and again you are indeed a liar; what is the use of your words? Go away!"—so saying in anger, she raises her very slender creeper-like arm.
As the crow wanders through the village, its throat adorned by bracelets slipped from that arm, it reveals the emaciation of the slender-limbed woman, which is so fitting for separation from you.

O long-eyed girl, with a stream of teardrops clinging to the tips of your lashes—drops that rival pearls—you create a necklace of ornaments upon your heart, as white as Shiva’s laughter; resting your face upon your hand, which is as beautiful as an ornament of young lotus stalks, O young maiden, who is this fortunate man being remembered by you?

In separation, he burns my limbs; in union, he arouses jealousy; when seen, he steals my heart; when touched, he renders my body helpless. When he arrives or departs, not even a moment’s happiness can be found. What more is there to say? That, despite this, he remains my beloved—how wondrous! *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 22.35. (734)
"Tell me, O fortunate one, who is that blessed man whose skeleton lies there, its bones jingling as they strike against the splashing waters of the Gaṅgā and Sarayū?
O fair-faced one, for her as she meditates upon him, incessant tears—dripping with the moisture of collyrium—wash away the decorative patterns painted upon her jar-like breasts."

O Lord, this separation from you has come upon me as the fruit of that act: when, out of curiosity, I made a female swan on the lotus-pond of my palace appear red-hued by scattering saffron—of which only the powder remained—upon its hand-like stalk, causing it to suffer a moment’s separation from its mate under the delusion that it was a ruddy sheldrake.

O slender-limbed one, why are these drops of tear-water being scattered in fragments upon the slope of your breasts, which ripple with the tremors of your sighs and are darkened by washed-away collyrium?
And why do these *hūṃ* sounds—crooked by the obstruction of your constricted throat, dripping nectar into the ears, and resonant with the sweet fifth note—break off as they emerge?
"Now, O friend, is it that the sun, surrounded by intense rays as if burning, rises in the night—this is a wonder to me?
Or is this the moon, O simple one, that manifests heat toward me? O child, what here does not become inverted for those who are without a protector?"
O Fire, do not release your rays; O Moon, let my life-breaths remain for a moment; O Sleep, close my eyes; O Night, become long, exceedingly long!
When I have joyfully embraced my beloved, found in a dream-union, you will once again experience the bitter taste of your own restless activity.
May that five-arrowed god grant you happiness, O friend—he who was drawn by you as your lord standing visibly before your eyes;
he whose fingers trembled as they formed the graceful lines upon his body, his bow, and his fish-shaped emblem.
When her friends asked, "Why do you wither like a crushed *mālatī* flower? the bashful young woman, though clearly distressed by the separation, did not speak aloud;
she merely suppressed the flood of tears in her eyes and somehow managed to gaze at the mango tree in the courtyard, its tips just beginning to break into buds.
With eyes slightly heavy and reddened from the flow of tears, the gaze somewhat languid; with the luster of her lips distressed by hot sighs and her locks disheveled over her brow;
pale across the surface of her cheeks which rest motionlessly upon her sprout-like hands—O innocent one, whose ripened fruit of asceticism is this state of yours? VidSrk_22.43 (742)

By whom was the conquest of the world achieved for Yaśovarman? Who is the virtuous man? Who is the master of the arts? And by whom has sincere devotion been directed toward the feet of the God of Love—that you, O fair-limbed one, by meditating upon him, bear a pallor fashioned from the mass of ashes rising from the many-flaming fire of Kandarpa? VidSrk_22.44 *(743) //
This bed of fresh lotus leaves should be burned by the spreading rays of her fevered limbs; what is the use of waving palm-leaf fans?
Let sandalwood water remain right there—it burns my eyes like the moon. O friends, this mental anguish is perverse, acting like a fire that uses water as its fuel.
She trembles at Abhinanda’s palace, abandons the garden, loathes the moonlight, fears the doorway, and considers her residence— a hall for painted pastimes— to be poison;
she remains only upon a bed spread with lotus shoots, her heart dependent on the nectar of your form brought to her by her own imagination.

At first, the streams of tears from this lotus-eyed woman emerge with trembling surfaces; then they become slightly swollen, and finally, with drops coalesced at their tips, they flow forth in a spreading cascade. Thus, by their own weight, these currents of tears perfectly manifest the anguish within her heart.
I believe that the Bodiless One, having released his five flower-arrows with blunted tips, now strikes the charming girl forcibly with a feathered shaft of water;
for otherwise, how could the flood of water, discharged from the mouths of the channels of her wide-open eyes into the forest of her three folds, attain the likeness of a flowing stream?

"O Rājaśekhara, you do not open your eyes to look at your friends; though addressed, you give no answer; you do not perceive that 'this is such,' nor that 'it is not such'; you have fallen into this vacant state. This bed is but a cage of visible skeletons, yet it is slightly moistened by life. What do you wish to do, letting go so little? Bestow your love upon one who has gone to another land. (VidSrk 22.49)
Was she struck by wind? No. Is she not afflicted by the great elements? No. Is she not delirious? No. Is she not shrouded by a wave of *saṃnipāta* fever?
No. Why then does she weep, faint, and gasp, yet bear a smiling face? Shall I say it? King Bhoja has been seen by her as an enemy without cause. (VidSrk 22.50)

Her breasts tremble at the sight of her lover; her cheek falls upon the palm of her hand; her sighs cause her straight locks of hair to dance wildly; and her tears repeatedly veil the power of her eyes. O friend, this display tells you something that dwells within your heart.
You do not abandon the bed of Narasiṃha; you do not look at your own condition; you do not straighten your hair, which is tied in a tangled knot.
O friend, do something at least that accords with the maintenance of your body; for never before have I seen a hundred women in separation like this.

*Colo iti virahiṇīvrajyā* // 22. Then follows the section on those separated from their lovers: "The gait is sluggish, the gaze is vacant, the body lacks its usual grace, and the sighing is excessive; but what could this be, or what else could it be?"
The command of Kandarpa wanders through the world, youth is subject to transformation, and those various graceful and sweet emotions cast away all steadfastness. (VidSrk 23.1) *(752)
Again and again, a flood of tears obstructs the emergence of my vision; my body reaches a state of numbness and paralysis from the exhaustion of longing for him.
This hand of mine, immediately perspiring with fingers trembling from incessant shaking, utterly fails in the task of drawing his portrait—what am I to do? (VidSrk 23.2)

O Wind, you who are filled with the fragrance of the thick nectar trickling from the hollows of the *kunda* buds, which are formidable with their opening blossoms—embrace that woman of curved limbs whose eyes are slightly trembling, and touch every limb of mine. (VidSrk 23.3)
The heart breaks with intense anguish, yet it does not split in two; the failing body bears delusion, yet it does not lose consciousness;
an internal burning consumes the frame, yet it does not reduce it to ashes; fate strikes at the vital organs, yet it does not cut short life. (VidSrk 23.4)
You do not eat green sprouts anywhere, nor do you seek stability; with eyes agitated, you gaze toward the quarters while crying out piteously.
O deer, you have been separated from your beloved by fate; why then do you wander for so long, from mountain to mountain, from valley to valley, from river to river, and from desert to desert?
Quickly strike the Malaya breeze on all sides with blows from *muñja* grass; O winds, place a heavy chain around its neck with repeated force!
Cast the King of Ragas, Pañcama, swiftly into prison, and grind the moon to powder upon a stone slab until it is reduced to dust!

When shall we behold the fawn-eyed one, her limbs entwined with modesty yet loosened by the command of passion, her body adorned with nail-marks like thin streaks of spreading madder, her thick thighs heaving like the mouth of a treasure-chest left unsealed as her silk garment slips away? Ah, when indeed shall we see it? (VidSrk 23.7)
These mango trees, too, are smoky with their dense swarms of bees; these aśoka trees are ablaze with the bursting forth of their bright new shoots;
even these kiṃśuka branches are turned to glowing coals by their dark buds. Alas! Where can I rest my eyes? Everywhere fate is adverse.

The swelling of a tumor, the thinness of one afflicted by disease, the blood from a wound, and the flow of saliva from a bite—none of these are present here; this is merely a poor traveler who has died. Ah, it is understood! By the honey-greedy bees raising a clamor, a reckless gaze must surely have been cast upon the mango bud.
O mind, do not slay the heart of this slender-limbed woman with your inwardly sharpened arrows that are like thunderbolts, as you have slain mine;
and O moon, surely do not release your merciless rays, which are like flaming torches, upon her who is as tender as a kandalī flower.

O Sleep, cruel one, why have you ceased? For my face withers from being denied the drinking of her nectar-lip through a kiss, and my hand hates itself for being prevented from wandering over her hips by the seizing of her hair; until at last, my limbs—having long since diminished her resentment—may sport upon every limb of hers in succession. (Rājaśekhara 23.11)
I know that for Abhinanda, she is utterly non-existent like a blossom on a sky-flower, and the pleasures of union with her are most unreal, like the fragrance arising from that very flower.
She was shown to me merely by a dream, like an enemy’s magical illusion; yet even so, my mind, filled with longing to embrace her, suffers in its distress.

By the power of fate, I have obtained this upper garment of the deer-eyed woman: it was the stake in the game of the Supreme Lord; the noose around her neck during their amorous play; the fan that dispels the fatigue of lovemaking at its conclusion; and [the veil] used in the midnight quarrels upon the bed. (VidSrk 23.13)
Though he knows that his beloved is separated from him by hundreds of lands, rivers, mountains, and forests, and thus cannot come within the range of his vision even with effort,

the traveler nevertheless stands with neck outstretched, one foot half-planted on the ground, and with eyes filled with tears; meditating on her in some inexplicable way, he gazes longingly toward that direction.

By that eye of Śrī Harṣa, which was agitated by the mature flavor of passion, cast down, turned aside, rolling, tender, delightful, and blinded by intoxication as it wandered on the road, we have come to this state;
our intellect is such, our consciousness is of this kind, our torment is this, our body is like this, and our condition is such—this is the report concerning her as well. (VidSrk 23.15)
This very same region of Vallana, like a lake whose lotus groves have been cut down, spreads inner torment; like the sky when the moon has vanished,
it now brings about a feverish pain of burning, more cruel than the heat of summer— alas, this very same winter season, during the separation from the slender-limbed one!
If we were created by Him, then what of this fawn-eyed woman? If she is He, then what of this spring?
And let that mango tree indeed exist as the rival of the world; why was it fashioned by the Creator?
Those arrows are said to consist of mango buds; that bow is said to be made of flowers; and Kāma himself is said to have been consumed by the flame of the eye-fire of the enraged Tryambaka.
What can we say? For even we have been pierced by this wretched one with arrows whose feathers do not even reach the shafts, yet such pain does not arise from a mere display of such equipment.
You are enamored of Vīryamitra’s red new shoots, and I too am devoted to my beloved’s praiseworthy virtues; bees released from the bow of Smara come to you, and likewise they come to me.
A blow from the foot of a lovely woman brings you joy, and it is true that it brings joy to me as well; O Aśoka, everything is equal for us both, yet the Creator has made me alone to be sorrowful.

These five arrows, with their very tips reaching to the feathers, have sunk simultaneously into my heart; by them, along with those very arrows, this body of mine has been consumed by the fire of separation.
Alas, O Kāma! You are now weaponless; you can no longer conquer people, for I alone shall be miserable while the entire world lives in happiness.
If the moon were to become a literal pool of nectar-essence belonging to Rājaśekhara, and if its spot were a forest of blooming blue lotuses, then perhaps,
with my limbs rendered cool by the sport of bathing therein, I might one day escape the torment inflicted by the fire of love. (VidSrk 23.21)
If Rājaśekhara’s form is emaciated day by day, if tears are in his eyes, if the face of a doe-eyed woman is on his ear with the thought of it being an ornament,
and if this is whispered into our ears by someone— then we desire the burden of separation to be replaced by union while dwelling in one place. (VidSrk 23.22)
O Vallaṇa, for those like me, both these qualities of yours appear contrary to their true nature: your status as one whose arrows are flowers, and the moon’s possession of cool rays.
For the moon emits fire from the tips of its rays that contain frost within, while you too turn your flower-arrows into the essence of thunderbolts.

May I behold once more that face of hers—the auspicious abode of the God of Love—which, when it descends within the path of vision, brings forth delight and spreads a supreme abundance of joys in the heart of Kālidāsa; a festival for the eyes which seems fashioned from the very essence gathered from the rising of the crescent moon. (VidŚrk 23.24)

The bow of the Mind-born God discharges arrows aloft with the humming of bees; the moon scatters rays that resemble fire; yet these have been surpassed by the splendor of her frown, her worshipful face, and the beauty of her loveliness. I know not what these, filled with wrath, will do to this deer-eyed woman.
For Śāntākaragupta as well, might that day ever come when my gaze, like a female bee, shall drink the honey from the blossoming lotus-face of my beloved;

and thereafter, may I too experience the union of limbs—those very limbs which serve as companions to love-making and are rendered playful through a sequence of soft and tender conversation? (VidSrk 23.26) [777]
The author of the *Vārttika* lowers his face with its long locks, yet this moon hates me and will not release its speech; the cuckoos, with their melodious notes, obstruct me;
she does not knit her brows, yet Love, with bow held firm, crushes me. Who indeed, upon seeing that frail woman, would not suddenly fall into distress? (VidSrk 23.27)
"O Bāṇa, withdraw your arrows; O bow-creeper, let go of your string! Your target is Tryambaka; who indeed am I here, whose mind is like a delicate *śirīṣa* bud?
Therefore, out of compassion for this submissive person, show mercy, O Lord Manmatha, and once again grant such a wondrous dream."
We, who take delight in the practice of the Supreme Person through discernment, somehow pass our days even when struck by the arrows of Rati’s lover;
but alas, we do not know how these days pass for my beloved, whose body is distressed by this fresh separation due to her youth. (VidŚrk 23.29) [780]

When shall that pure face of the deer-eyed one be seen—its speech faltering with playful charm, the petals of its ear-lotuses fallen away, moistened by the sweat of exhaustion, eyes languid from the cessation of love-play, and made beautiful by rows of curls straightened by the sport of pulling her hair? *VidSrk_23.30* (781)
The forest is empty as if of me; the waters have reached a state of thinness as if they were we;
and the days are long and scorching as if they were our own sighs.
She is as if dissolved, as if reflected, as if painted, as if carved in form, as if inlaid, as if fashioned from adamantine cement, and as if deeply engraved within.
That beloved is fixed within my heart as if nailed there by the five arrows of the god of love, or as if tightly sewn by the web of threads from the continuous strands of my anxious thoughts.
If that maiden were a pond, with her eyes as blue lotuses, her face a lotus, the waves of her creeper-like brows, and her pair of arms as lotus stalks;
then, with my limbs numbed by plunging into the water of her beauty, I might escape these peerless, life-cutting agonies that emit a mass of flames from the fire of Love.

"Where is the striker—the bodiless one with a bow of flowers and but few arrows—and where is the mind, which is fickle, subtle, concealed, and formless?"—this manifest inconsistency that has arisen in my mind is pacified by the experience of the emergence of pain. (VidSrk 23.34)

I repeatedly recall her half-glances as she was unable to say anything appropriate to the Venerable Tathāgata, due to a succession of internal, heavy indignations; her breasts heaved as she uttered indistinct *hūṃ* sounds. (VidSrk 23.35) [786]

Today I remember how, as she sighed with her lips trembling and her intended words failing their purpose because the meaning of the syllables was not clear, she wiped her eyes with the hem of her garment and said something— or rather, said it over and over again.

I remember that young girl, whose face bears the mark of the young moon; she is like a cluster of blossoms on the Madana tree that has sprouted from the ashes of its burning, like a lotus risen from a bed of loveliness, and as if fashioned from the nectar dripping from the orb of the cool-rayed moon. (VidSrk 23.37)
Resounding with the *hūṃkāra* sounds of bees, smiling as they regurgitate honey, and appearing like the very bow of the Fish-bannered God (Kāma) discharged in victory,
the mango sprouts— nestled one upon another— gaze at separated lovers through the tremulous pupils of their eyelashes.
If that fawn-eyed woman does not exist, what is the point of speaking of others?
If there is no digit of the moon in the sky, how many stars can there be?
Above is a thick mass of clouds, and my beloved is far away; thus has this calamity befallen me.
While the divine medicinal herbs grow upon the Himalayas, a serpent, seized by anger, rests upon my head.
With my face turned upward, I gaze at the sky shrouded by fresh rain-clouds.
The traveler seems to transfer that flood of water into his own eyes.

Victorious one! Those are your shanks, that is your hip, that is your belly, those are your breasts, that is your smile, that is your eloquent speech, that is the pair of lotus-eyes, and that is the mass of your braided hair.
And that face of that fawn-eyed woman, raining down drops of the nectar of loveliness—thus meditating upon this one thing alone again and again, we remain just so.
O charming girl, if the moon has been forcibly eclipsed by your face, why does this merciless one thus show malice toward me?
For while it gladdens the entire world with showers of nectar-like rays, it inflames me with these beams that are harsh like flashes of fire.

The glances of that fair-eyed woman—glances which possess the overflowing nectar of a smile from the Supreme Lord whose eyebrows dance in play; which are dense with the luster of blooming blue lotuses and beautiful with slightly curved rows of lashes;
and which are moist with love and tremble with a multitude of sidelong looks—reach the path of memory for that separated lover and spread deep sorrow.

Flashing with rays that quiver most tremulously at their tips, those barbed arrows of sidelong glances—smooth yet harsh—which she released after repeatedly deceiving her eyes with skill, have cut my heart again and again; by those merciless shafts, my heart is being torn even now.
"O, bring the dark luster of the Supreme Lord's consort [Śyāmā] here with thick brushes of ink! Having employed the ritual procedure and the mantra, take away the smile of the white lotuses!
And grind the moon into powder in an instant by reducing it to fragments upon a stone slab, so that I may behold the ten directions marked with the seal of her face. (VidSrk 23.46)
When that Smara, the five-arrowed one, had been reduced to ashes by the Lord Bharga, I know that the Lotus-born Brahmā fashioned another Kāma with inexhaustible arrows;
for by these shafts of his, which are plunged from here and there into my very marrow to their feathers, my mind has become like a bursting kadamba bud.
Born from the ocean of milk, you share a brotherly affection with the Lord’s Śrīkaustubha gem; your rays are like those in beds of night-lotuses, and you scatter streams of nectar.
You even vie with the lotus-faces of deer-eyed women. O Moon, crest-jewel of Śiva, why then do you pour upon me these agonizing, flame-spewing pains?
O cakora birds, drink up the entire water of the moonlight with your beaks flickering as they are straightened by the upward-thrusting of your necks;
for it is by means of this that the deer-marked moon becomes impoverished of its splendor, serving as the cause for saving the lives of those distressed by separation.
These two [verses] are by Rājaśekhara. (VidSrk 23.49) (800)

The moon has poison in its belly; sandalwood is the playground of hooded serpents; pearl necklaces are clouds of salty water; and the lotus, the dear friend of the sun—alas, what indeed can these do to extinguish the fire of love? For we, having abandoned the truth, have been deceived by the delusion of external appearances.
The breezes from the fans increase this succession of sighs; the sandalwood paste is capable of expanding this flow of tears;
the bed of flowers assists the arrows of Love. How, indeed, will the torment of the God of Love, whose blackness is doubled, ever cease?
For Rājaśekhara, there are these pearl necklaces, beds moist with water, lotus petals, and breezes from the snowy mountains that shed droplets of frost;
even when his fuel consists of fresh sandalwood, how shall that fire of love ever be extinguished?
Surely Madana, having grown indifferent toward his delicate flower-arrows, now wields the wind as his weapon;
for otherwise, how could these sighs, straight as the finest strands of a necklace, escape through the edges of her silken garment?
It is better indeed never to have experienced love than to have it arise and then be shattered;
for one whose eyes have been plucked out suffers in a way that one born blind does not.
O Lord, be gracious in a dream and show me my beloved once more, even if only for a moment.
Once she has seen me clinging to her with my arms firmly entwined around her, she either leads me right there or does not go at all.

"O neighbor, will you grant me a moment's glance even here in my house? For likely the child’s father will drink nothing but these tasteless waters from the well today. "Alas! [she replies]. Thus begins the section on those separated by lovers, followed by the section on unchaste women.
It would be better for me to go from here alone toward that stream thick with *tamāla* trees; let the dense, reed-like knots of the riverbanks carve into my breasts like the cuts of a saw.

O Bhadra, I know that the leaves of those vine-bowers on the banks of the daughter of Kalinda— companions to the dalliances of the cowherd women, witnesses to the secret trysts of Rādhā— are now turning old and their dark luster fading, since the practice of preparing couches for amorous play has been interrupted. Vidyaśataka 24.2 (808)

O Muralā, tell me, by whom were these *nicula* trees created— trees with sandy banks, providing dense shade, serving as playful dwellings for cool breezes that linger at their edges, where water-rats chirp, and which bestow upon women an unceasing expenditure of love?
O traveler, abandon your leisurely pace and set out immediately; the forest ahead is utterly terrifying with elephants, boars, serpents, and gavayas.
Even the rays of the sun have grown faint in every direction; you alone are young, there is no place for you in my house, and I am but a single girl.
"O travelers, rest here for a moment under the cool shade of this tree and then proceed;
beyond this point, the path is without trees or water and is difficult to traverse due to its uneven rocks.

"Here lies my mother, an old woman; here is my father, the foremost among those advanced in years; and here is the servant-girl Kumbhadāsī, her body weakened by the exhaustion of all the household chores."
"In this [city], I am a sinful woman alone, whose lord of life has been away for several days"—thus did the young woman speak her desire to the traveler, under the pretext of these words.

Only those know true happiness who, by chance, find themselves unexpectedly in a deserted place and are kissed most tenderly by a lotus-eyed woman— she who is helpless with passion, whose refusal is charmingly feigned, and whose eyes dart repeatedly in every direction out of fear.

Free from conversation, devoid of any exchange of various arts, with the edge of her silk garment slipping as he began to touch her hand, Ahalyā and Indra’s union became as if momentary—trembling repeatedly and casting glances in every direction. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 24.8 (814).

He who took my maidenhood is indeed that same bridegroom of the Lord of Yoga; those nights filled with moonlight are the very ones fragrant with blossoming new jasmine; and those breezes from the Vindhya mountains are the same.

And yet, I am still this very same person. Nevertheless, why does my heart long for the groves of cane-reeds on the riverbank—those places where one can enjoy the playful arts of love with steadfast composure?
"Where are you going, O girl with thighs like an elephant's trunk, in the thick of the night, where dwells my beloved who is dearer to me than life?
Tell me, young girl, how is it that you do not fear being alone? Surely Madana, with his feathered arrows, is your companion."
