"Which auspicious lunar day is attained by the fortunate, wherein the enemy moon does not rise?"—as if lamenting thus repeatedly with distress, the cuckoo cried out "Kuhū! Kuhū! (the name of the new moon day). (VidSrk 24.11)
"Mother, housewife, if this parrot whose mate has been killed is to be raised by me, then have a sturdy iron cage made for this ill-behaved creature.
For today, while I was dragging him from his hiding place in the hollow of a jujube thicket toward a fierce serpent, my very fingernails have become stained with blood. (Vidūṣaka 24.12)

"By whom was the ointment on your pair of breasts destroyed? By whom was the collyrium in your eyes removed? By whom was the red dye on your lower lip rubbed away? By whom were the garlands from your hair taken?

"O friend, by Kṛṣṇa—the son of the Yamunā, who steals the sins of the entire multitude of people and possesses the luster of a blue lotus—was it not done? For your passion for Kṛṣṇa [has been washed away] by his water. VidSrk_24.13 (819)

"O girl, he who first pulls my mass of hair with a firm grip, presses his face against my face, clings to my neck, again embraces my breasts with a tight bodily contact, and, fixed in attachment, falls upon my hips and then at my feet—such is my beloved. O crooked one, shame is utterly destroyed; indeed, it is not so, for what cause for shame is there in a bodice? "With its fragrant scent, mixed with honey, greyish-white, and falling before me in a restless, wandering motion..."
"O friend, I have been exhausted by that intoxicated lover at the close of day; for what indeed has not been done by the *kesara* tree? (Vidśrk 24.15)

When a traveler lay down on the grassy ground within a lotus pond, spreading out his garment's hem, you were exhausted and I too had traveled the road; the village for lodging was not yet reached, nor did the time of day pass away.
With our thighs slightly uncovered as we lay alone, our knees and bellies pressed together in an awkward, doubled-over position with our garments slipping off—what indeed is this?
Where the moon of Vallaṇa is not disparaged, where the sweet words of a messenger are not heard, where conversations clouded by tears do not fall, and where the body does not undergo emaciation—
where one sleeps embracing one's own submissive wife who is under one's control— is that love? This is merely the painful observance of the householder’s vow.
Casting a glance from her face that is clear with affection toward Lakṣmīdhara, she is filled with apprehension; she embraces him tightly around the neck while her breasts tremble;
though held back with effort, she repeatedly says, "I am going"—oh, how much more does the passionate woman delight him even as she stands at the trysting place!
When the husband has gone abroad, there is supreme pleasure for the woman fickle of hip, while the city streets are deserted by the wind of a stormy midnight— thus says Śrī Harṣa. (VidSrk 24.19)
Thinking, "The path is muddy, the darkness is thick with rain, and movement is silent; today, O innocent one, you must go to the dwelling of my beloved," she takes this to heart.
With her anklets removed as far as her knees and her eyes firmly covered by her palms, she practices the path in her own home, having attained her footing only with great difficulty.

Bearing fresh nail-marks upon her hips—on no other part of her body out of fear—and possessing eyes languid with sleep, reddened by kissing yet free from wounds, she indicates her rendezvous with her lover nearby by a sign of the brow; thus this widow, a unique wish-fulfilling creeper for the libertine, attains success, for she cannot be won without merit.

O traveler, did you not see him today? Having heard that his own mother had gone far away this morning in a fit of causeless anger, the householder went from here at midday to bring her back. With a body worn out by lameness and decrepitude, he was likely seen by you; O traveler, stay for a moment and tell me.

Having fastened their girdle-jewels and secured their anklets—which had slipped from beneath their garments—with the hem of their tightly drawn upper cloths, these fawn-eyed women set out for their secret trysts;
alas, on the road they were clearly distressed by the humming of swarms of bees, agitated by the fragrance of the jasmine flowers in their tresses.
This husband is difficult to deceive; the moon is dim; the path is treacherous; people are looking for faults; and the words of a lover are hard to resist.
Therefore, a certain slender woman, in order to reach the place of assignation arranged for love, went out from her house again and again, and then entered it once more.

The paths of the moonstone pavements—moist with droplets of light from the rising nectar-rayed moon and bearing the thick lac-dye of frequent footsteps—reveal at every step the backward glances of immodest women; these glances cause the startled cakora birds to fly up suddenly, as if they were apprehensive.
With their bodies smeared with sandalwood paste, adorned with fresh strings of pearls, their faces radiant with exceptionally white ivory ear-ornaments, and clad in beautiful, spotless garments,
the *abhisārikās*— fearless and having reached invisibility as the moon spreads its light and whitens the earth— proceed happily indeed to the dwellings of their lovers. (Vidvadbhañjikā 24.26,
Bāṇa)
In the darkness of night, these utterly innocent women, having set out for secret trysts, curse their friends here;
stumbling on the path, alas, they long to embrace the torrents of water from the clouds. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 24.27) — by Puruṣottama.

Having silenced her anklets on her feet, bound the jewels of her girdle which produced a tumultuous sound, and while her attendants were somewhat drowsy—just as she was about to set out, whom can you be angry with? For, impelled by fate, the moon has risen, stealing away the splendor of the jar-like breasts of the Kashmiri women.
A pearl necklace with a central gem is placed upon your breast, a tinkling girdle is fastened around your hips, and your feet bear jingling jeweled anklets;
thus, O charming girl, you set out as if to meet your beloved amidst the beating of drums—why then do you look repeatedly toward the quarters of the sky, trembling with fear?

As if with the consent of Devagupta to bring him back, women going to meet their lovers— darkened by the mass of shadows in every direction, casting their glances about, their beauty sprouting like collyrium,
and veiled in black cloths with the hue of smoke from the fire of passion— set out toward their beloveds with limbs whose ornaments made no sound.
By Bhaṭṭa Śivasvāmin.
Thus ends the section on unchaste women;
next follows the section on the reproach of female messengers.

The sandalwood paste has vanished entirely from the slope of your breasts; the luster has departed from your lower lip; your eyes are completely devoid of collyrium; and your body is dripping with drops of water.

O messenger who shatters my hopes, you have gone from here to bathe in the pond—having failed to realize the arrival of this suffering for your kinsmen—but certainly not to the presence of that base man.
"Why do you conceal your breasts and face with your hand, O messenger? For the lips of heroes and their breasts shine all the more when they are wounded. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 25.2 (838)
"Excellent, messenger! Excellent again! What more could be done than this, that you have clung to me even with your teeth and your nails? (VidSrk 25.3)
Your dwelling is in the region of your throat, your eyes are dyed saffron, and your lips are free from passion; O messenger, have you perhaps become a female renunciant?
Messenger, what is the use of that sinner who transgresses the scriptures, by whom you—the sixth among the five five-nailed animals that may be eaten—have been devoured? (VidSrk 25.5)
"Since he could not be brought under control by either conciliation or bribery, it was well that you, despite the display of dissension, inflicted punishment upon this ill-behaved man. (VidŚrk 25.6)
O messenger, by this lower [man] who is free from passion, like a Buddha, emptiness has been declared to you without artifice regarding all things. (VidSrk 25.7)
O messenger, with your two sides wounded by blows and your lower lip torn by sores,
you are fit for battle, not fit for the work of a messenger.
O messenger, the deed you have performed is difficult for anyone else to achieve:
he who sought out our vulnerabilities and was intent on destroying those who had sought refuge has been struck down. (VidSrk 25.9)
Your body is emaciated, your gait is weary, the pupils of your eyes are sunken, your speech is indistinct, and your garment is loose; O messenger, why are you feverish?
On another night, during a change of lovers, my garment—which was improper [for me]—was somehow taken by that friend of yours;
how is it, O messenger, that you, so skilled in providing remedies for such lapses, have now brought this back to me with affection by giving me your own clothing? VidSrk_25.11 (847)
O messenger, if my beloved did not come even after making such an oath, why then was your lower lip bitten by your own teeth in your anger?
Abandoning this trembling that sheds drops of perspiration, regain your composure; for who, O friend, can know the inner heart of a person whose nature is crooked?
"You bear horripilation, you breathe incessantly, you have resorted to some kind of meditation; your gaze wanders, trembling and unsteady, and your sighing is manifest.
O messenger, having encountered that man skilled in the arts of love like a harlot, are you feverish? Or rather, calamities arise from touching what is sinful. (VidSrk 25.13)

"Why is your breath so hurried? Why are you trembling with horripilation? Why have you come to propitiate me? Why does your braid fall as you prostrate at my feet? Why are you so emaciated?"—O messenger, with such words, what will you say when your face is wet with sweat from the heat of the sun, your lower garment has slipped from its position, and your own lip steals the luster of a withered lotus? (VidSrk 25.14)
"O messenger,
my mind has been agitated by you— lowly yet exalted, and tormented by a lover— as the ocean is by Mount Mandara.

(VidSrk 25.15) It was not considered whether, as a messenger, you have suffered the defeat of passion because you have approached with true sincerity and equal affection, or because you are the wife of another.
O messenger, do not go again even in a dream to the abode of that man who has lost all virtue, by whom the pallor of your lotus-like face was brought about.
O messenger, by you who always maintain your activity for my sake with the thought that it is your own business,
this doctrine that our bodies are one has been demonstrated through the very result.
Of Vittoka.
Thus ends the section concerning the reproach of the female messenger;
next follows the section on the lamp.

When the wind is stilled and darkness is dispelled, its power of light blossoming through the force of auspiciousness, why should the lamp not attain extinction upon seeing the lover—who, during the nights, is agitated by the impact of Cupid’s arrows as he rushes toward him, drawn by the tinkling sound of the girdle that steals away the garments from the hips of sleeping women—as if it were the Supreme Brahman? (VidSrk 26.1)
Unable to endure that excessively thick mass of darkness,
this slender lamp seems to slowly vomit it out under the guise of soot.
Even though it has entered the domain of extinction, does the lamp repeatedly recall what occurred at the conclusion of the lovemaking of the two youths? It [the lamp] was [once] exceedingly bright.
Thus does the lamp of Rati raise its neck as if in shame at the sight of all these blemishes. (VidSrk 26.3)
Seeing his son-in-law embracing his young bride— who is slender-limbed, unacquainted with sexual union, and newly wed— with such intensity, this lamp at the window trembles in fear.
Colo iti pradīpavrajyā // 26.
Then follows the section on the afternoon:
Having gathered the luster of the day-maker’s rays from the lotuses, which were blinded by sleep, these rays now bear a deep redness as if it were their own manifold quality.
Being extinguished by the incessant waters of the wheel-marked [lotuses], they attain coolness as if through the touch of breasts that have experienced the pain of separation. (VidSrk 27.1)
The power of the forest fire becomes cool, and the hearts of the young *kokila* birds burst into flame;
what can we say? The darkness that shrouds the world rises up, yet those blind by day become possessed of pure vision. (VidSrk 27.2)
Now, having been released throughout the day, this entire universe appears as if veiled by those very shadows;
with the ocean blazing at its borders and the jeweled peak in the center, this earth, with its variegated form, delights us with the playful display of masses of darkness. (VidSrk_27.3)

The openings of the venomous serpents appear intensely radiant with their shimmering crest-jewels; from the sun-stones, fire enters the hearts of the female *cakravāka* birds. Moreover, these lamps shine as they pierce the darkness on both sides, rivaling the mass of evening twilight particles crushed by the violent collision of dense glooms. (VidSrk 27.4) [And] within the hollow cauldrons of the mountain whose ore is the metal of its peaks, the light of the sun boils with the sharp heat of pungent spices.
The sky, suddenly joined with a fresh twilight that surged upward as if from a heavy burden, shone brilliantly.

When the sun, the source of light for the eyes of the world, has set, the quarters of the sky— like women performing the virtuous deed appropriate for their class by dissolving their radiance into the fire—
seem to bear the dark antelope skin of the deepest gloom, with the flickering fireflies as their rosaries, as if out of a desire to practice ascetic penances.
Just as the lion of the sun, resplendent with the spreading mane of his rays, having slain the elephant of the day, has taken his stand upon the western mountain;
even so, the assembly of owls shrouded in deep darkness drinks in the twilight-weapon, while these stars shine with the luster of pearls scattered from the fall of its frontal globes.

Having cast off her saffron body-unguent, the sky—once bearing rows of stars like slender bamboo poles that moved in succession like waves of a garland of pearls—is now sorrowful, its beauty obscured by contact with the faded garment of darkness; due to its separation from the newly risen sun, it no longer brings comfort to the eyes.
The cows have returned; the flocks of birds warble among the trees; the heart of the female Piśācīs is touched by the inclination toward household duties;
and this Nandin, intent on completing his tasks at the time of twilight, beats the drums in a manner that accords with the intention of the Three-Eyed Lord.

When the darkness— possessing the luster of rising streaks of smoke from the throat of Śiva— had slightly enveloped the sky with the appearance of sparks in the form of emerging stars, the Lord of Day reached the western quarter;
and as his beloved lotus-ponds bowed down as if in grief, their tongues of bees faltering, the beauty of the day was consumed as the Sun entered the fire of the twilight glow.
The fall of moths has begun in vain upon the jeweled lamp-stands here; on all sides, swarms of bees, blinded by fragrance, remain with their wings upraised;
and here, the excellent women, their activities signaled by the jingling of bracelets as they gaze with creeper-like arms, apply various cosmetic pigments.
Having assumed a slightly dimmed light, this sun, with the fresh crimson hue of the *javā* flower, now moves toward the quarter of the Lord of Waters (the West), visible only at his own will;
in every direction, birds that have finished their feeding alight at ease upon the crests of the trees where they dwell.
Seeing the sun falling from the sky, struck by the serpent of Time,
the Mother of the Ancestors seems to run along, taking up the Lord of Herbs (the Moon). 27.13 (870)
The light of the world’s eye slowly drinks up the blinding darkness; the crows, drawn into their nests, have momentarily ceased their cawing;
and thus the owl, his fear slightly dispelled, peers out from the mouth of his hollow with neck submerged in his body and head shaking, surveying the directions.

The twilight quivered in the sky like the tongue of the night-demoness— whose body was as dark as the gloom and whose row of fierce teeth was white with the sprouting stars— as she sought to swallow the sun, red as raw blood and flesh, like a morsel of meat.
Now that his friend the sun has set, the Mandara mountain seems to bathe in the waters of the rays streaming from the moon-jars tossed up by the ocean;
this thick darkness, which steals away the eyes of the world, spreads its splendor over the mountain’s back like a mass of disheveled hair.
Is this the broad neck-disk of a headless trunk in the sky, or is it the blood-stained skull of a Kapalika of Death?
Is it perhaps a fragment of Garuda’s egg filled with quivering serpents? The orb of the sun at twilight indeed gives rise to such conjectures.

In the radiant sacrifice of the sky, where the crimson hue of the heads of aged cranes rests upon the peaks of the setting sun, the firmament is smeared with darkness as dark as the throat of a ravening crow;
and even this eastern quarter, its lotuses blooming and longing for the moonrise, shines with a pallor like the cheeks of a Śabara woman long separated from her lover.

The sun appears like a safflower due to its rays, which possess dense veils of clouds, as it rests upon the single branch of a *spandana* tree whose foliage is surrounded by exceedingly green leaves— [the tree] belonging to Acala-siṃha.
The sun, the jewel of the day belonging to Cakrapāṇi, was displayed for sale at an invaluable price by the merchant Day throughout the world; yet,
failing to find a corresponding price, it has been placed back, as it were, into the ocean, the mine of jewels.

Bearing the likeness of a life-sustaining orb of day departing for the illustrious Dharmapāla, the solar disc— reddened by its rays and still warm— descends from the vault of the sky onto the western mountain;
moreover, the world begins to take on the form of an ancient painting, slightly smoky-grey and turning dark with the gathering of a small measure of twilight gloom.
As the sun, following the path of shimmering jeweled slabs, descended upon the ridges and slopes of Mount Meru,
the twilight blazed forth, tossed by the wind like the dust of rubies crushed by the hooves of galloping horses. (VidSrk 27.22)

The Kāla-kaula, as if for the sake of his own success, leads the bull of the sky somewhere away from the mark of contact with the fresh lac-dye of the solar disc resting upon the summit of the eight-peaked mountain.
First, the lotus stands with its broad filaments drooping at their tips due to sluggishness; then, its internal petals become very sparse and slightly closed together.
Thereafter, as the petals began the process of closing, the full-blown lotuses underwent a certain distress at the mere turning of their faces outward.
The glow of twilight assumes the splendor of a great heap of glowing embers by the seven-rayed fire that has arisen from the sun—the day-maker—that has burnt away the darkness;
meanwhile, the fresh shadows of night, having first scorched the heavy mass of darkness, now spread a dark hue like a spray of water from its extinction.
The Sun,

the traveler on the path of day, whose rays curve toward the quarters of space as they rest upon his head— which is like a sun-disk placed upon a soft pillow— wears a blanket of darkness while reclining upon the bed of the gods.

Count the courtyard of the sky as painted by the Lord with moon-white drops of ash, moist with sweat, drunk and then vomited from the hollows of his fingernails through the exhaustion of dancing to the Malaya breeze— thus abandoning the popular notion that it is "star-spangled."
Of Lakṣmīdhara. Thus ends the Section on the Afternoon (Aparāhṇavrajyā), [Section] 27. Next is the Section on Darkness (Andhakāravrajyā), [Section] 28.
"Is it Rahu who smears the world with the expansive radiance of his body? Or is the sky, its hand outstretched, falling as the sun descends?
Or is Hari placing the earth, along with its oceans and mountain ranges, within himself?"—such are the thoughts that the thick darkness, dark as a flock of swans, spreads abroad.

As darkness—anointed by the throats of intoxicated female cuckoos—smears the world, the mountains are discerned by the rays of medicinal herbs shimmering with their natural luster; living beings by the sounds of birds perched on their peaks; trees by the breezes carrying the fragrance of flowers; and houses by the beams of lamps flickering through the openings of the lattice windows.
The sun, crimson as a ruby, now sets with its rays suddenly overturned, casting the courtyard of the sky into a twilight glow where two or three stars flicker;
the sacred trees at the edges of the groves here and there are being mourned by flocks of birds, and moreover, heaven and earth are being shrouded by darkness whose power is drawing near.

The sky, clinging as it were to the eyes, appears excessively thick with the color of ink; alas, the quarters of the horizon appear as if standing at one's side, their internal spaces blocked without any gap.
This surface of the earth is known only by the measure of the space occupied by one’s own feet; moreover, even regarding one’s own limbs, conviction is possible only through contact with the hand.
As if the timbers of the quarters had been eaten away by swarms of woodworms in the form of dense darkness, these stars fall as sawdust through these holes under the guise of rays. (Vidvatsabhā 28.5;
Anargharāghava 2.53)
Standing at a secret trysting-place for Murāri, repeatedly casting his eyes along every path— eyes whose opening is rendered futile by being shrouded in a mass of deepest darkness—
the youth grows weary with anxious longing, his arms flailing in confusion as he mistakes even the slightest rustling sound for his beloved approaching in silence.
No.
Alas, what a tragedy! Who here is capable of providing a remedy? To whom can this be told? Alas, the entire world is swallowed up by masses of darkness as if by night-stalkers.
Is there even such a time when the Blessed One, the Cool-rayed Moon, having arisen, will lift the earth from the flood of gloom, as Hari [lifted it] from the depths of Pātāla?
To whom does this belong? To Vijayendra.
Driven away from their cheeks by the radiance of smiles, as if shaken off from their breasts by single-string pearl necklaces,
darkness— finding no pleasure in enjoying their limbs— seizes women in their braided hair as if out of rage.
The horizons are enveloped by creepers of darkness as if by clusters of *tāpiccha* blossoms; through its peripheral movement, the earth seems to sink into fresh water.
At its very onset, the night brings forth its own blackness within the forests, appearing like the vast, swirling glow of smoke-circles spread in all directions by the force of a whirlwind.
Having pushed far outside the dark shadows of the eaves and the curved cornices, the rays of the lamps emerge through the sparse openings of the latticed windows;
at night, they appear like the tawny, coarse, and sparse sprouts of a beard on the face of darkness as it has grown old under the burden of youth.
Like the directions clinging to the body of Bhaṭṭagaṇapati, the circle of the earth becomes as if traversible by his feet alone;
and the sky, reaching only to his forehead, makes the darkness graspable within his fist. (VidSrk 28.11)
With crest-ornaments of peacock feathers upon arms as dark as emerald bracelets; with necklaces of choice sapphires and elaborate facial designs made of musk;

with the beauty of blue-lotus topknots and the wearing of dark garments—such is the fashionable style of the fawn-eyed women now, during their secret trysts, that it acts as a companion to the heavy burden of darkness.
These two belong to Rājaśekhara. [End of] the Section on Darkness, 28. Next, the Section on the Moon, 29.

Victorious is the white-rayed god born from the ocean of milk, the lover of the night-lily; he who is the stage-manager in the realm of love, a celibate student in the hermitage of the sage with the flower-arrowed bow, the primordial deity of women, honored by the three worlds as the priest in the kingdom of passion, who maintains a sacrificial session of moonlight and reclines upon the crest of the matted locks of the Destroyer of Cities. VidSrk_29.1 (897)
The moon, the friend of the lily-beds and the master at closing the clusters of lotuses, rises like Vasukalpa,
as if stroking the limbs of the quarters with his hand that possesses the luster of saffron. (VidSrk 29.2)
O people of royal fortune, abandon your grief; it does not endure for long. O auspicious night-lily, go forth; O cakora bird, cast off your delusion.
Here rises that glorious moon, the common lamp of the universe and the sole mountain from which flow the rivers of the nectar-essence of pure moonlight. VidSrk_29.3 *(899)
Was the form of heaven and earth filled with camphor, smeared with sandalwood paste, washed with mercury, or fashioned from crystal stones by the Fortune of the King?

Thus one might conjecture regarding the full moon—the remover of the lily’s fatigue, the preceptor for the initiation into love, the mirror for the beauties of the quarters, and the friend of the cakora bird. (VidSrk 29.4)

Like a gallant man, the moon—possessing its digits as ornaments, curved, with the glow of its shimmering lower lip, and possessing a fresh body—kisses the young women whose passion for pride is melting away;
he kisses them on their heavy orb-like hips, their bud-like eyes, their lower lip, their cheek, their neck, and their jar-like breasts. (VidSrk 29.5)

"O beautiful one, look here at this moon— the kinsman of Śrīkaṇṭha, the initiating preceptor for the amorous dalliances of the Raghu kings, the familiar standard of comparison for the faces of fair-limbed women,
the beloved of the star-brides, and the crest-jewel of Caṇḍī’s lord— whose pure luster has been freshly polished by the teeth of southern young women."
O slender-waisted friend, behold this letter, which possesses the splendor of an archway to the city of the Bodiless One;
for even between two youths separated by distant lands, their glances surely meet within it.
These two are not the horns of Rājaśekhara;
this is not the sky, but the salt-ocean; look, this is not the path of the moon's shadow, but its bridge;
this is not the moon with its densely coiled body, but Śeṣa; and this is not a spot, but Hari sleeping. (VidSrk 29.8)
In a skull, the cat licks its paws thinking it is milk; the elephant gathers the moonlight streaming through the gaps in the trees like lotus stalks;
and at the end of lovemaking, the woman thinks she is picking up her garment from the bed. Alas, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, brings this entire world to such confusion!
"Is it now, or will it be so? Will this reflection of the moon fall from the sky?
I too shall make my body free of marks with streaks of sandalwood paste. — By Bhikṣu Sumati.
The moon is the funeral pyre of the flower-bowed god whose body was consumed by fire; the spot upon it bears the likeness of a dark charcoal ember.
But this light of his, white as slightly crushed camphor, spreads in every direction like scattered ashes carried by the winds.

Making the courtyard of the sky appear as if smeared with the fresh paste of sandalwood, this moon rises—its form comparable to the severed tusks of the lovely elephant Airāvata—with rays hanging down like necklaces of clear pearl-jewels; it is the playful lamp for the art of reading the love-letters of charming women.

Gradually manifesting its digits— one, two, three, and so forth— the moon rises as if in secret, fearing the sidelong glances of women whose eyes are kindled by the fire of separation from their beloveds, for those glances possess the luster of the sprouts of a fresh lotus root.
A few rays of the moon of nectar are unfolding, possessing the delicate luster of lotus stalks and performing the function of closing the petals of the day-lotuses;
even as the mountains turn white with the first light of dawn, this ocean of darkness, agitated as if by the emerging universe, suddenly foams forth.
This lunar orb expands, anointing the vault of the sky with saffron from the faces of fair-browed women, establishing a dual sovereignty over the moonstones, and piercing the veins of the waters;

it causes the deer in its lap to become intoxicated by the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass offered as an *argha* welcome by the city women of Indra’s capital who have come forth to meet it. VidSrk_29.15 *(911)*.

The Blessed Moon does not even rise so high as to reach the sky at a distance of two leagues; yet even now, the rays that flatter the glory of the Kuru lineage continue to churn the earth's surface, obstruct the mountain thickets and their interior recesses as if taking them alive, and seize hold of shadows here and there.

Is this a dark ocean that has become entirely clear below due to the rays of the moon acting like the powder of *kataka* nuts, and thus all its mud has vanished under the guise of shadows? Or is it that the sky itself has been polished bright on all sides by the blades of those very rays, and these are merely the shavings falling here and there in the form of shadows?
Beneath the trees laden with spreading foliage, the moonlight here was like sesame seeds interspersed with rice grains;
in various places, it appeared as if made thin by being pecked at by the tips of the beaks of cakora birds restless with passion.
Thus, in the eastern direction, the moon tosses up a wave of rays that shatters the buds of the lily-fields;
for on every side, the moonstones (*eṇāṅkamaṇi*) appear like clusters, each globule of them emitting a dense spray of water-drops. (VidSrk 29.19)
Since these stars are far more numerous during the nights of darkness and sparse during the moonlit nights,
we infer that this moon is filled with the very stars melted down by the fire of twilight within the crucible of the sky.

People live only to behold the deer-marked moon, which bears the names of the directions—east, west, south, and north—and which, with its shimmering, rippling nets of moonlight, dispels the blinding darkness on all sides; it emerges from the Eastern Mountain like a sprout from the seed of light for the three worlds. (VidSrk 29.21)

The moonlight of the moon—whose foot-water has been offered by the moonstones on the peaks of the eastern mountains, whose handfuls of parched grain for the guest-offering are its own stars, and whose body is its own—is spreading thickly from its orb in all directions, dense yet hollow with a mature internal spot, shattering the mass of nocturnal darkness like sprouting shoots. (VidSrk 29.22)
For the sake of Murāri, the eastern quarter has given birth to the moon, Madana dances, even the quarters laugh,
and the wind scatters the pollen of night-lotuses like fragrant dust in the courtyard of the sky.

As the moon embraced the night, whose garment of darkness was slipping away, with its lovely fingertips—cool from their immersion in the interior of night-lotuses—the quarters of the sky, like young brides, gazed at one another;
and as joy reached its peak through glances that overflowed with affection born of long acquaintance, they clearly seemed to break into laughter. (VidSrk 29.24)

Even today, this pride of women desires to dwell in their hearts, which are as difficult to penetrate as the mountain-fortresses of their breasts; yet the moon, rising with its rays suddenly extended far and reddened as if with anger,
instantly draws forth the sword of the rows of bees emerging from the swelling buds of the night-lilies.
When the sun had set, the moon, assuming its form and filled with passion, freely extended its ray toward the lovely night-lily to embrace it;
but perceiving the thick touch of cold, the beloved of the night-lily closed her lotus-face, turning as pale as if from embarrassment at her smile.

By the unrestrained rays of the moon, which bear the luster of the stalks of a lake-born lotus and have suddenly drunk up the darkness on all sides, the night— feeling itself to be day— became terrified, while the family of owls somehow remained asleep as the lotuses blossomed. (Rājaśekhara) 29.27 (923)

The orb of the moon, resembling the impression left by the pressing of the high and curved breasts of a young Hūṇa woman during dalliance— her bosom once emptied of her garment— is revealed as the first footprint of Viṣṇu by his foremost rays, which are pale-white like the pith of a mature lotus stalk. (VidSrk 29.28)
Where has the darkness gone, having transcended even the quarters, time, and the sky? Where has even the seal of the fresh lotus bud suddenly vanished?
And where is that patience of the ocean? Now that the moon sits in the midst of the plateau of the rising mountain, this entire world is thrown into agitation.
At the onset of night, the moon— first possessing the hue of dawn, then the luster of gold, followed by the glow of the cheeks of a slender woman distressed by separation,
and finally capable of destroying the darkness— spreads forth with the brilliance of a sliced stalk from a juicy lotus.
The moon incessantly pours forth even milk in thousands of upward-streaming jets, as if the thirsty night-lotuses were now drinking the water of moonlight;
the world, exhausted by the labors of the day, seems to be immersing itself in the waters of the Ocean of Milk, and from its agitation, the reddish stars float up like water-bubbles.
In the garden of the sky, the lunar disc bears the beauty of a crystal basin for the single sprout of the young *tamāla* tree that is its dark spot, which is moistened by the water of its rays.
Here, the moonlight has been thickened by the radiance of the moonbeams, which are marked by the beak-prints of female cakora birds reeling with intoxication,
and which reveal the playful breaking of sprout-like hands by young women as they fashion couches for the exhaustion of their intense passion.

The moon rises in the lake of the sky, like a swan laughing at its own grace—a saffron tilaka upon the forehead of the city’s women, a lion for the herd of elephants that is darkness, a silver consecration-vase for the flower-armed lord of the earth, and the unique crest-jewel of the mountain of sunrise, serving as a fresh mirror for the quarters. (VidSrk 29.34)
In the dense darkness at the edge of the sky, which is as dark as the turbid waters of the Yamunā,
this cool-rayed moon shines like a royal swan with its beak hidden within its folded wings. (VidSrk 29.35)
On the edge of the pond that is the expanse of the sky, this moon shines forth as it is being dug up by the powerful boar of nightfall;
marked with a stain, it appears like a root-tuber for its own lotus-fiber of rays, lightly smeared with mud.
Her body became pale as a ripened lavalī fruit with a darkened belly,
like the whetstone for the sharp arrow of Love, whose shafts have grown blunt from piercing the hearts of men— [the stone] belonging to the moon.

When his friend the moon had risen, the white ocean— having attained its own increase and disregarding its proper bounds as if desiring to seize the jewels extracted from the gods— plunged into the interior of the quarters and the world under the guise of moonlight.
The ocean, as if grinding sandalwood-foam with the tips of its waves for Gaṇapati, takes it up with its rays;
the moon, as it were, anoints the women of the quarters with it. (VidSrk 29.39)

The Lord, the beloved of the daughter of Dakṣa, reigns supreme— he who is the entire wealth of the splendor of the sky, the trusted friend of the Lord of Love, the resident upon the head of Hara, the one who swallows the mass of darkness from all worlds with his fist, the elixir of the milk-ocean, the sprout of the medicinal plant that slumbers within the lotus, and a treasury of great radiance.

As if submerged in a great mist of spray from liquid camphor, as if smeared with a thick coating of fresh nectar-foam paste, or as if cast into the interior of a house made of pure crystal, this lord of the full-moon night shines forth with unrestrained splendor, making this earth appear so. (VidSrk 29.41)
If the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), intoxicated and bearing a coppery luster, becomes the moon stumbling upon the peak of the eastern mountain— the abode of the Supreme Lord—
then even this darkness, which steals the brilliance of fresh tamāla leaves, will fall away like his own swaying garment.

Just as this moon, the lord of yogis, shines while scattering rays as white as jasmine in every direction, so too does this deer— though possessing the luster of a fragment of a fresh cloud— attain a resemblance to the decorative leaf-patterns drawn with musk upon the beauty-pitchers of the breasts of Kashmiri women.
Just as this glorious moon, the producer of nectar, causes the mind to suspect it is a golden lotus upon the edge of the ramparts of the Western Mountain,
so too does its spot assume the beauty of a swarm of bees falling out of thirst for the liquid nectar of the spreading flow of its loveliness.

Then, having gradually transcended its charming childhood state, the orb of the moon shines before us— first as fierce as a blooming red lotus, then with the tawny glow of Jāmbūnada gold, and finally resembling a fragment of crystal.
The moonlight seems to glide through the sky, to multiply among the night-lotuses, to reflect upon the cheeks of women as pale as the stalks of reeds,
to blossom in the waters, to laugh in the dwellings whitened by plaster, and to dance upon the fluttering tips of the banners' silken fringes as they sway in the breeze. (VidSrk 29.46)

First, the orb of the moon shines in the vault of the sky with the hue of a cluster of *analasa* and *javā* flowers; then it takes on the glow of the cheeks of intoxicated Yavana women; then it becomes honey-tawny; then it possesses the luster of a mirror of fresh gold; and thereafter, it appears like a young *tagara* flower. (VidSrk 29.47)
The red moon, having shaken off the veil of darkness from the night, scatters its rays upon the tips of the pale breasts of the quarters;
seeing this, the women of the directions, filled with curiosity yet feeling bashful, seem to withdraw far away with a smile. (VidSrk 29.48)
With his body reddened by fragments of yellow orpiment and rock-crystal, the Lord of Stars gradually and smoothly advances;
about to become rich, he covers the sky, which is as white as a canopy of fresh lotus fibers.
Having surveyed the interior of the forest, with his clearly visible rays for a mane, the moon has emerged from the mountain of sunrise like a lion that has seized a motionless deer. (VidSrk 29.50)
From the direction of Indra (the East), Pāṇini’s moon was born; Sarasvatī, with her rows of waving arms, began to dance;
the fish-bannered god (Kāma) rejoiced; and the bees attained liberation from their imprisonment within the white water-lilies. (VidSrk 29.51)
Like the rays of the moon, acting as the claws of the lion-like Abhinanda, the stars shine with the luster of pearls shed from the elephant of darkness that has been torn asunder. VidSrk_29.52 (948)
The bright rays of the moon begin, as it were, a sudden burst of laughter upon the slopes of the breasts and the surfaces of the cheeks of the fawn-eyed women of fair complexion;
they spread, as it were, a playful undulation across the spotless strings of pearls.

The lunar orb, its distinct markings clearly visible, shines like the skull-bowl of Śiva, its center darkened by the smoke from the fire of the venomous breath of serpents bound at the base of its rim. (VidSrk 29.54) [Of Dakṣa]
When the moon’s orb has attained a resemblance to the eye from its palace of the sky,
white with moonlight, its dark spot acts like a blue pigeon.

That moonlight, which previously possessed a splendor worthy of being woven into a string of pearls—bearing the beauty of rows of freshly split filaments from the heart of a *ketaka* flower—is now present with its power diminished;
it can only be grasped by cupped hands trembling with uncertainty or measured out by sprouts of lotus stalks, and must be drunk.

Those rays of the nectar-rayed moon which formerly were friends to the stalks of grass, which bore the luster and shade of the petals at the tips of *ketaka* flowers, which possessed the loveliness of lotus tendrils, which for a moment mimicked streams of water, and which thereafter shared the beauty of shimmering pearl necklaces— those very rays have now become surpassed by the splendor of crystal staffs.
Of Rājaśekhara: These two [verses] concern the moon, which is pale as night: "The moon, possessing cheeks as soft as a lotus, is not more bold than her cheek; its rays remain unimpaired.
This boundary of its eye is this slight shadow of a deer upon its breast; by fate, this spot was not formed again. (VidSrk 29.58) (954)

The moon—this abode of the playful charms of women bewildered by moonlight, a lake of nectar-waves, a mass of butter from the ocean of milk, a cooling stone for the waters of the earth’s heat, the tilaka mark of the night, the digit of the deer-eyed women, the sole hermitage for the vow of love, and a rain of camphor for the cakora birds begging for its light—now moves across the sky. (Vidvadbhañjikā 29.59)

In the garden of the sky, which possesses rows of *tārā* (stars) as its blossoms, contemplate with certainty that the moon— a white spider— shines amidst this pair of trees, the mountains of sunrise and sunset, with these spreading webs of rays that devour the flies of darkness falling upon the sprouts of twilight.
[This was] the twenty-ninth [chapter], the "Course of the Moon," of the Vasukalpa.
Then follows the thirtieth, the "Course of the Dawn."
These stars, whirling in circles like the waist-bands of the sky, mimic the rapid tossing of handfuls of cowrie shells by a multitude of gamblers;
moreover, this Lord of Night, his beauty now fading away, seeks the luster of a piece of smooth, hard chalk lying at the edge of the gaming board.
While the nectar-bodied moon has reached the end of its life, the quarters of the sky are being drunk up by the darknesses of Kaimalla, as if by the smoke from a mass of sun-stones about to blaze;
drawing away the bees from the lotuses like a magnet draws out an internal splinter, the Lord of Light still does not shine even now. (VidSrk 30.2)
The stars, casting a sweetly pale shadow like that of a ripe onion, sprout a faint radiance in the eastern quarter—the very lifeblood of the lotuses.
Meanwhile, the moon, its orb here round as a spider’s web, kisses the western mountain from the vault of the sky at dawn, its light departed.
Two or three lovely rays of the jewel of the sky are now ascending toward the heavens, acting as the pericarp for the lotus-bed that is the eastern quarter.
And this lotus, though its opening is slight, is blooming wide with the heavy agitation of swarms of bees emerging from its calyx together in eager haste.
As if counting these rays of the sun as they set, one by one in sequence, the lotus-plant closed its hundreds of eyes—the folds of its petals;
now, as if curious to count them again, it gradually opens them once more to number the thousand rays of the sun as they rise.
Having drunk the heavy rain of nocturnal darkness from the shells of their lotus-buds, they now burst open;
under the guise of emerging swarms of bees, they vomit forth pearls that seem to bear the very qualities of their cause.
This remaining circle of Murāri’s stars, possessing the luster of *tagara* flowers, stands diminished in number; the lamp-flames, their radiance extinguished, vie with the sprouts of turmeric.
There, at dawn, the moon has become as inert as liquid mercury that has been solidified, and the eastern sky possesses the sweet hue of aged rum.
In the sky, two or three stars remain, possessing the luster of ancient pearl-jewels; the female cakora birds sleep, their bodies languid from the weight of drinking the moonlight;
the moon has gone to the peak of the western mountain with the faded splendor of a honey-bee's parasol; and the eastern quarter has become the vessel for the glow of the eyes of young cats.
The darkness has indeed vanished, yet the eyes do not clearly perceive; the garments of the women have indeed been covered, yet they do not abandon their lords;
and by the pairs of ruddy geese situated on both banks, there is indeed a faltering cry of joy full of meaning, yet they do not fly up with a loud rustling sound.
Having made a *vajra*-sound (*vajrakṛtya*),
having uttered a cry of satisfaction (*sātkṛtya*).

"Twinkle, O stars! Move about, you circles of thieves! Spread forth, you darknesses! This is indeed the time for those such as yourselves—before the sun, with its dust raised from the mountain of sunrise, ascends and makes the expanse of the sky rosy with its mass of radiance. (VidSrk 30.10)

The darkness has been destroyed on all sides by the sun, red with anger at dawn; therefore, the bees, resembling that [darkness] in color within the cups of the lotuses, have been dragged away by his rays.
"Alas, what a tragedy! We too are clearly struck down by the splendor of the darkness"—thus these crows now cry out in fear, using their own name, "kāka."
Worthy of long worship with the lotus of one's eyes, possessing the splendor of a circle as pale-red as a mass of saffron,
dispelling the darkness, the god rises in the direction protected by the Lord of the Immortals— the seed-vessel of the day.
Wherein the moon, marked by a deer, appears like a single lock of hair remaining from Viṣṇu-Hari, while the God of Love has submerged himself in a lake of sandalwood paste;
there the deer-marked moon has gone to its setting.

Behold, now that the Moon— the lord of the digits— has gradually set through the power of his changing course, the Night, wailing with the cries of birds, her mass of hair in the form of darkness loosened,
and her teardrops in the form of stars rivaling a heap of large fallen pearls, offers up her body as an oblation into the sacrificial fire of the emerging dawn.
"I have traveled a very great distance, mounted upon the king of birds, and alas, I have become deeply attached to wine"—
having reflected thus with certainty, the moon suddenly leapt from the entire western mountain into the ocean.

The sky, the domain of Narasiṃha, has gradually become devoid of stars as they have set behind the peak of the western mountain; following them, the moon, its luster impoverished by shadow, has vanished.
Then, with the crimson glow from the orb of the sun standing near the eastern horizon, even the eastern quarter unfolds, red as the juice of madder.
The rays of the sun, which have stolen away the light of even the stars like frost-drops, now meet at the base of the eastern mountain; meanwhile, the moon,
its beauty as clear as a ripe lavalī fruit held in the hollow of the hand, rests upon the shore of the western ocean with its expanse of shadow growing faint.
The moon, white as a mass of silver, is departing for the western ocean; the stars, with the luster of water bubbles, bow down;
the sprouts of lamps assume a radiance pale as *kuruṇṭaka* flowers; and the southern quarter (Sautrāmaṇī) becomes as red as the eyes of a *cakora* bird.
Having received the awakening of Rājaśekhara, as the Day-Elephant rises with pride from this long bed of the sky— its starry garland scattered—
the Moon falls like a loosened conch-shell earring, its cord of rays frayed and its body stained by the flowing ichor of its trunk. (VidSrk 30.19)
When the sun— a mass of splendor that drenches the very edges of the horizons of the ocean of worlds— drinks up the waters of the mass of darkness, like Agastya drinking from the sea;
Like intoxicated crocodiles, tortoises, and large fish, these great mountain ranges situated within [the ocean] emerge from their internal state by way of the process of manifestation.
Sealing the edge of the lake as if with darkness, their feet embraced by foam like a multitude of stars through grief for their mate;

with their circular beaks eager to bite the clearly visible lotus stalks they have seized in their confusion, these ruddy geese appear like the crescent moon itself, captured as a prisoner by the Creator who brought about their separation.
Having hidden his feet within the work of Bhaṭṭa Śivasvāmin, the moon— now sinking with its dark spot appearing like a streak of excessive mud—
is like the King of Tortoises lying on his back, clinging to the western shore of the ocean of the sky. *Vidagdhamukhamandana* 30.22 (978).
This son of Śatānanda rises, the breaker of the seal for the lotus-beds—the young mandāra blossom from the forest groves of the Mountain of Sunrise;
he is the friend of pairs of cakravāka birds distressed by separation, dispelling the darkness that is as copper-red as the wrathful cheeks of an angry monkey. (VidSrk 30.23)
In the cities,

the songs that dispel the morning sleep of the citizens— the songs introducing the mutual secrets of Rādhā and Mādhava— are sung by the masters of yoga, who, like mendicants on the streets, have warded off the suffering of winter’s onset with great woolen blankets sewn from hundreds of rags, their throats and bellies now clear and resonant.
Of the child.
Thus ends the "Practice of Dawn" (Chapter 30).
Next is the "Practice of Midday."
At midday, the deer beneath the trees resort to the thickly gathered shade; in the pond with its belly burst open, the insects spend the day in profound stillness.
In the forest, a monkey—his face resting upon his two forepaws loosely released from his lap, refreshed by the sprinkling of water droplets from crickets—sleeps soundly.
At this midday hour, even the wind does not stir, as if terrified by the fierce heat of the sun’s orb scorching the forehead;
moreover, the shadows, though they have moved far away, turn back and huddle together at the foot of the trees, as if unable to endure the burning of rolling in the parched dust.
At first, having been raised far aloft by the heavy grasp of pride, and later reduced to thinness by the weight of remorse, she has been brought to extreme lightness;
now, because she follows those who dwell within her lap, the shade of the tree clings to this earth as if it were a beloved embracing all her limbs.
While the sun scatters its rays in all directions, the shadows of the people’s bodies, becoming exceedingly short, move about like land-tortoises;
meanwhile, the deer lie upon the marshy ground, cool and sweet with the fine water-droplets sprayed from the trunks of lordly elephants.

Alas, these empty quarters at midday—where the edges of the wilderness are scorched by the massed flames of sun-stones playing in the intense encounter with the radiance of the fierce sun; where the lapwings remain silent on the arid slopes; and where the cruel glare of the sun’s rays floats upon the terrestrial heat—bring to an end the very lifespan of one's vision. VidSrk_31.5 (985)

May this midday of the Lord bring about appropriate auspiciousness on all sides— this midday which causes the royal swans to leave the surface of the rows of tall lotus petals to seek out the quality of playful children within the courtyards of the mansions, and which brings a slight exhaustion to the limbs of those who study, making their eyes exceedingly languid.

At the *kāśmarya* tree of Puruṣottamadeva, which is covered in *kṛtamāla* and has sprouted new leaves, the *koyaṣṭika* birds are perched; the *pūrṇikā* birds, their beaks touching the pods of the *aśmantaka*, run toward the water.

On the trunk of the *tiniśa* tree, which possesses hollows, the *dātyūha* cranes remain hidden; below them, the wild cocks (*kukkubha*) cry out, echoing the warbling of the young pigeons in the nests upon the creepers.
As if their intensity were rendered futile by the rays of the fiercely blazing garlanded sun, the shadows now form a single mass at the roots of the trees;
moreover, this lake possesses a false parasol formed by the flocks of birds that fly up in agitation from the plunging of the host of daughters of the king of the Dānavas.

At midday, Dharmāśoka’s elephant holds its own ear-fan above its trunk, desiring not to touch the lotus surface; the peacock restrains its head within its plumage, withholding the taste for the shoots of young grass; the boar vainly licks at the tip of his tusk with the impulse of a lotus fiber; and the buffalo longs for the great mire of his own shadow.
When the water from the bathing antelope-eyed women, reaching the bank of the pleasure-park pond with the curves of their hips,
enters once more into the deep expanse of the hollows of their navels, it produces a resonant *kuhuṃkāra* sound and bows down.

On the paths of Rājaśekhara, the abundant dust within the hollows of the roads—bearing the playful roar of the wind and purified by masses of cloudless rays released from the bright sun—is wafted along.

Furthermore, the traveler, mistaking the shadow of clouds for water, runs ahead toward a patch of scorched dūrvā grass; moreover, he grows weary with the delusion that the shimmering waves of heat-rays are a flood of water.

Cuckoos dwell in the hollow-houses of mountain caves whose dark foliage is like a forest; travelers drink the turbid water as if it were a ship; and thirsty deer, standing amidst herds of boars, buffaloes, and wild asses swollen by the mass of rays from the sun—which is powerless against the dense thicket of forest darkness—drink the heated water that has flowed down from them.

The smoke drifting through the forests causes swarms of crows to flock together; moreover, by these waves of wind from every side, laden with a towering mass of rising dust, it creates the illusion of spreading forest fires. Furthermore, the deer at the edge of the lakes mistake the waters of the western direction for a multitude of shimmering ripples of clear sunlight.

At midday, in the waters of the Buddha-Ākaragupta’s pond which were perfectly clear, a *śakula* fish—its fear overcome by the thickness of its body amidst the garlands of moss—scattered the rows of hair on its tail-tip with the grand display of a playful dance; then, having disgorged a pellet of water it had swallowed for a moment from the tip of its snout while its belly was full of water, it settled down. (VidSrk 31.14)
Thus ends the section on the Midday Journey (31).
Then follows the section on the Journey for Renown (32):
"O King, we brahmins, wishing you well, desire to bathe in the waters where the Kālindī and the celestial river meet at the holy ford, as we are desirous of bathing here and there."

Therefore, we entreat you: may you maintain your vow of being solely intent on purifying the seven worlds; let there be for us a discernment between the white and black waters through the manifestation of your own glory.
What is the use of inquiries concerning the affairs of others' households? However, being naturally talkative and possessing the disposition of a Southerner, I am unable to remain silent.
Alas, your beloved Fame wanders like a madwoman from house to house, through the marketplaces, the squares, and the drinking halls.
Your fame, which far outshines learning, the moon, sandalwood, the white blossoms of the kunda flower, the ocean of milk, the serpent Śeṣa, the laughter of the fierce Lord Śiva,
and even the luster of the white ivory earring of a Karṇāṭaka woman, wanders through the three worlds as you have conquered your enemies by the prowess of your arms.
The three worlds are the cage for that royal swan of glory, the author of the Vārttika;
and even these seven masses of water are but drinking-cups for him. (VidSrk 32.4)
The salt water of the ocean, which was both brackish and turbid, was taken by the clouds and, with great effort, placed within oyster shells so that it became sweet and pure; thus,
through its priceless value and beauty, it vies with your fame and shines forth— surely, this transformation of material elements is wondrous!
O lover of Ujjayinī,
your fame, as white as the moon, has been beheld by witnesses of battle, proclaimed by throngs of bards, fixed in the hearts of the virtuous, circulated in the poems of great poets,
engraved by skilled artisans upon panegyrics, and is ever sung by the wives of the gods. (VidŚrk 32.6)
The salt-water ocean has attained the splendor of the surging sea of milk; the gods' discrimination was cast aside as they wondered, "Who is the Vindhya? And who is the father of Gaurī?
The horses of the sun’s chariot were turned into crabs, and O King, the moon, having lost its mark upon its lap, was made white by the unrestrained brilliance of your fame.

O King, this entire world has been illuminated by your glories— glories that are as white as the remnants of [the ocean] after it was churned by the Lord of Mountains, as pale as the interior of the Milky Ocean when agitated by the churning of the mountain king, and as radiant as the fragments of the moon severed during the dark fortnight; thus did it shine through Abhinanda.

Hail! From the midst of the Ocean of Milk, with a lotus held in her hand within the embrace of her own beloved, Lakṣmī sends her greetings to the great sovereign Bhojyadeva, whose fame is as vast as the earth.

May you enjoy well-being until the end of the age; may the Lord Hari—who is kept awake by the proclamations of your fame—render the abundance of my youth fruitful. Your fame, as if rendered numb from immersion in the seven oceans, [spreads abroad].
O Lord of the World, your majesty has gone to the orb of the sun. (VidŚrk 32.10)
Who are you? You are the fame of Kuntalamalla! Alas, where do you dwell? Nowhere at all. Tell me, where are those friends of yours—where is your speech, your fortune, and your beauty?

Your speech has gone to the mouth of the Four-Faced One (Brahmā), your fortune to the chest of Murāri (Viṣṇu), and your beauty to the lunar orb; but for me, there is still no place of rest even today.
That seed of pearls which was sown by you upon the battlefield from the frontal globes of the elephants of your enemies has produced this tree of your fame throughout the three worlds:
Śeṣa is its root, the Himalayas its trunk, the milk-ocean its basin for irrigation, moonlight the spreading of its branches, the clusters of stars its flowers, and the moon its fruit.
O virtuous one, today the host of celestial nymphs sings loudly of your fame, bright as the moon; meanwhile, the moon remains in a state of spotless pride.
"Tell me, Master, with its desire for mouthfuls of grass abandoned due to the joy of listening to songs, how many more days will this deer on your lap survive?"

"O King, we declare that your wife, the sword-blade, who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus and reclines upon the chest of the enemy, has given birth to a noble daughter—Fame, who is easily obtained at the proper time; and she too wanders through the entire world, as if blinded by passion, in order to delight him."

Your fame covers the heavens of Amarasiṃha, spreads across the surface of the earth, and dispels the darkness at the very roots of the netherworld; it resembles a string of pearls, the deer-marked moon, the loud laughter of Hara, the tusk of Heramba, and the conch of Hari. (VidSrk 32.15)
O King, as your fame spreads abroad, Lakṣmī, the nectar, Uccaiḥśravas, Candra, Airāvata, and Kaustubha seem to have remained behind in the Ocean of Milk.

Yet there remains one singular blemish: that Śrī does not, out of delusion, approach Kṛṣṇa; that Pārvatī does not approach the Blue-throated One (Śiva); and that Revatī does not approach him who wears blue garments (Balarāma).

By your glories, all elephants act as Airāvaṇas, all serpents indeed act as Śeṣas, alas! even birds act as swans; the blue lotuses act as white lilies, and all mountains are intent on becoming Mount Kailāsa. (VidSrk 32.17)
That Rāma, accompanied by an army, formerly crossed to the far shore of the ocean after constructing a stone bridge, would not cause wonder today;
for, O Lord, your wife Fame, though alone and without the aid of a bridge, effortlessly leaps across even the seven oceans.
It is no wonder that your royal serpent-like arm, with its fierce tongue of extended sword-blades, is capable of bearing the burden of the earth;
for this orb of the world has been covered by the slough of your fame, which is as pure as a fresh lotus-stalk fiber.

The glories of your fame, possessing the pale luster of white sandalwood and surpassing the radiance of clusters of blooming white lotuses, pierce the circle of the sky and the quarters with dense successions of forms as they coalesce within it. (VidSrk 32.20)

O King, remove this great delusion with this sword of yours; tell me, how and where was this marvelous feat of deceptive play learned, that while repeatedly drinking the enemy's blood as red as saffron dye, he suddenly vomits forth fame white as a stream from the Ocean of Milk? (VidSrk 32.21)
O Kāmboja, you shine upon the earth as the son of Dakṣa; your father shines in heaven; and his father, that incomparable ornament, radiates in the abode of Brahmā.
With these three of you who have offered their bodies [as support], your expanding fame bears the beauty of a necklace adorned with a cluster of three rubies.
As your fame, mingled with the affection of the people, spreads forth like Vasukalpa,
it has suddenly become like half-applied saffron upon the faces of the women who are the quarters of the sky.

The mark of the moon, the base of the throat of the conqueror of Tripura, and the temples of the world-elephants—stained with the ink of rut-fluid—still appear today as if smeared with blackness, O ornament of the earth’s circle; tell me, what has been whitened by your glories?
The Chapter on Fame, "Colo," is the thirty-second.
Then follows the Chapter on Indirect Address, the thirty-third:
"O pearl-jewel, spread abroad and illuminate even the palaces of the lords of the earth; make your own virtues bear fruit!"
Why do you waste yourself here in vain within the hollow of a seashell? This ocean is vast and deep; who here would take you into account?
To dwell in the ocean, the refuge of all, whose majesty and power are beyond measure—that is the fruit of no small austerity; yet there is this one great defect:
even a common shellfish, by virtue of sharing that same dwelling, absolutely desires to rival the most rare and priceless jewels.

A lotus-pond, though limited in size, is better than that great ocean whose waves, when provoked, seize one by the throat even on its own shore; for it is the former where prosperity is enjoyed according to one's own will. (VidSrk 33.3)
O curious one, do not descend into this water of Dāmodara out of a desire to grasp the moon in your hand; for here below is only its reflection.

Where in the mortal world can there be the seizing of it, even the nectar of its sight is denied to those whose eyes have lost their splendor; and even in the heavenly realm, it is but a tiny fragment, the sole crest-jewel upon the matted locks of Śiva.

O emerald gem, by what heartless person were you uprooted from the mine while still seated comfortably for Vallaṇa? Or by whom was it desired that you be sold in this foreign land, where— at least for now— there is no buyer capable of bearing the burden of the expenditure of wealth, O brother, nor even anyone capable of examining you?
The petty birds in every direction have departed, honored by the crowning of its summit; the timid deer have vanished, their fatigue dispelled by the gift of its shade;
alas, what a pity, the restless monkeys, greedy for fruit, have fled; yet by that single tree alone has the calamity of the forest fire been fully endured.
"This is the sole abode of waters," "this is a mine of jewels"—thinking thus, we have resorted to the ocean with minds agitated by thirst.
Who could have known that a sage would, in an instant, drink it up along with its gasping whales and sea-monsters, having brought it into the hollow of his own cupped palms?

The birth of Kavinanda was in the hollow of a lotus in the lake of the sky; his friends were the wish-fulfilling trees; his play was with the celestial nymphs; and his familiar garlands were of golden creepers.
Even from this [birth], your descent was not merely the sound of a drum of madness; rather, O bee, these repeated attacks are truly the sport of fainting.
What need is there to speak of the embrace of limb with limb, or the clashing of trunks and so forth, when even the mere scent of the lord of scent-elephants causes other elephants to flee?

That elephant which was marked by Hari as his sign is yet to be conquered; therefore we revere that [lioness] from whose womb was born Śarabha himself, who, though hearing that he was "conqueror by his own power," remained unmarked.
These two trees, which stood here on the bank since Vallana’s birth, have been uprooted by the waves; yet those waves, though momentary in their destruction, have again reached the highest state.
Within, they carry a mass of stones; without, even the fragrant trees fall away. O brother Śoṇa, there is no one who does not laugh at the ruin of your prosperity.
"O shameless one, abandon this delay! What is the use of these deep and sweet sounds? Release the water instantly with a splashing roar!
Alas, look at the condition of this tree, its body entangled in the mass of flames from the forest fire flickering due to the encounter with the pitiless wind! (VidSrk 33.11)

It is fitting that the honey-bees should abandon this tree at the time when its flowers perish; let that be so. But this is something never seen before, nor have we heard any report of it: that these bees should abandon even the bark of the branches, which are as thin as slender stalks.
That cloud is worthy of homage; it truly produces joy for the eyes and, though lowly, attains lightness for the sake of others by becoming as dear as a petitioner.
Even its name is worth hearing, yet it does not bring about the destruction of people; indeed, even its rising serves to uplift them.

He beheld the splendor of the lake, sweet with the humming of swarms of bees summoned by the thick fragrance of night-lotuses awakened by the contact with the rising rays of the moon; there, a colony of frogs dwelling within the hollows of blind wells lives happily, as if they were partaking of nectar.
"O goldsmith Maitrīśrī, you have come here to sell articles worthy of being heard [prized] by the ears;
it was not heard from anywhere that the village chief here, Aviddhakarṇa, was still alive. (VidSrk 33.15)
The rivers of rutting ichor belonging to the elephants of the quarters, which used to dry up instantly at the roar of that lion— the abode of majesty whose wrath was never in vain—
now that he has fallen by fate into a miserable state, this aged elephant drags the mass of his mane with his trunk.

Your leap, your claws as hard as adamant that endure the scaling of mountain peaks, your fierce splendor, and that great roar which shatters the mountains—all these means for the sole conquest of the world have been acquired by a lion who, out of laziness, did not leave his mountain cave while sleeping; yet he has accomplished nothing at all.
O people! Let the trees indeed stand along every path and in every forest, laden with fruit and bending low;
yet the state of the Malaya tree is truly unique, in that even its mere fragrance dispels all distress.

That you are called "kinsman" by those crows because you are born from a nest, because you have the luster of collyrium, because you move in the sky, and because you are a bird—that sound of yours, which is a rich outpouring of a flavor that delights beyond the senses, has become a fault; O leader of sweet-voiced birds, for that is simply their nature.
O Aśoka tree, what is the use of your humility, what of your height, what of your dense shade, what of the playfulness of your young shoots, and even of this splendor of your flowers?
For indeed, alas, the multitude of weary travelers seated at your root, though praising you, do not eat your sweet and soft fruits to their heart's content out of longing.
What greater blessing could there be for us than this means of livelihood, that you, alas, O brother charcoal-maker, cut down these trees and burn them?
But what remedy is there for the travelers distressed by sunbeams as piercing as lightning in this shelterless desert wilderness?
The quarters are stretched out with ropes, the waters are filled with poison, the earth is bound with snares, and the forest edges are ablaze with fire;
the hunters, bows in hand, follow his tracks—where can the leader of the deer herd find refuge?

Having taken water from hundreds of rivers on all sides, what indeed has been accomplished by this great ocean? It has been turned salty, offered as a libation into the submarine fire, and deposited within the hollow cavity of the underworld.

Having endured the hardship of intense frost, certain trees—bound by a vow of ingratitude—gradually shed their leaves as if out of a desire for more foliage; they did not mind even the loss of their own shade at that time. Yet, on the very trunks of those same trees, those who act with gratitude remain seated, even as they wither away.
In that very same pristine, excellent lake, where once herds of wild elephants with upraised trunks plunged entirely into the mud due to the heat and torment of the summer season,
now— having by fate reached a state of desiccation— the restless minnow enters the silt out of fear of being swallowed by a crane.
That you touch the sky with your waves, that you illuminate the depths of the netherworld with jewels, and that you cover the earth with your waters—
all this of yours, O Ocean, is a mere trifle, since you are abandoned on the shore by travelers eager to take water, who instead release streams of tears.

Fortune is fickle; the moon is stained by its dark spot; the king of jewels (the sun) is cruel; and even the beloved of Abhramu (Airāvata) is ever intoxicated. Thus, reflecting upon the misconduct of his own kin within him, the ocean is intensely consumed by the fire named Vāḍava under the guise of a flame.

/var{@bhramu@/lem /emend/ /Ingalls, @trabhramu@ /edKG}/ var{@bhramu@/lem /emend/ /Ingalls, @trabhramu@ /edKG} means "delusion" (Sanskrit: *bhrānti*). It refers to an error or cognitive distortion. In the context of Buddhist epistemology and philosophy, it denotes a state of mind that perceives things incorrectly, such as perceiving what is impermanent as permanent, or what is selfless as having a self. It is often contrasted with non-delusion (*abhrānti*), which signifies a clear and correct cognition. In this specific textual instance, the manuscript reading is *trabhramu*, while Ingalls emends it to *bhramu*. Thus, the corrected term is **delusion**.

While the herds of deer—whose chests are curled up in the corners of various caves and whose heads and tails are hidden out of fear and pain from even a tiny particle of the foul-smelling wind rising from the road—are terrified, this śarabha, though he has been praised at will for his victory over proud and intractable scent-elephants, stands smiling; remembering his former births, he feels the utmost compassion in his heart.

By even a single ocean, those clouds have been filled by the crores; yet not even a loss of water as fine as a drop of dew resting on the tip of a blade of kusha grass has occurred for him. Alas! By the turning of fate, the clouds, though gathering together with their waters, are unable to produce even a momentary stillness in his dust.
Out of fear of breaking their bounds, and due to their possession of infinite essence, fortitude, and depth, all these oceans with their waters restrained do not indeed become agitated.

However, if by some stroke of fate they were to undergo agitation at any time, then neither the earth, nor the multitude of mountains, nor even the sun and moon would remain; everything would become a single vast ocean. (VidSrk 33.30) We have heard from afar the supreme name of the ocean, "the mine of jewels," but we have not seen the gems that fall within the range of our vision.
High waves have arrived before us on the shore, eager for prey, and there are crocodiles with clearly visible, formidable tusks. (VidŚrk 33.31)
Having beheld you, O tree, with your beautiful shade and your crown bowed down by the weight of fruit—granting the pacification of all suffering—we have come here, abandoning our path.
If, however, within your hollow there is the terrifying sight of the poison-fire vomited from the throbbing mouths of a row of serpents moving inside, then you are truly worthy of our worship.
O cuckoo chick, maintain silence for now until these two wings are capable of flying into the expanse of the sky;
otherwise, you will surely be seen shattered by the blows from the beaks of crows, enraged by sounds alien to their own species.

Even a lion—whose mass of mane is smeared with streaks of blood from the flayed skin torn by claws upon his maw—is possessed of an inviolable majesty; yet even a decrepit monkey bears the name "hari. What more need be said here?

Where is your birthplace on the slopes of Malaya, and where are those forest-dwellers? Where indeed is the cutting by the axe, and where is this journey to distant lands? Where is the whetting on the surface of a hard stone, and where is this beautiful form smeared with mud? O friend sandalwood, do not fall into despair; your very virtues are your blemish.
Tell me, you who know the news of what has occurred in Jambudvīpa:
has the throat-pipe of the cātaka bird—dusty from its intense thirst—ever been placed upon a river, a lake, or the ocean, even for a moment, after it had abandoned a rain-cloud?
When the ocean, whose wealth was violently churned by that powerful Fate through a contemptible act, was robbed of its riches, did it lose its depth by so much?
Does it cease to nourish the clouds? Does it break its bounds? Or does it fail to protect the submarine fire? (Vidyākara’s Subhāṣitaratnakośa 33.37)
O leader of the herd of young *śarabhas*, what other mountain here is capable of supporting you as you stride from the peak of Bheruśikhara, which captivates with its unrestrained majesty?
Therefore, O you whose soul is pampered by the art of leaping over difficult peaks, go; that very Lord of Mountains, strewn with golden moonlight, is the fit dwelling for you.
Vallaṇa’s dark days have passed; you, a treasury of splendors, have been seen.
Now, while filling the quarters with light, why are you obscured by clouds?

The greatness of the ocean—pervading the quarters, scraping the sky with the crests of its surging waves, and visible to the eye—is rendered wondrous by those [waves] which, having become silent as they entered the hollows between the fingers of the Sage’s joined palms, were seen to be no larger than the interior of his water-pot, with the schools of crocodiles and sharks nestled within the gaps of his interlaced fingers. (VidSrk 33.40)

In that very lake, which had seemed dead with frogs dwelling in its hollows, buried within the earth with tortoises, and repeatedly fainted from the wild boars wallowing upon its broad bed of mud, Abhinanda’s efforts were such that a cloud out of season arrived and caused the water to be drunk by herds of wild elephants submerged up to their temples.

"O young lion, you who are a mere cub, if you would abandon your anger toward this elephant, we shall say this: what has been gained by your long-lived self in slaying this entire thousand of elephants?
If you say, 'I am indeed capable of doing this,' then fie on you, fool! Is the ocean not able to flood the world on all sides? It is because it maintains its fortitude. (VidSrk 33.42)
Truly, O Pippala, best of trees, this path of the righteous has been graced by you, who stand tall with dense shade; what more can be said? You are a manifestation of Hari himself.
Furthermore, that the birds taking refuge in you—merry-mouthed with the enjoyment of your fruit—should produce the warbling of male cuckoos is nothing short of supreme excellence.

On a banyan tree laden with fruit, some fruit ripens with its flavor fully manifest; even among those, only a few seeds reach the stage of sprouting; and yet, among those too, only a single excellent sprout attains that height toward which wayfarers run as if to their own mother to quench their weariness. (VidSrk 33.44)
Thinking that from this flower of the *śālika* tree— which is already great by its very nature— one will likely obtain a fruit that is exceedingly large, beautiful, sweet, fragrant, and cool,
the parrot remains there with such hope; yet, through his perception of the timing of the *śālmali*’s ripening, he sees the downy cotton emerging from the suture of the fruit’s opening.

Because of its sweetness, extreme coolness, purity, and capacity to soothe the fever of distress, this water—belonging both to milk and to the ocean—is called "milk" (payaḥ) in the same sense as the liquid itself.
Yet, regarding that very ocean, a further description occurs to me: that upon meeting it, the milk increases; whereas by that same [ocean], its friend [the milk] is itself consumed when boiled.
With his wives he sported like the intoxicated preceptor of the gods; by him alone, and not by this other, was the vast host of gods and asuras shattered in their conflict.

This one is certainly not he, nor is he like him, for he is no maker of darkness (the moon). Who is this, O friend, who is like a blemish upon the sun—equal to the spot on the moon to those with eyes?
They constantly come and go to Madhukūṭa; they do not take account of whether the water is cold or harsh. Alas, we do not know whose days these are, nor what they will do.
This navel-lotus of Hari, whose majesty is a marvel to the entire world, is not to be blamed; for destiny prevails everywhere.
For here Brahmā drinks his own life-span as honey, yet the bees plunder that nectar, which is more fragrant than ambrosia, with an excess of sweat.
When the sun, having destroyed the entire mass of darkness and attained great majesty, prevails as the eye of the world—that opportunity has passed.
Now, as he resorts to the mountain of setting with his power of light dissolved, let the demons frolic and let the gloom shroud the quarters of the sky.
"O travelers on the path to the Lord of Virtue, return once more to that lake, the ornament of the road; having reached its clarity, sport there with the weight of your fatigue dispelled.
But from this salt ocean, whose waters are churned by aged crocodiles, retreat is auspicious, for entry is not possible by any means."

In that beautiful lake where a flock of swans drinks the pure water with ease, a young *cātaka* bird, out of delusion, does not drink the water—whether by nature or through pride. What does this matter to the bird? Does it cause the lake to become high or light?
Cease from this onset; desist and restrain this anger, O Hari. This rising sound belongs to the clouds, not to elephants.
Indeed, these masses of water, flame, mountain-peak, and wind are roaring by their very nature; but when you are present, this world is rendered free of pride.
