O Amarasiṃha, why do you suddenly strike the tree by the road like one mad? Why do you tear at the lake with its blossoming lotuses with blows from your trunk?
Then we shall recognize your incomparable outburst of strength, O noble elephant, if you touch the mane of even a sleeping lion cub.
"O jewel, abandon your distress here, thinking, 'I have been cast up by merciless waves upon the shore within the ocean.
Surely some king, whose heart is drawn by acquaintance with your virtues, will make you the object of kisses from the makara-designs upon his crown."

Why are you afflicted with grief at the *aśoka* tree, agitated in mind at the *bakula*, and joyless at the *kunda*? You take no delight even with the *sahakāra* mango trees; since you place your trust here in the *kusumbha*, O wretched bee, you will undoubtedly have your body wounded by its hundreds of thorns.
The rising of the sun brings great joy and not at all weariness, for who in this world has not gone to their setting in the course of time, or who is not going, or who will not go?
Only this causes distress: that darkness, excluded from light, has found a place even in that very sky which is vast by nature.
One scatters a painful mass of hailstones; another thunders excessively; yet another hurls down fierce lightning-fire;
and another produces a swift wind—know this first, O bird: why do you open your beak at every single cloud?
Do not hoard the abundance of fruit, nor conceal yourself with your leaves, O tree on the riverbank; bestow this very gift that is so appropriate.
Surely, today or tomorrow, the pitiless river, with its waves as high as palm trees and turbid with the onset of the rainy season, will cast you down from your splendor.
"O sandalwood tree, drawn from afar in every direction by your fragrances, we have come here in person to see you, the very embodiment of Fortune.
What do we see, O fortunate one? A serpent is playing right upon your chest! May it be well with you; release us, for we must depart."
Indeed, not even an atom serves as an ornament for his chest; yet you partake of this very thing, which is likewise his own manifestation.
In this charming lake, who among the lordly elephants, submerged by the exhaustion of their labors, has not constantly drunk the water?
O Cloud, for the Cātaka bird who has long been languishing in the supportless sky of Śrīdharmakara, with his upturned beak extended toward you,
let alone the showers from the ocean— your sweet sound itself was never heard by him.
"O Ocean, though we are overcome by exhaustion, we desired from you not even a small amount of water for the sake of our extensive prosperity.
Why are you so excessively agitated with waves? Be gracious; salutations to you! In every direction there are hundreds of auspicious lotus-pools for us. (VidSrk 33.63)
Having wandered and wandered from direction to direction and gazed again and again, we have seen no tree equal to this Acala,
which, like sandalwood, spreads an ever-increasing and heart-stealing fragrance even when scorched by fire, cut down, or rubbed against a stone surface.
This *cātaka* bird flies toward the clouds, hears their thunder, endures the hailstones, and withstands the waves of lightning;
it fans its wings, utters its cry, and even at the cost of a few drops of water, it persists. (VidSrk 33.65)
"O bee, you are bound to the immovable lotus; know first that such is the nature of this addiction! O heedless bee, why do you flutter fruitlessly over the closing flower? (VidSrk 33.66)
"O friend, even after these clouds have stolen his entire wealth,
they still act as friends; what then can be said of those who do unpleasant things?"
What does this monkey not do with this very *śrīphala* fruit?
He laughs, leaps, swings about, and looks down at the people below. (VidSrk 33.68)
Another too, bound by thirst for its virtues, strives to water the sandalwood tree of noble form, which delights the sun;
but for this śākhoṭaka tree, which is devoid of merit, even the great-hearted cloud is its only refuge.
Thunder, O cloud, if you will; release water, if you will; threaten once more with streaks of lightning, if you will.
But behold: as for this bird, whose own activity is dependent on its past karma, you alone are its fate.

This is the churning vessel, the ocean of milk itself; this is the churning rod, Vāsuki; and this is the mountain used as the pivot—now that the gods and demons have raised their staff-like arms, which are no longer sluggish with pride, it is truly the moment for them to scratch their itching limbs. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 33.71)
O Bhaṭṭagaṇapati, why do we say much about this tree? This natural sap of service toward others is ever-present;
for even though it was uprooted by the wind on the path through the difficult terrain of the ocean, alas, it has here become a bridge for people. (VidSrk 33.72)
His body is foul-smelling, his deeds are intent upon the slaughter of others, and his discernment between good and evil is said to be that of a beast;
thus, there is nothing at all admirable in the lion, yet he possesses some inexplicable majesty by which the wretched world is sustained.
Tell me, O lake on the path of the virtuous, whose thirst do you not quench? Who does not plunge into you, provided that the crocodile does not dwell within your embrace? — [Thus spoke] the Hero.

The great cloud does not flash, nor does it thunder; it scatters no hailstones and produces no lightning; it releases no whirlwind, yet it rains silently. How could the *kadamba* tree fail to have its every limb covered with dense horripilation?
Free from any desire for recompense, the cloud nourishes the entire world. Stretching out its trunk like the hand of a lion, the sun, resting upon the southern quarter, [sustains all].
Not only has he made himself light by this act, but even the day itself has been shortened.
It is impossible to dry out the receptacles of oil or even to cover them with a canopy,
for even while being burned, they burst open after manifesting the oil within.

The earth cannot serve as a support, nor can even the seven oceans quench the pain of thirst, nor does Mount Meru provide wealth for one whose human effort has been brought under the sway of previously accumulated evil karma; even the wish-fulfilling tree does not grant his desired object. (VidSrk 33.79)

Having comforted the mountain ranges scorched by the heat of the sun, having quenched the forests distressed by forest fires, and having filled hundreds of various rivers and streams—you are now empty, O cloud; that very state is your exalted glory.

O tree of rest, tell me where now, in this time of calamity, are those living beings whom you previously nurtured with fruits, leaves, and shade? Blessed indeed are these bark-skins, for which a reward was prepared merely by their presence; had it not been for the cutting away of them, this axe would not have fallen upon you.
O cloud, even if you cast Vittoka far away with winds of terrifying speed, or crush him firmly with rocks,
or repeatedly strike his eyes with lightning bolts— even then, O water-bearer, there is no other refuge for the cātaka bird.
When it arose, something was conceived in the mind of the cātaka bird, languid with many desires;
alas, what a tragedy! Now, from that very cloud which was the cause for the rite of bestowing desired fruits, a stroke of lightning falls.
Now that the divine Laḍahacandra has fallen under the power of time, alas, O Darkness, why do you swell in every direction, having found an opportunity while the Sun is obscured?
But here rises before you the full moon, endowed with all its digits, having seized the hundreds of rays of that very [Sun] who has set, and utterly destroying you.

O mango tree, you are fortunate now, filling the mouths of crows and parrots with your fruit. But that bee who once sported for a moment upon you when you were awakened by the weight of your blossoming clusters—since he does not come to you now that you bear fruit, is it not his nature to seek fruit, even in the wish-fulfilling tree?

That sprout of coral which was first seen within the opening of a split shell, having generally begun its growth through the stages of the two leaves and so forth, eventually established its seat upon a branch.

Glossy with new shoots, dense with buds, flowering with wide-spreading radiance, and bearing fruit with excellence, this is some extraordinary mango tree that has bowed down deeply. Many are born here in this lineage of tortoises; however, not even a single female tortoise has ever given birth to one, nor does she give birth now, nor will she ever give birth—one who would be capable of granting even a few days of rest to that tortoise whose soul is exhausted by contraction from bearing the burden of the earth until the end of the aeon.
O Hanumān,
you are a boat made of the wood of existence (bhava) that possesses a heart;
otherwise, how could you be drawn by the virtues (guṇas) belonging to another?
O Blessed Night, I bow to you; it is upon you that the virtue of a devoted wife is seen on earth.
When the lord of the night has departed, you bear a form as dark as collyrium.
Fie on this profundity! Fie on the nectar-like nature of the ocean! Fie on these long, trembling arms of its waves!
At the very outset, its body was devoured by forest fires; neither the groves on the banks nor even a mere spray of water could provide it any relief.

O Great Sage, even that water which served as the consolation for the ocean— which is shaped like a whorl and is a peerless mass of virtues— when Uccaiḥśravas and others had been forcibly seized, was drunk by you who are devoid of compassion.
O river, though the flood that stays for only a few days during your ascent through the forest may rise very high,
it will pass; but the single sin of felling the trees on your banks will endure for a long time.
The waves are stilled, the water is clear, motionless, and smooth; this humble appearance of the rivers seems to proclaim their tranquility.
Nevertheless, because of those various trees fallen all around upon their banks, that very same lack of restraint—which was previously held in check—now manifests before the mind.
"O lotus pond, is it fitting for you now to cast down that staff which, standing firm, has always proclaimed you to be established as one who remains impartial?"—
thus [spoke] the Protector of the Virtuous.
This has been done improperly by the deer,
that they have abandoned the forest— the place of their lifelong play— out of fear while the forest fire blazes upon the heads of the trees.
(Of the *khadira* tree.)
The beasts and birds are scattered, the deities of the groves are brought to distress, and the quarters of the sky and the earth itself are scorched by fumes naturally dark with soot.
Having reduced those various great trees—along with their flowers, shoots, and leaves—to ashes, the wicked forest fire has left the wood as nothing but a mound of ant-hills.
This bee, having been separated from the contact with the temples of elephants, now resolves to partake of the bitter ichor of their enemies.
When the lotuses have become worthy of being contemplated, fie on this wretched life of this filthy creature! (VidSrk 33.97)
It is truly marvelous that those very stones, when heated, do not emit fire even when touched by the rays of the moon;
yet how is it possible that moonstones produce a purifying and cooling liquid? VidSrk_33.98 (1116)
O gold, though you have been rendered perfectly pure by burning, cutting, and rubbing, your heaviness is in vain,
since you have mounted the scale together with guñjā seeds.
(VidSrk 33.99) [Of the cow] Surabhi...

A conch shell from the Southern Sea, driven to the shore by waves tossed high by the force of the wind, has by the power of cruel fate been taken up by village women who, mistaking it for a sea-snail, carry it away along with their shells, wondering: "Has it been burnt, or will it turn into ink? VidSrk_33.100 (1118)
A flaw in good conduct is like a flaw in a gem; for the sake of its virtues, it is the cause of its being set in the position of a leader.
Otherwise, how could it roll at the feet and upon the crest of the lords? (VidSrk 33.101)
How can a roasted parrot from a royal aviary ever disparage you, O mango, whose taste is sweet and whose texture is tender upon ripening—
especially when compared to the coconut, which possesses limitless hardness and whose essence and beauty have vanished for one whose heart is enslaved by passion?
O *kiṃpāka* fruit, you possess a red exterior at ripening, yet you seek beauty with an interior that is bitter and black when seen;
for this much alone, I do not know whose wall of heart-delight you are, once the crow has been cast aside.
—By Buddhākaragupta.

Cease your roaring, O ocean, and abandon your restlessness; what is this pride for a few pebbles of gemstone? Cast your gaze upon Mount Meru, for it is honored by its plateaus of jewels and remains in great silence; moreover, through its steadfastness, it makes the very world stable.
Placing the command of the Sage upon your head, remain on the Vindhya mountain if you desire that exceedingly lofty station; yet you must never again overstep this [limit].
For one who drank the ocean—which found its abode in mountains such as Maināka—would even the slight discomfort of your touch against his cheek arise when he swallows you?
Who can deny that those śallakī shoots are fond of being seized in his upraised trunk, and that lake of the mountains is capable of withstanding his splashing?
Yet, O Lord, because of its very long sighs, this lordly elephant, exhausted as he rests upon his pillar-like tusks, is a lover separated from you—that Vindhya mountain.
Thus ends the section on "Designations for Others"; next follows the section on "Winds":
Winds that fill the atmosphere with the fragrance of lotus stalks crushed by wild elephants, and which are enriched by breezes from the wings of swans as they flutter.
The breezes from Lake Pampā, touching the pride of the swift-moving cranes who leap over waves far-reaching in the distance, seem to anoint the quarters with sprays of liquid camphor.
Moving slowly due to the exertion of rubbing against the firm, swelling breasts of Andhra women, setting in motion the beautiful, golden-brown tresses of lovely Dravidian brides,
smelling the lotus-faces of Siṃhala women, and kissing the cheeks of Kerala women, the southern breezes, fragrant with the scent of the Malaya mountains, blow gently.
Having touched this flowering creeper belonging to Vasukalpa and having bathed in the pool,
the wind blows very slowly, as if apprehensive of contact with her once again. (VidSrk 34.3)

The winds blow, carrying the spray of the Revā river, shattering the seal of pride of the women of Andhra and Murala, made resonant by the *hūṃ* cries of young female cuckoos; they are thieves of the jasmine pollen from the braided hair of Kerala women, restless as they pull at their lovers, and have come to a standstill upon the slopes of the breasts of the broad-hipped women of Coḍa. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 34.4)
Shaking the *campaka* trees on the grounds surrounding the Kāverī river, the breeze from Śrīkaṇṭha’s region blows gently, scattering the nectar of the *kunda* clusters;
it causes the curls of hair on the foreheads of the women of Lāṭa— already disheveled by the tugging of their lovers’ affection— to dance wildly, falling straight down to their very roots.
This one southern breeze, gentle and charming, blows to loosen the bonds of a lover’s pride;
shaking the waves of the ocean waters within, this fragrant wind bestows the scent of camphor while sporting playfully.
Having long enjoyed this bride of the southern quarter, the wind, out of fear of her, gradually abandons her;
adorned with ornaments made of sandalwood and other fragrant woods, he departs for the north as if toward a beloved mistress.

The wind blows, scattering the groves of *lavaṅga*, *lodhra*, and *lavalī* trees; shaking the *karañja* trees, it is chilled by the garlands of waves from the waters of the Muralā, which have been enjoyed and left behind.

A breeze blows at will from the vicinity of the marshy groves of plantain trees on the banks of the Southern Ocean, intensified by the rustling sound produced as it strikes the slopes of the Kāverī riverbank.

Kissing their faces, rolling over the slopes of their breasts, tossing their locks of hair, and scattering the hem of their garments, the Malaya breeze—arousing the sports of the Mind-born God, agitating their limbs, unsettling their minds, and utterly uprooting their pride—embraces every limb of women like a lover. (VidSrk 34.9)
In the expanse of the flowering forests, the breeze— possessing the majesty of a mass of matted locks fashioned from garlands of *alīna* flowers,
and displaying a coating of ash-like pollen from blossoms— moves slowly, slow as a wandering mendicant intent on gathering flowers.

The evening breezes, fragrant with freshly blossomed jasmine and not yet touched by the dust of the earth, gently awaken the sleeping god of love in longing lovers who dwell in the courtyards of their pleasure-garden houses— courtyards flooded by water from the irrigation channels falling into basins darkened by young grass.

Today, as the evening breezes—fragrant with fresh jasmine—settle upon the mountain peaks, they generally cause the deer-eyed women to slacken their passion for the flower-bowed god; for those women who frequent the palace terraces, these winds now dry the sandalwood paste from their breasts, which had been so intensely pressed against the broad chests of Acala-siṃha that they instantly withered it. Now that the spring has passed, the winds evoke a new sense of despondency.
While the wind carrying cool droplets blew, the mind-born god, as if hurrying out of fear of the cold,
entered the hearts of women separated from their lovers, where the fire of grief had already been kindled.

Having been released from the long slopes of the Malaya plateau, the southern breeze—suddenly revealing the fragrance of sandalwood that betrays its affection—descends very slowly upon the Mādhavī vines; having arrived after a long time, it seems to announce a supreme terror. (VidSrk 34.14)
At dawn, these breezes blow very gently, fragrant everywhere with blossoming wild jasmine; they possess the majesty of thundering clouds ready for battle,
and they steal away the drops of perspiration from the foreheads of young women exhausted by the combat of love.
Worn out by the playful drinking bouts of the serpent-maidens exhausted from the weight of their breasts,
the Malaya breeze here grows robust once more through the sighs of those separated from their lovers.
These breezes are the adversaries of the fatigue produced around the full breasts of the wives of village chiefs, who were distressed by intense amorous play.
In every pond, the breezes blow at their own will, catching the excellence of the fragrance of *gundrā* grass as it breaks under the pressure of the boars' tusks.

In Dvārakā, the winds—whose movement is momentarily suspended by the lofty moonstone palaces of Śaṅkhapāṇi, and which cause the waters of the western ocean to tremble—are ever enjoyed by the fortunate. These breezes carry within them the exhalations of guggulu resin, released by the weight of the roars of angry lions awakened at the stroke of the hard trunks of the city’s foremost elephants.
Causing a dense network of horripilation to arise on the limbs through their touch with the cold, and licking the blossoming mango sprouts as they break from the beaks of cuckoos,
these Malaya breezes blow very gently, removing at the day's end the eye-fatigue caused by the day for the fawn-eyed women.

O friend, at dawn this breeze blows, crushing the dense drops of perspiration on the surface of the high, full breasts of sleepless Dravidian women; it is refined by the fragrance of the oozing sap of sandalwood trees and is the remnant left over from being enjoyed by female serpents.

Those southern winds—the great witnesses to the victory of Love—which cause the swinging play of the fawn-eyed women, which instantly sever the sting of grief, and which are the preeminent masters in the ritual initiation of passion throughout the three worlds; now, rolling upon the throats of cuckoos, they breathe forth the fifth note, the king of melodies, at their own will. —By Rājaśekhara. (VidSrk 34.21) [1145]

Fragrant with the emerging buds of its crest-cluster opening wide, having become intimately acquainted with the ritual of the dance-play of the creepers, and moving slowly due to the fatigue of carrying away the abundant flow of nectar, the breeze shatters the gardens and, by means of the arrows of the Mind-born God, brings them to ruin.

Exhausted by the swaying of the thickets of mango groves, these gale winds—charming with the overflowing river of fragrance from the dense clusters of opening jasmine buds, scattering sprays of young frost-mist from the surging waves of rain shimmering near the dwellings—now sport. (VidSrk 34.23)
[This is] the work of Buddhākaragupta. Thus ends the section on winds; next is the section on castes. 35.
Rolled in mud mixed with cumin and dusted with black pepper, causing a tingling sensation in the tongue and lips due to their pungency and heat;
their bodies smeared with copious oil from which the fire had not yet died down—I immediately fried and swallowed several pieces of *kavayi* fish.
Casting his gaze repeatedly at the chariot as it pursues him with a graceful turn of the neck, he has drawn his hindquarters far into his forebody out of fear that an arrow might strike him;

scattering the path with half-chewed grass falling from his mouth opened by exhaustion, behold, because of his high leaps, he travels much more in the air and but little upon the earth. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 35.2) — By Kālidāsa.
Circling repeatedly above at will in accordance with its flight-path, the hawk— having established itself firmly, cast its gaze forward,

and fixed its aim upon a piece of meat in the courtyards of the outcaste hamlets— spreads its broad wings wide as they flutter and expand from the force of its sharp downward swoop, and snatches the half-burnt morsel from the belly of a cooking pot in a Cāṇḍāla settlement.
With necks outstretched and the cavities of their mouths wide open and crimson, their palms fluttering from thirst and their bodies trembling as they have not yet grown wings,
the young *śarāri* birds rise slightly from the ground at dawn on the riverbank and drink the dew-water trickling through channels made of *vīraṇa* grass leaves.
With one breast clearly revealed as her vine-like arm rises with the force of pulling the rope, making a jingling sound from the row of conch-shell bangles that tremble as the cord snaps;
with her pair of thick thighs spread wide across and her expansive hips made prominent by the bending of her back—the low-born woman draws up water from the well again and again.

Stretching out his feet one by one along with his two wings, and drawing them together against his sides, the pigeon yawns from within the interior of his nest, slowly extending his pale bellies and wing-roots over his neck; his eyes are particularly red from the remnants of sleep, and the openings of his mouth are split wide as far as his corners.
Awakened at dawn by the sweet sounds of the tinkling anklets of courtesans moving about the golden water-pitchers, the pigeon shakes his wings and,
having long and ardently kissed his mate whose eyes are slightly closed, coos with longing, his throat faltering as it is gently shaken.
Having leapt far up from Vikramāditya and the ascetic,
and having shaken its wings, the fish-hawk, fixing its aim for a moment and watching below,
plunges into the middle of the water and emerges with a fish.

Having departed from the nest of Vākpatirāja, shaking his wings and ascending to the top of a tree, the cock thereon gradually begins to crow with his neck outstretched, his tail raised, one foot lifted, and his crest bristling. (VidSrk 35.9)

O friend, the cowherd milks the cow in a manner that captivates the mind with the sound of the stream trickling from between the mouths of the jars held fast by the mechanism of his two knees bent downward; his fingers are curved by the pressure of his big toes, the ground is covered by the half of his foot, and he repeatedly strikes away the biting insects with both elbows, causing them agitation on his sides.
With his ears pricked forward and his head bowed, the dog of Upādhyāya Dāmara— his tail-stalk quivering as it was tucked into the cleft of his hips, which were worn out by age—
spies from afar a rival dog whose neck is throbbing with mature, aggressive rage; then, baring teeth like jasmine buds and whimpering slightly, he moves away.
If a pot-bellied man kisses his beloved, he falls away from his own interest; if he pursues his own interest, he does not obtain the taste of his beloved’s lip.
Fools of dull intellect, blinded by lust, pursue both, because when the body is occupied by a protruding belly in sexual union, there can be neither one nor the other. (VidSrk 35.12)
With clusters of clear water droplets clinging to the ends of her disheveled, curly hair, arranging her hands in the *svastika* gesture while pressing against the fullness of her new breasts,
wearing her silk garment tucked between her plump thighs, this young girl rises from the water, slightly bent over, her eyes flickering with a sidelong glance toward the bank.
At midnight in the palm groves, the elephants of King Bhoja— standing silently with their ears like fans,
eyes half-closed, and trunks resting on the tips of their tusks— hear the sound of the downpour from the clouds as they discharge water. (VidŚrk 35.14)
In the surrounding ground dug up by the tips of the plow belonging to the elephant-keeper, village sparrows roll about at will, scattering the earth with the tips of their claws;
their eyes are repeatedly closed and opened as they are bewildered by contact with particles of dust raised by the wind produced from the movement of their pair of wings.
With his back arched, his head and tail-tip raised and quivering, one eye fixed inside the house out of fear, and both ears motionless;
with a face made terrifying by bared fangs and gaping corners of the mouth smeared with saliva, the dog—his throat swollen from the suppression of his breath—leaps upon the cat. (VidSrk 35.16)
In the clear water of the lake, a crane, desiring to catch fish, places his steps very slowly while turning his eyes here and there;
with one leg raised in the air and his neck twisted sideways, he gazes again and again at even a moving leaf with hopeful expectation.
With their reins loosened, these chariot-horses— stretching their forebodies forward, with the tips of their chowries motionless and their ears pricked up rigidly—
gallop as if unable to endure the speed of the deer, remaining unassailable even by the dust raised by themselves.

Then, stretching out his hind legs and extending his body by bending it low at the haunches, the horse— raising his neck high and pressing his face against his chest, shaking his dust-grey mane— rises from his bed and, with his muzzle constantly flickering in its desire for a mouthful of fodder, scratches the earth slowly with his hoof while making a soft sound.

Having sniffed the surface of the earth, with dust drawn up by the tips of his hooves, the horse—having gathered all his legs together, his knees bending in succession, and his body released from tension—twists his limbs two or three times out of a desire to remove the itch from his back and flanks; then, rising quickly and remaining motionless for a moment, he shakes his body starting from the face. First stretching their legs, lowering their necks, raising their faces, and repeatedly striking with their hooves, the calves [play].
With their faces turned toward them by their mothers, they drink from the breast while their minds are at ease, as the back half of their mouths licks it.

While his beloved was acting wantonly, the deer—exhausted by the extreme heaviness of her womb and by the Kirāta running close behind with his bow drawn to his ear—is bewildered by a mixture of love for his mate and the fear for his life; he looks back again and again, yet continues to move forward.

With his small umbrella shattered, his belly coiled with the complications of many stomachs, a bilva leaf tucked into his crest, and his throat terrifying with its deep cavernous folds, the aged student—exhausted by wandering long distances—somehow slowly restrains the pain in his feet and approaches the house of a Brahmin at evening to split firewood at his own leisure. [And there is] the fierce [peacock], whose trembling crest-tip is deceived by its darting, restless beak, as it falls; its neck quivering with the expansion of its mane of bristling filaments, formidable like a circle of wheels.
A pair of cocks, their feet repeatedly struck by the thickly throbbing claws that sweep upward again and again, fight with swift steps and cruel maneuvers.

These gale winds play with the clusters of water-troughs—shaking them, tossing them, letting them go, striking them, clashing them, uprooting them, hurling them up, and whirling them about—while the trees, their branches trembling and birds distressed and ill at ease, are shaken; these winds, matted with the black hair of decayed nests, drag along heaps of dust. (Vidvatsamvāda 35.25)

These village settlements on the dry upland plains captivate the mind, where the scent of chickpeas being constantly roasted prevails and the shadows are worn by long exposure to the parched soil; they resound with the noise of heavy water-lifting machines swung by the exuberant hands of young, rustic women, while their deep interiors of houses remain empty.

In this sky, the column of smoke from the forest fire— slightly curled, spread out, somewhat broken and bent, its power gradually accumulated through a gentle grace, heaped up and then rising again, dark as the shoulder of a young buffalo— creeping at its own will, creates fleeting leaf-patterns.

In some places, villages—where the lords of the land have become devoid of compassion and where the local clans, though impoverished by groundless calamities, do not abandon their ancestral lands because they are few in number—are filled with withered walls and overgrown with weeds; there, mongooses wander at will through gardens made resonant by the cries of pale-necked pigeons, yet these villages hardly ever reach a state of desolation.

The bull enters the dwelling of the peasant with his horns bent back, catching the streams of water that are diverted by the wind; nearby, the doors are barred by plows poorly yoked, and household vessels are cast down in alarm by the startled women.

Leaping from the corner of the house, they move forward with a few hesitant steps; then, approaching with slow, deliberate movements of their jaws while slightly trembling at the throat, these frogs—falling upon the putrid matter with half-opened eyes and making the sound "micimici"—render the place free of flies by opening their mouths wide like crocodiles.

The songs of the women threshing the *kalama* rice are enchanting, made jagged by the clinking of bracelets as they slip against one another on their sprout-like arms which move restlessly with pestles smooth from constant play; they are further enriched by the breaking of melodic cadences as their chests tremble violently at the sounds of quarrelsome *hūṃ*-cries. (VidSrk 35.31)
He opens his eyes wide, touches them with his hand when they are squinting, looks far away and then again toward what is very close by;
he goes outside into the sunlight and remembers his eye-salve as he gazes at a book, a man overcome by old age.
O Varāha,
on the dusty roadways where the dūrvā grass is covered in dust, the hungry bulls— having had the flies driven from their backs by the base-born— move about at will; yet,
their lives scorched by the entry of the dust stirred up by the wind of their own breath, they eat with difficulty, their grazing interrupted by constant shaking.
In the fields where the mud has dried, the sparrows, their breasts outstretched and white with the color of young sprouts,
move about, leaping most lightly as they peck for seeds.

With their arms raised for a moment, their rows of tinkling bracelets jingling, the sprout-like stems of their arms reveal the series of nail-marks upon the slopes of their breasts as their garments slip away.
Raising repeatedly her hand-lotus that holds a shimmering pestle, with a long garland of jewels hanging down, the woman threshing the *kalama* rice shines forth.

With his tail raised high, his body swelling with joy like a woman's, and his two wings drooping downward, the sparrow circles gracefully around Vāgura again and again with a series of spontaneous leaps;
then, with a longing and languid warbling, he approaches his beloved— who has momentarily set aside her desire for amorous play— trembling for a moment as he utters his sweet call.
On the stalks of the Siddhārtha plants belonging to Sonnoka— wherein the succession of fruit-stalks is bound in shapes that diminish progressively upward,
and whose flowers are falling away in the order of their birth— the process of ripening imparts a tawny hue.
These cranes, with their beaks tucked under their feet, bring delight to the eyes of travelers traveling along the shores of cool lakes;
shaking their heads, they have eyes clouded with tears from the clear contact with the shimmering tails of large fish falling from their gullets.
With his pair of sharp horns turned sideways and his neck and face bent low as he moves, his eyes slightly squinted, and his hooves striking the ground, the bull—
scattering clouds of chaff with his incessant breaths— having achieved victory on the outskirts of the cow-pen, charges toward the herd of cows.

Not far from the forest fire of Mount Acala, which, terrifying with its garland of flames, is licking the very heavens, these cruel smoke-eagles wander from branch to branch in their own haunts; having flown up again and again, their movement is slowed by the joy of devouring moths, they shriek ever louder as they go, their smoky forms difficult to discern due to the heavy fall of soot.
The forest deer drinks its fill of the warm, sweet scum of wild rice porridge— more delicious than that which has just been drunk by his mate who has recently given birth;
and the fragrance of cooking vegetables mixed with *karkandhū* fruits, accompanied by the faint wafting scent of ghee-rich food, spreads all around.
Uttering a welcome as it were with the sweet humming of bees, these trees perform a bow as it were with their heads bent down by fruit;
scattering a rain of flowers as if offering me the guest-offering (argha), tell me, have even the trees learned the ritual of respectful homage?
In this [work] of Śrīharṣa,
these deep forests— with peaks that have been marked with the five fingers by the palms of aged forest-dwellers,

with interiors made formidable by towering summits, and variegated by the bones of men tossed about after being treated like sacrificial animals at the thresholds of the dwellings— seem to bring a trembling to the heart. (VidSrk 35.43)

Having worshipped the goddess Kāntāradurgā, who dwells here in the crevices of rocks, with various offerings of living creatures, and having given blood at the foot of a tree to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), the Barbarians,
accompanied by young women, enjoy aged liquor from the husks of wood-apples at day’s end— their passion for women being momentarily set aside by the diversion of the lute and the gourd-pipe.

The orange tree of the Lord of Yoga shines in its entirety, its yellow hue overcome by a crimsonness manifested through the sequence of its ripening; it bears a fresh seal upon its face, possesses a small well-like depression for its sacred thread, displays a loose and expansive girth, and has branches that breathe forth flames. *Vidagdha-śālabhañjikā* 35.45. (1192)
[The section] of Abhinanda.
Thus ends the "Chapter on Lineages" (jātivrajyā), [numbered] 35. Next is the "Chapter on Greatness" (māhātmyavrajyā), [numbered] 36.
Somewhere here lies that cosmic egg, somewhere the earth, somewhere the clouds, and in other places the oceans garlanded with rows of islands; and in various spots, the mountains.
A wonder is the indescribable majesty of the sky, for despite all these things being situated within it, its emptiness has not even been covered by their names, let alone filled. (VidSrk 36.1)

Behold the ocean of milk, which has Keśaṭa for its stalk, with clouds acting repeatedly as bees drinking from it, and with its thousand trembling ripples as its petals— the single great white lotus of the vast lake that is the three worlds.
The Lord Viṣṇu bore the entire earth; the serpent bore him as well as that earth; and the ocean bore even him along with them.
But Agastya, born from a jar, swallowed even that ocean with effortless ease. Truly, there is no limit to the greatness of the great.

What can we say of the ocean’s glory? For it is indeed the birthplace of Śrī herself. What need is there to speak of its greatness, when even the earth is known by tradition as merely one of its islands? Its generosity is beyond compare; even the clouds become its supplicants for water. And what talk can there be of its power, when its mere agitation brings about the end of an aeon? — Vācaspati.
Having taken some drops of water from this ocean, the clouds then fill the earth, obstructing the sky with their waters;
yet, having obtained from it but one water-nymph whose eyes rolled in fear at the impact of Mount Mandara’s peak, the illustrious Acyuta became the lord of the three worlds.
The wonder of King Muñja is that very Lord Vaḍavānala (the submarine fire), and the wonder of the ocean is that, upon reflecting on their extraordinary deeds, a trembling arises in one's heart:
for the one who devours his own support, no satisfaction arose even as he drank; yet for the other, the Great-Souled One, there was not even the slightest depletion of water from his body.
The sage by whom Keśaṭa was swallowed now dwells upon his bank; that fire of Aurva, which burns with an internal heat like a garland of flowers, is there.
And Hari, who was greatly tormented by him for the sake of all his possessions, sleeps on his lap—oh, what an indescribable majesty belongs to the ocean!
of the mountain (Dharādhara),
bestowing [it].
May that other fire of the pot-born sage Agastya be for our protection—that digestive fire, upon whose reflection the submarine fire (Vāḍava) appears like a mere flame on silken cloth;
that venerable belly wherein the ocean, with its rows of fish, crocodiles, and sharks, wanders roaring, having filled its sides and the sky within.

Salutations to that Agastya, by whom the lord of the waters was drunk— though not even his belly was filled— even as he drank, that ocean remained the very limit of all great wonders, wherein Hari, in the form of the sport-lordly boar, repeatedly submerged himself while creating the illusion of a porpoise, his breath having uprooted Mount Meru and spread across the vault of the sky.
The names of Vācaspati possess many great splendors, and even the moon is sufficient to adorn the circle of the world; yet,
apart from the sun, there is nothing that rises or sets such that by its rising there is day, and by its setting there is night.
His birth was from Jamadagni; that blessed Lord Pinākin was his guru; his renunciation extended to the unfeigned gift of the earth sealed by the seven oceans;
and as for his valor, it is surely not within the path of words, but is made manifest by his deeds. What indeed could be another world for that blessed one, a treasure-house of Brahman and austerity?
(VidSrk 36.11) To this side dwells Keśava; to this side the cities of his enemies; and to this side sleep the winged mountains who have come for refuge.
Moreover, from this [ocean] comes the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction; oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the body of the ocean!
The splendor of the moon remains truly great only so long as the orb of the sun has not yet risen;
once that treasury of all light has appeared, what difference is there between the moon and a patch of white clouds?

A female boar generally gives birth to ten offspring at a time; yet there has never been, nor will there ever be, another capable of bearing the burden of the earth here, who—having placed his own foot upon the circle of the hoods of the Lord of Serpents—lifts up the world and the ocean as they sink within.
Their thirsts are not quenched here and there, nor does anyone else possess such an abundance of water;
yet the oceans fulfill the clouds' success in their resolve to bring about the welfare of the entire world. (VidSrk 36.15)

How can the greatness of the great ocean be described, wherein even Mount Maināka—terrified by the blow of Indra’s thunderbolt—found refuge in the hollow of a wall within a hut made of the tips of moss-sprouts shimmering on the back of a pāṭhīna fish rolling in the deep waters; there, he remained at ease, taking the form of a small boat tossed upon the waves.
What can we say of Vallaṇa? Hari is within his belly; or rather, what of the serpent’s hood, upon which Hari himself lies? Even that ocean occupies but a single spot [within him].
It is a marvel that for this pitcher-born Agastya, that ocean becomes a mere mouthful, the serpent a lotus, and the Lord of Śrī a bee.
If the ocean did not possess such vastness, or if it did not have such depth, or if its compassionate favor toward all sentient beings were not so extensive,
then who would not be reduced to mere ashes by the powerful submarine fire, which blazes within, consumes the waters, and emits wreaths of flames?

Victorious is that sage Keśaṭa, whose blazing fire digests the ocean within his belly, so that only the water remaining after the rest has been vomited up has somehow reached the end of the sea; moreover,
from that gastric fire, as if fresh, the submarine Vāḍava fire has emerged again due to the recent process of vomiting, having once more entered the waters for Yama.
The fire whose waters belong to the illustrious Daśaratha ceases at the end of its dwelling when the cloud departs, along with those very waters;
yet there is another fire which, remaining sleepless even during the onset of the night of universal dissolution, incessantly offers these oceanic waters into its own radiance.
[The story] of Keśaṭa.
Thus ends the section on Greatness (Māhātmyavrajyā), number 36. Next is the section on the Righteous Path (Sadvrajyā), number 37.

The wicked are not to be entreated; even a friend who possesses little wealth is not to be asked for a favor; one’s livelihood should be righteous; and one’s conduct should remain stainless even at the cost of life.
One must stand firm in adversity and follow the path of the great and the virtuous—who taught this difficult vow, which is like walking on the edge of a sword? (VidSrk 37.1)
The conduct of Dharmakīrti is for the most part pleasing; his restraint in speech is sweet with humility; his mind is naturally auspicious; and his acquaintance [with the world] is beyond reproach.
Whether in public or in private, this pure secret of the virtuous, whose flavor is never inverted, reigns supreme. (VidSrk 37.2)
Whether those skilled in ethics censure or praise, whether fortune arrives or departs as it pleases,
whether death comes this very day or at the end of an eon, the steadfast do not stir even a single step from the path of justice.
How could a flaw ever somehow be found in the stainless works of Bhartṛhari? It is only by their virtues that such a flaw is concealed, just as in the case of a pearl. (VidSrk 37.4)

When I knew only a little of Tryambaka, I became like an elephant blinded by rut; then my mind was arrogant, thinking, "I am all-knowing. But when I had acquired some small measure of knowledge from the presence of wise men, the intoxication left me like a fever, as I realized, "I am a fool. (VidSrk 37.5)
Imitating Kālidāsa, the wicked and the good man are indicated by the first and last lines [of this verse] respectively:
"One creates a flaw; the other, being virtuous, fills it. (VidSrk 37.6)
The virtuous, who are like stalks of sugarcane from Puṇḍra— possessing sweet water and being friends to the cow— bend themselves as much as desired if they so wish;
yet when shaken by another with a desire for them to bow, they simply break into a hundred pieces and no longer bend.
Fault, once it has entered the hearts of the wicked, acts like liquid lac;
but in the case of the virtuous, it either does not enter at all, or if it does, it passes through like quicksilver.
Like a cluster of blossoms, the conduct of a wise man is twofold:
he either stands at the head of all the world or withers away in the forest alone.
"You are the king of Vyāsa; we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom served under our gurus. You are renowned for your riches; poets spread our glories in all directions.
"O giver of honor, thus the difference between us two is not very great. If you are turned away from us, we too are entirely free from desire."

The earth is bounded by the ocean, and that reservoir of waters extends for only a hundred yojanas; the sun, ever a traveler, measures the dimensions of the sky—thus, for the most part, all things are closed in by the seal of a manifest limit. Yet, this boundless flash of wisdom belonging to the virtuous triumphs. (VidSrk 37.11)

The virtuous are like arrows: they possess good feathers, are straight, pure, effective, and seekers of merit; yet it is a marvel that, despite having equal qualities, the virtuous are "santaḥ" (peaceful/good) while arrows are merely "śarāḥ" (arrows). — Rājaśekhara, Vidagdhamukhamandana 37.12.

Fortitude in adversity, forbearance in prosperity, eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle, devotion to fame, and dedication to sacred learning—these are indeed the innate qualities of great souls. (VidSrk 37.13)
He is a virtuous man who renders assistance to those in distress,
but not one who is clever at preserving things that were poorly executed or long past.
It is true that in this Kali age, the virtues of the virtuous, even when acquired through great effort, become fruitless due to the adversity of fate;
yet their very fruitfulness is this: they cause the hearts of the wicked to burn with envy.
The fire of anger in both the virtuous man and the wicked man is something unprecedented:
in one it is extinguished by affection, while in the other it increases even when restrained.
They provide shade for others and stand even in the heat;
like trees, virtuous people bear fruit for the sake of others.
They have no regard for affection, nor for a worthy recipient, nor for their own circumstances;
always intent on the welfare of the world, these supreme ones are like lamps filled with jewels.
They regard Fortune as a blade of grass, yet they bow under its weight;
oh, how truly wondrous are the deeds of the great-souled! (VidSrk 37.19)
The flowers held in the hollowed palms perfume both hands;
oh, how uniform is the conduct of the *sumanas* (well-minded ones) toward both the left and the right! VidSrk_37.20*(1232)
"Accepting the reality of others' virtues, concealing one's own virtues, maintaining silence regarding the misfortunes of others,
and speaking words that are sweet and sincere— this is what has been taught to the noble by someone.
Indeed, when reflected upon, a person of good character causes wonder through their far-reaching and virtuous conduct.
But when he comes within the range of vision of embodied beings, he sprinkles their minds as if with nectar. (VidSrk 37.22)
Through association with the wise—who dispel darkness and destroy the evils of the world—even a cruel person abandons his innate impurity and adopts a state of goodness.

For that very water which a person, though parched by thirst, does not wish to drink, instantly loses its saltiness when it stays within the belly of a cloud and becomes the water of the Lord of Waters.
Who can count those who are angry without cause? Those who do not become angry even when there is a cause are but five or six in this world.
If even virtuous people speak harshly, who else could possibly be sweet-spoken? If the rays of the moon were accompanied by fire, would nectar surely not be produced from something else? — Maṅgala.

How few are those virtuous people who are compassionate toward the wretched, whom even a slight display of wealth does not affect, who rejoice in performing service for others when requested, and who remain composed even when afflicted by the great malady of the onset of youth? They alone are the singular ornaments adorning the circle of the earth. (VidSrk 37.26)

They protect their reputation rather than their lives; they fear sin more than an enemy; they seek out those who need help rather than wealth—this is the natural disposition of the great-souled. (VidSrk 37.27)
Just as the highest pinnacle of excellence ascends,
so too do those whose nature is like that of a bowstring come to rest.
"This one is my own, that one is a stranger"—such is the calculation of those with small minds;
but for those of noble conduct, the entire earth is indeed their family.
Those whose minds remain unperturbed even when calamity strikes, who do not become arrogant in times of prosperity, and who never turn their backs on a supplicant even at the cost of their own lives;
who possess modesty regarding the act of praising their own virtues and are wise in the praise of others—fie upon the pitiable Creator who did not make them long-lived until the end of the aeon!

Praiseworthy generosity in the hand, devotion to the feet of the guru upon the head, truthful speech in the mouth, unblemished learning in the ears, a pure disposition in the heart, and incomparable valor in victorious arms—this is the ornament of the great, which shines even without worldly sovereignty. (VidSrk 37.31)
Harder even than a diamond, yet softer than a flower—

indeed, who is able to understand the minds of those who have transcended the world? (VidSrk 37.32) Until the learned are fully satisfied, I do not consider one's knowledge of technical application to be truly excellent.
Even for those who are highly trained, the mind lacks confidence in itself.

(VidSrk 37.33) Not everything is good simply because it is old, nor is every poem flawed simply because it is new. The virtuous, having examined them, resort to whichever is superior; the fool, however, has a mind that is led away by the opinions of others. (VidSrk 37.34)
These two [verses] of Kālidāsa are always like a garment for the good man, intent solely on concealing his secrets;
this mockery of yours is that it would unravel him through these flaws.

"Tell me, what are these that appear on fresh pumpkin fruits—those by the mere pointing of a finger which cause proud men to lose their lives?"* VidSrk_37.36 *(1248)* *The answer is "worms. The word *aṅgulīkathanāt* (from the pointing of a finger) is a pun: it can mean "by the mention of the word 'finger'" (referring to the answer "worms," as *aṅguli* means finger), or it can mean "by the pointing of a finger" (as in the riddle).*

That which Giriśa does not behold with three eyes, nor even the Lotus-born with eight, nor Skanda with twelve, nor Maghavan with a thousand eyes—even if the eyes of the three worlds were combined—that cannot be seen; yet, having withdrawn their sight, the wise, whose minds are composed, perceive it. (VidSrk 37.37)
Even though they are sapless, we find pleasure in the fruits of the cotton plant,
whose birth is full of virtue for the sake of concealing the private parts of others.
Perceiving that the essence [of your teaching] is to be grasped solely by those who possess the vessel of virtue,
the world understands you as its own kinsman and runs to you.
Those who are constantly afraid of untruth say "do not fear" to those who are terrified;

O tongue of the virtuous, you have achieved your purpose by eating only the remnants left for guests. Even if, through fate, the affection of a good person perishes, it nevertheless [remains] toward sentient beings.
The latent impression (saṃskāra) persists for a long time, like the resonance of a bell's sound. By Ravigupta. Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, "Association with the Virtuous."
Therefore, when an extremely base task must be performed, the intellect of the wicked becomes exceedingly skillful;
for in the darkness, the vision of owls attains its proper form.
A wicked person seeks out faults in a poem adorned with excellent qualities, just as a young camel seeks out thorns in a forest strewn with blossoms. (VidSrk 38.2)
The creation of a talkative, unfriendly person who thwarts the affairs of friends, as well as that of a cloud, leads only to the destruction of one's hopes. (VidSrk 38.3)

A fan for the windless, a goad for the pacification of the pride of elephants blinded by rut, a boat for crossing the difficult-to-traverse ocean, a lamp at the onset of darkness—in this way, there is nothing on earth for which Providence has not devised a remedy; yet I believe even the Creator’s efforts have failed in the task of capturing the mental disposition of the wicked.

Whose fear does not arise from the wicked person who is cruel due to manifesting enmity without cause—a man whose mouth always harbors unbearable, venomous speech, like the poison of a great serpent? (VidSrk 38.5)
When the multitude of the wicked and the cremation ground are diminished, it is then certainly understood that there is welfare for the worlds. (VidSrk 38.6)
Who has not been deceived by a rogue, who is foul within with a filthy body yet pleasing on the outside, like the fruit of the *mahākāla* tree?

Everywhere, indeed, the wicked person exerts himself with the bold arrogance of a slanderer to bind the virtuous—who are straightforward and unattached to worldly existence—by means of their very footsteps;
having immediately produced some entirely unprecedented "sutra" from his own belly, he creates a marvelous web, crooked like the mass of threads spun by a spider.
Even while the gods look on, he is indeed eclipsed by his splendor;
for the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose wheel has been cast away, there is no longer even need for a garment.
With a slight [weight] it rises, and with a slight [weight] it goes downward;
oh, how the behavior of a scale-beam and that of a wicked person are alike!
What have the wicked learned from mice, or what have the mice learned from the wicked?
For neither of them possesses any occupation other than digging up the houses of others. Men whose minds are corrupted by the wicked have no trust even in their own kin.

A child who has been burned by milk-porridge eats even curd only after blowing upon it. (VidSrk 38.12) Out of hatred for excellence of virtue, a wicked man composes and disseminates some unworthy statement, even regarding those who are great by nature.
If this were not so, how could there be such a clamor that the ocean was contained within a single mouthful of the Sage, which was like half a lotus bud? (VidSrk 38.13)

O dear friend, having placed our minds upon the wheel of anxiety—which is unstable due to its familiarity with a succession of falls at the edge of the staff of calamity—the wicked Creator has forcibly kneaded them like a lump of clay and whirls them about like a skilled potter; we do not know what he will fashion from them here.
A snake kills only that which it strikes with its foot, or that which it stirs with its raised staff, or that which it touches with its fang;
but this other, a slanderer possessing the nature of a serpent, touches another in the ear and destroys yet another along with his very roots.
Even when relying on a completely pure livelihood, a wicked person causes distress to others;
even serpents that subsist only on air do not refrain from harming others. (VidSrk 38.16, Ravigupta)

Beyond the reach of mantras, outside the domain even of natural physicians, incurable by the nectar of ambrosia, and dense with its most extraordinary onset, wicked people are clearly created by Fate—whose intellect has matured—to cause the world to wander; they are a malady as unnatural as their very nature.
How can there be courtesy in this wicked man—who, like a serpent of fierce wrath, first stains even his own virtues with villainy—when he crushes the virtues of others? (VidSrk 38.18)

What excellence can be found in a wicked person—who seeks out vulnerabilities, who is poisonous with evil glances, who hates those of pure intent, who is quick to anger, who withers away happiness, and who consumes the world without cause; who speaks softly only for his own sake, who is utterly delighted when his desires are thwarted, and who is as treacherous as the coils of a furious serpent?
Two verses of Guṇākara on the nature of virtue:

In one possessed of modesty, dullness is counted; in one who delights in vows, hypocrisy; in the pure, deceit; in the brave, cruelty; in the upright, mental instability; in the sweet-spoken, wretchedness; in the spirited, arrogance; in the eloquent, garrulousness; in the steadfast, incapacity. What indeed can be called a virtue in the virtuous that has not been branded by the wicked? VidSrk_38.20 *(1273)

The wicked man reviles those worthy of honor, mocks the suffering, and afflicts his kinsmen; he hates the brave and insults those deprived of wealth; he commands his dependents, reveals secrets, and fomenting mutual enmities, he quickly utters what should not be said; having abandoned all virtue, he seizes upon faults. (Vidura-śataka 38.21)
Whatever is most dear to oneself, that indeed should be given to one who possesses virtues;
for this very reason, a wicked person bestows his own faults upon the virtuous.
A wicked person afflicts a virtuous man who is melted by compassion all the more;
for a thorn pierces what is soft, while it becomes blunted against what is hard. (VidSrk 38.23) [The fire of grief] is heavy at its onset, diminishing gradually, light at first, and increasing later.
The friendship of the wicked and the virtuous is like the shadow of the day, divided into its forenoon and afternoon portions.
Where is the mind of the wicked, as hard as the date-palm tree, and where are the words of poets, as delicate as a blossoming jasmine flower?
Abandon this delusion and hear these wondrous tales, just as the moon, though made of nectar, melts a piece of stone.

O Blessed Earth, how can you support that person who breaks his word and commits evil against one who has been helpful, pure-minded, or a benefactor? Like drops of milk falling into the mouth of a base serpent, they are wasted upon him.
In an instant, the drops of the nectar of well-spoken words turn into poison.

Who indeed does not incur misfortune from a wicked man— who is fond of shaven heads, who bestows long-lasting suffering, who has cast out the springtime, whose splendor has blossomed, and whose circle of friends has been scorched— just as one does from a day of penance?
Born equal to Narada, these two—Śaṅkha and Soma—are naturally white; yet among them, Sthāṇu bears the moon upon a head that is unlike it.
Śaṅkha is cut by shell-workers with a multitude of saws that cause pain; indeed, who that is crooked within by nature does not meet with misfortune?
Failing to distinguish between his own nature and that of others, he perceives even his own fault as residing in another;
like one standing on a boat who imagines the motionless things on the shore to be moving.
This wicked person is a consumer of his own support, a black-pathed fire, and a burner.
Even so, it would be as if an oblation were poured into ashes; in this [case], the offering would be truly offered only into fire.
It would be better for the moon and the wicked man to remain forever waning,
rather than to wax and thereby manifest their spreading spots.
In every place, those who are talkative and fickle prevail; the virtuous, though esteemed by the world, do not.
Waves remain upon the surface of the ocean, while the jewels lie at its bottom.
Undertakings that are delightful at the start become tasteless in their conclusion.
Associations with the wicked generally end in enmity.
A virtuous person places even a mere fragment of merit upon his head, like Śiva bearing the crescent moon;
yet a malicious person cannot tolerate the virtues of others, just as the moon cannot endure the beauty of the lotus.
We are utterly afraid even of the "virtue" of a wheelwright.
He who cuts down even a worthy recipient by means of his own virtues alone.
That day which fails to reach completion because it is the cause of tormenting others—
the wicked person, being dejected, does not count that as anything within the span of their life; rather,
they rejoice in those days and highly esteem them as the true gain of their birth.
Those who proceed with a malicious intent, devoted to the practice of tormenting others...
A wicked person, overflowing with excessive arrogance toward those who are gentle with compassion, undergoes a supreme transformation; for he perceives no danger from them.
But where he is touched even by the slightest suspicion of fear, he behaves humbly like one who is disciplined, his arrogance subsided.
If even wicked people can be countered by noble men with sweet words,
then what effort would it take for the ocean to bind Śūra with the pollen of the *ketakī* flower?
Surely, out of pride, the moon was taken by the Creator to wipe away the heart of the wicked man; yet it was not whitened by him in sport, nor was it returned.

The children of Dharaṇīdhara, emaciated by hunger, are like corpses; my kinsmen have little regard for me; and a cracked water-jar smeared with bits of lac does not trouble me as much as the neighbor woman who, every day, having broken into a piteous smile, demands a needle from me to mend her torn garment while she pretends to be angry.

These children of the poor, with their bodies bristling with goosebumps, place a thin, worn, and soiled rag upon their shoulders and engage in squabbling during the cold season for the sake of gaining a spot on a wall dappled by the rays of the sun. (VidSrk 39.6)
In that very same interior of the house is the kitchen; right there is the mortar, right there the utensils, right there the children, and right there his own dwelling.
Even for such a wretched householder who has endured all this, what can we say of his miserable state, when tomorrow his wife, about to give birth, will be grinding grain in that very same place?

"Today's meal for the children has been secured by my strength; how indeed will it be tomorrow?"—thus reflecting, with her cheeks stained by the falling of tears, the wife of a poor man cannot bear the end of the night.
She grieves for the soaked barley meal, she remedies it; she splashes water from a bowl toward the crying children; she protects the straw of her bed.
Having placed a broken shard of a winnowing-basket upon her head, the distressed mistress of a ruined house—what is there that she does not do when the god rains so heavily?

Your harems— adorned with ornaments consisting merely of palm-leaf earrings and *tāḍī* fans, wearing garlands of blooming *sinduvāra* flowers, clad in aged, heavy *bhūrja*-bark garments upon their thick hips,

and with decorative leaf-designs on the borders of their breasts fashioned from mineral ores on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains— sport without ceasing in the company of young monkeys clinging to their chests.
A river was formed by the saliva trickling from the coils of serpents distressed within, as they were falling due to the weight of the elephants dispersing during your *nāsīra* (vanguard);
moreover, in that river, lotuses arose from the rows of hoods—adorned with jeweled filaments—of the Naga women who were moving about, eager for water-sports.
O God, listen as you stand upon the battlefield of Gaṅgādhara and have strung your bow: behold what has been achieved by each successive power.
From the bow came the arrows; from the arrows, the enemy's head; from that, the circle of the earth; from that, you; from you, stainless fame; and from that fame, the three worlds.

O Lord, what king indeed in this world can endure the twang of your bowstring, which is rendered useless by arrows on the field of battle yet remains expert in the undertaking of conquering the three worlds?
Upon hearing it loudly, even the Lord of the Gods, out of fear of combat and shame, looks toward his side and most silently lets go of his own bow.
O Hero, at the gate of your enemy’s city during the season of frost, as the bear Nāhiḷla lay nearby with his body curled into a circle and his snout thrust into the joint of his chest,
the hunters in the morning beheld one of his eyes— opened in the process of waking from sleep— as resembling a spark of fire resting upon chaff and ashes.
They possess nothing but their loincloths as wealth, yet they alone enjoy the finest *dhātrī* fruits; at their gates herds of horses neigh, and by them alone has the earth been won.
By them this very family has been adorned—what more need we say?—those who have been beheld by you, the Supreme Lord, whether in anger or in favor.

O Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa— whose formidable mass of arms was once made to slacken by Your conduct, which was as profound as the wonder of granting fearlessness to Indra— now sleeps peacefully upon his high serpent-couch, filled with the breath of his own vital energy, which is composed of the cool fragrance of internal contentment, for the protection of the three worlds. (VidSrk 41.31)
"O child Mādhavī! O father Campaka! O young mango tree! O beloved Kauntī! Alas, mother Madayantī! O brother Kurabaka!
O sister Mālatī!"—thus do the night-stalkers hear the cries of the garden goddesses in the houses of their enemies, driven by the frantic agitation of being trampled by monkeys.
O Vajrin, abandon this thunderbolt; O Blessed One, Lord, what need is there for the trident? O Viṣṇu, you too must lay aside the discus; let all the immortals cast away their weapons.

Today, for this king who has conquered the armies of his enemies, it is his own staff-like arm—skilled in shattering the masses of formidable foes—that is raised up to bear the yoke of the three worlds.
Your arrows, possessing a brilliance as dense as the rays of the sun, when hurled at enemies who have become targets for the instruction of the art of intimidating rival kingdoms,

appear like side-long glances cast by the assembly of the Goddesses of the Quarters— eager in their play of beholding the battlefield— with necklaces dangling from their hands as they move restlessly.

The serpent maidens dwelling on the slopes of the coastal mountains sing of your virtues, their heads—weighed down by the burden of jewels—nodding gently; from the swelling joints of their sloughs, where great horripilation has arisen, flows a surging flood of intoxicating sweat; and they are lovely as they unevenly utter syllables of joy, their voices filled with the resonance of their double tongues.
May the dust of your feet, O Murāri, be victorious— dust that possesses the grace of woodworm powder whirling within the hollow trunk of the world’s poverty (which is like a *karṇaka* tree),
and which is the friend of the pollen of the lotus-abode of Lakṣmī, and the sands of the river formed by the moonlight of the rays from the jewels in the crowns of kings bowing down in service.
O King, you are as broad as Vallaṇa in virtues, like Rāma in fame, like Nala, and like Bharata; in great battle you are Śatrughna, and in war you are ever Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus, by your noble deeds, you bear the likeness of ancient monarchs; how then could you not be Māndhātṛ, O Lord, even though you are the conqueror of the three worlds?
You are our master, and we are committed to the vow of a garland-maker; therefore, these flowers of our words have been respectfully offered to you.
If they are flawed, do not place them around your neck, nor put them upon your breast—just listen for a moment to this new [garland] and let our labor bear fruit.
O King, it is a great wonder that this single thing bestows fear upon many enemies simultaneously and perpetually. (VidSrk 41.39)
"You are always a giver of all"—thus you are falsely praised by the wise;
for enemies have never gained your back, nor have the wives of others gained your chest. (VidSrk 41.40)
"From where have you learned this unprecedented science of archery?
For while the flood of arrows comes forth, the bowstring reaches the ends of the quarters."
Even when surrounded by a grove of *sāla* trees, she is as if devoid of a *sāla* grove; though her neck is encircled by a necklace, your enemy’s wife is as if without a necklace. VidSrk_41.42 (1422)
These [women], by pulling the hems of Vīryamitra’s garments out of excessive passion, embracing him,
seizing his hair, scratching his lower lip, and pressing against his breasts—
Even before the eyes of the King of Kaliṅga’s harem, alas, what indeed was not done by those branches [of trees] like profligates in the forest? Oh, fie on this misery! (VidSrk 41.43)
Those very rays of the sun that reduce even the deep, waterless lakes of Vasukalpa to mere mud—
how is it that they are thwarted in drying up even a drop of the tears from the eyes of the wives of your heroic enemies? This is my reflection.

O Lord, Sovereign of the Circle of the Earth, as the water from the hoods of the Lord of Serpents— exhausted by your army— falls drop by drop in an unbroken stream into his wide-spread, expanding hood-mounds,
the circle of the earth appears clearly to the families of serpents as if supported by one thousand and one massive pillars.

O Lord, this army of yours is once again ready to conquer the earth—to exhaust the remaining quarters, to shroud the directions, to crush the mountains, to turn the oceans into mud with a mass of dust, to block the very sky with those same clouds of dust, and to raise a tumultuous clamor of "Move! Move! repeatedly at the front of the march; yet it is your two arms that must do so.
O Lord,

as the earth was being bent down by the weight of your army, the King of Serpents was seen at the crossroads, having raised his neck with his vast body; supporting the earth with his hundred hoods— which were closed due to his hissing and roaring— he appeared like a banyan tree in full growth, bearing fruit in the form of the red jewels upon his heads, while thick streams of saliva fell from them.
Water suddenly turns to mud; liquid mud becomes dust; dust, driven by the wind from the flapping ears of elephants, becomes mist at the horizons;
mountains become lowlands, level ground becomes uneven, and uninhabited places become crowded with people—O Rājyapāla, when you depart, the world loses its very nature.
"Lest our women's parting of the hair be marked by the red lead of the great ocean," for this reason those enemies avoid the sword in battle from afar.
"O King, you are indeed fond of seizing hair; having quickly loosened her girdle, you, with swift hands, have begun to strike even her limbs.
When the bard, seeking to praise you, spoke thus, the women were ashamed as they glanced at one another, while your enemies trembled with fear.
When Bhīma sets forth, his flashing sword-blade concealing the fire of his enemies, let all the lords of the world immediately take up either the fly-whisk or the quarters of the earth.

If you do not do so, then the vultures, impetuous in their swiftness, will swiftly carry your heads aloft into the sky—heads pierced by the arrows released from the bow held in battle. —Vasukalpa’s *Vidvadbhañjikā* 41.51.

"You always accomplish what is desired; you reside on the Himālaya mountains. Therefore, you are indeed Śaṅkara, and Skanda is nothing more than that to you. (VidŚrk 41.52) "Since his childhood, he has been brought by me alone to the highest pinnacle of excellence; now this prince feels ashamed because of our very conversation."
Thus, as if distressed by his own fame, the aged multitude of your virtues has reached the penance groves on the shore of the ocean, having found support through that very fame.

The pair of breasts of your enemies' wives, bathed in tears from the fire of grief residing close at hand in their hearts, practices a vow of fasting, as it were. [Love] sprouted during the mere thought [of you], then put forth two leaves when the time for your departure arrived; it budded on the road as you entered the city, and now rises up with a hundred branches.
When the morning dawned, my tree of desire was merely budding; but now that you, O King, have been seen, it has blossomed and even borne fruit this very day.
With bodies adorned with ashes, having attained greatness through their passion for the wilderness,
and placing their hands upon the three *liṅgas*, those who were your enemies have become your equals.
I know, O Vikramavardhana, that as you bestow wealth upon supplicants, there will arise an unfathomable ocean of jewels, like the Śoṇa river bedecked with stones.
And I see that Mount Rohaṇa, its interior swelling with a weight of jewels, will in a few days reach the state of a pomegranate fruit bursting open at ripeness.

It is a marvel that you, though one, always dwell in three ways within the hearts of enemies, the learned, and gazelle-eyed women—extending, respectively, heat through the fervor of your valor, joy through your humility, and passion through your grace. (VidSrk 41.58)
O Lord, I entreat you: the long-awaited arrival of the rains has passed, and now my heart runs hither and thither to wander from sacred ford to sacred ford.

Therefore, O Hero, let your bow rest from the firm binding of its string through your prowess; let not the path of your journey become impassable due to the tears from the eyes of your enemies' wives.
O King, in battle, the single sword-blade maiden was of two forms: she was a courtesan to the elephants of the enemy and a procuress to the brave warriors. (VidSrk 41.60)
Repeatedly stroking the circle of her breasts, repeatedly kissing her cheeks, and clutching her neck with hands agitated by excitement,
a mosquito— driven mad by the mountain-river breezes— is buzzing something in the ear of your enemy's wives as they sleep in the depths of the mountain-cave thickets.

With drops of water from their hanging eyes, with locks of hair dangling upon the surface of their cheeks, the wives of your enemies wander through the deep caves of the mountains. May you never hear that report concerning your enemies which is heard from the suffix *kvip*.
Together with the kinsmen of Aṅga, [there was] that which occurs in the *sici* [augment] of the *parasmaipada*.

O Kamboja, you were clearly fashioned by the Creator by taking from the sky the pollen of the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree, the milk of the cow of plenty, the fire of the flower-weaponed god whose body was consumed by the eye of Tryambaka, the breaths of Lakṣmī, and the very essence of the autumn season; homage to you!
O Lord of Heroes, the enemies of Vasukalpa, having been deprived of their weapons by the prowess of your arm, do not stand face-to-face before you.
The ocean of milk was not cast into the house of milk; the golden mountain was not placed in your treasury; nor were the guardians of the quarters brought and appointed to protect the borders;
nor were the elephants of the directions, with bees humming upon them, employed in the sport of being mounted in turn—tell me, what exactly have you accomplished in your conquest of the world?
When the sky was shrouded by the dust born from the earth, churned by the sharp tips of the hooves of Dakṣa’s sacrificial horse-arrays during the festival of your departure,
the sun— scattered in every direction and lengthening the day for the sake of long life— wastes away as the team of horses wanders the wrong path, bewildered by the loss of the cardinal points.

This one is renowned throughout the world as a giver; what does he give? Indeed, it is well known that he bestows all things beneficial upon the world. From his very birth, he has desired a worthy recipient for his gifts; if even the wish-fulfilling gem were to give, let it do so!

O ornament of kings, as you set forth, these signs will surely appear before you for those who seek you: a full water-pot at the tip of a branch, graceful women, smiling maidens, an elephant with temples moistened by the flow of rut, a white bull, and a sweet-voiced crow on a milk-tree— all these, O auspicious one, manifest themselves to you.
O King, wherever your eye— pink as the back of a fingernail— moves as you show favor,
there the Goddess Kamalā, who dwells in the lotus groves, runs after it, as if out of a desire for that very eye.

Even by the forest-dwellers living on the Vindhya mountains, the weeping of the Supreme Lord was heard as he extended his hand toward the forest-women holding fruits in their hands for the sake of your enemy’s child.

O King, at the front of the battle, your very self has appeared before you under the guise of the shadow of your own sword-blade— bearing a forehead with a deeply furrowed, terrifying frown, and with his lower lip trembling as he turns his back to the enemy.
When the wild peacocks had not arrived, though summoned by the names of the peacocks in his own home,
your enemy’s wife was made to weep long and bitterly by her crying young son. (Vidvatsarvasva 41.73)
— by Yogeśvara.
Those which are incessantly and excessively consumed by those afflicted by thirst, yet remain clear and inwardly present, becoming instantly full of virtues;
wherein, when bowed down, a fresh fruit is surely obtained—could these be wells fashioned by merit, or are they men such as you?

O Lord, if you were not a sugar-cane for the person, then how could this Dharma—lame and standing on only one foot—continue to wander? For it wandered with all four feet during the Age of Truth (Kṛtayuga), with three legs in the Tretā age, and somehow with two in the Dvāpara; but in this most degenerate Kali age, it would not exist at all. VidSrk_41.75 *(1455)
You are the Dharmarāja; you are Bhīma at the head of the battle; you are Arjuna in fame; you have a likeness in Nakula;
Sahadeva alone is your equal—if indeed there is anyone else. But as for Duḥśāsana, he is surely some kind of enemy to you!

O King, the lamp of your majesty blazes forth: Halāyudha is its base, the Tortoise is its stand, the Lord of Serpents is the wick, the Earth is the vessel, the oceans are the supply of oil, and this Golden Mountain is the growth of the rounded wick; the rays of the sun are the flame, the darkness of the sky is the soot, and the ranks of your enemies being consumed are the moths.

I know that hearing of your passion for giving and your heroism, O Lord of Generosity, the ocean bears as it were an inner anguish as it rolls incessantly, while the golden mountain remains motionless as if established in meditative absorption; for one fears the churning of the former, while the other fears the blows of the axe.
"Have you not indeed seen anyone anywhere who is equal in virtues to King Kalikandarpa? Have you perhaps heard of such a person?"—
thus, as if agitated by the desire for an answer, the eye of the deer-eyed women, tremulous with its most flickering pupil, reached to the edge of her ear.
