Though you possess the eightfold prosperity (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*), you are not wretched; with the playful charms of celestial nymphs born of your merit, your inner apartments shine resplendent; and though your majesty is as great as the sun's, you are never subject to anger. O Lord, though you are not distinct from the ocean, why are you not a true ocean within your own domain, having conquered the gods by your own power?
Thus ends the "Colo," the section on flattery.

Then there is the life of renunciation for the fortunate, who, dwelling in the interior of mountain caves and meditating on the supreme light, have birds sitting fearlessly in their laps drinking the tears of their joy;
but for us, whose lives are spent merely in the pleasure-pavilions of gardens by the banks of ponds within palaces constructed only by our desires, our existence is utterly wasted away.
Having experienced it myself, I say that the great, heart-piercing pains of begging must not befall anyone in this cycle of existence;
behold, brother, for this begging is a playground for the mockery of dignity and old age, a stain upon one's pride, and a miscarriage of the boldness inherent in the possession of virtues.
"Look, Gobhaṭa, what can we do? Such is the course of actions: for us, as if from the verbal root *duṣ*, a virtue has resulted only in the production of a fault. (VidSrk 42.3)

"Disregarding propriety and paying no heed to immense shame, those who—agitated by the wicked hope for a mere fragment of wealth—must gaze upon the faces of the rich, whose brows are knitted by the fever of false pride; fie on this belly that is so difficult to fill! (VidSrk 42.4)
Let my birth sink to the underworld; let the multitude of my virtues go even deeper; let my character fall like a stone from a mountain cliff; let my noble lineage be consumed by fire;
and let a thunderbolt swiftly strike my valor as an enemy—let there be for us wealth alone, without which all these other qualities are no more than mere blades of grass. (VidSrk 42.5)
Are the hollows of the mountain caves now stemless? Are the barks of the trees withered? Are the rivers dried up, their waves stumbling over the heavy, shimmering rocks of the mountains?

For even the learned sit here day after day, rising from their seats again and again, casting their eyes toward the king with loud cries of praise. What have we not done, devoid of discernment, for the sake of these lives that are as fleeting as water on a lotus leaf?
If, in the presence of lords, those whose minds are blinded by the delusion of even a tiny fragment of wealth have shamelessly committed the sin of speaking of their own virtues; (VidSrk_42.7) *1467*

That these wealthy men turn their faces away from the virtuous is not out of contempt for them, but rather out of fear of expending their own wealth; therefore, there is no resentment in this, but only compassion. For what insult could there be toward deer who are terrified of the loss of their own flesh? (VidSrk 42.8)
I have not bound upon my wrist the bracelet white as the light of the autumn moon; nor have I tasted the face of a young bride, tender and slow with shame.
Neither by arms nor by learning have I brought glory to the abode of the Lord of the Gods; instead, my time has been spent in dilapidated monasteries, wasted among impudent and malicious students.
We are unskilled at whispering into the ear, nor are we capable of deceiving our master’s mind with fabricated conduct;
furthermore, these dullards have not learned how to speak even pleasant words falsely—what virtue, indeed, could there be that would make us favorites of the lord of men?

Desiring to please others, I have somehow endured the taunts of the wicked; suppressing my inner pain, I have even laughed with a vacant mind. I have even offered salutations with joined palms to those whose intellects are paralyzed by the intoxication of wealth. O Hope, you who are vain hope! What more can you do than this to make me dance? VidSrk_42.11 *(1471) //

I wandered through Janasthāna with a mind obsessed by the golden deer; I wailed "O Vaidehī! in every direction with tears streaming down; I engaged in conversations with the faces of the Lord of Laṅkā; I attained the state of Rāma, yet I did not achieve the status of having Kuśa and Lava as my sons.
First, he creates a jewel among men, an abode of all virtues and an ornament of the earth;
yet if he subsequently makes that very being perish in an instant—alas, what a tragedy! What ignorance on the part of the Creator!
Homage to you, O Blessed Destiny, who are partial toward the virtuous;
for you yourself do not touch the ungrateful, the dull-witted, or the base-born. Bali was the donor and Viṣṇu the supplicant; the gift was the earth, and the time was that of the horse-sacrifice.
Homage be to that destiny, the fruit of which has become nothing but bondage!
Our dear daughters appear to us as if they were calamities;
otherwise, how could those possessed of virtue be given away to men of noble birth? (VidSrk 42.16)
O noble Speech, first arrange the pure succession of syllables in my mouth; O Mind, attain composure; go to that dignity where the proud reside!

O Modesty, stand for a moment with your face turned away from here; O Desire, listen and stand before me while I, a wretch, speak these piteous words: "Give to the wealthy man!"* VidSrk_42.17 *(1477) *The original Sanskrit text contains a pun on the word *dīna*, meaning both "wretched" and "beggar. The translation reflects this dual sense.

Having abandoned his beloved young wife—who was newly and intensely devoted to him—he becomes a beggar, studies for a long time while sleeping upon the bare ground, and even after mastering the scriptures, his body wastes away as he wanders through the forest. Therefore, O learning, you are such that there is neither happiness here nor even spiritual merit. 42.18 (1478)

O ascetic woman, whose creeper of knowledge is laden with blossoming white flowers of speech—cease, for it is better! O you who are free from the wandering bee [of passion], you shall bear neither the fruit of worldly enjoyment nor liberation.
Those whose voices are faltering with madness, whose eyes are unsteady with intoxication, and whose natural dispositions have fallen away, no longer remember what has been done.
Whom among men does not the intoxication from drinking the wine of sovereign power cause to stumble at every step?

We possess but a tiny fragment of wealth, yet these virtuous ones suffer in poverty; there is not even a trace of a desire to give in their hearts. Shame on you, O Creator! Why do you mock us? (VidSrk 42.21) Even though one is learned, of noble birth, and endowed with other virtues, if one does not obtain the desired fruit of the mind, that is the fault of fate to be censured.
But this much causes pain in the heart: that even a fool, having obtained fortune through past actions, considers himself worthy despite being unrighteous.
(VidSrk 42.22) For here in the house of the Lord, poison, the bull, and ashes are held in high regard;
but what account is there for one who possesses neither poison, nor the bull, nor ashes? (VidSrk 42.23)

Who, like a bee, does not wither before a lord who destroys desires, who is like poison, who is arrogant with prosperity, and who delights in the company of serpents? Do not desire fruit from one devoid of virtue.
Even if it means friction with a thunderbolt or being trampled underfoot, [one should not seek such a lord].
If they are indeed jewels, they endure [all things] out of a longing for their own virtues.
How can those possessed of merit rise when they have fallen into an improper place?
Has anyone ever seen a ball emerge from the mud?
Whatever I write upon the tablet of my heart, Fate carefully effaces it. Now, due to this repeated erasure, not even a line of my desire appears upon the smooth surface.
What would he not do for his wealthy kinsmen? Would their conduct not bring solace to my eyes?
If his mind were not devoid of the false suspicion that "he has come to beg from me," [then he would have acted otherwise]. VidSrk_42.28 *(1488) //

For those like us who truly possess no merit, this treasury of the jewels of virtue—though present—is perceived only as something non-existent; it serves neither ourselves nor others, being sealed with the mark of poverty. (VidSrk 42.29)
Tell me, how is it that you go to another's house, and once there, how is it that you begin a hundred flatteries?
And then, how is it that you praise yourself? O son of noble family, you are proud! Alas, you fool, you have been mocked by your own wretched belly!
The cranes have lost their food and do not sport; the herons do not move about.
Just as in a lake when Vikramāditya has passed away from this earth, leaving behind only his fame—so it is now.
(Subandhu)
"Appropriate action does not bring prosperity, while anything else is indeed worthless to the discerning.
Thus, having been severed from all connection with happiness, how could a wise man not despair because of this? (VidSrk 42.32)
Having cut the snare, cast off the trap, and forcibly broken through the net, the deer has emerged from the forest thick with a mass of flickering flames;
leaping with great speed beyond the range of the hunters' arrows, it falls into a well. What can human effort achieve against adverse fate? (VidSrk 42.33)
Granted that deer in the forests live on grass that is easily obtained without effort;
yet they do not display cruelty toward the wealthy—those are indeed beasts, while we are the wise.
Those who, out of greed for even a tiny fragment of wealth, settle upon a friend who possesses riches...

And yet, holding them like blades of grass, tell me, for whom do you feel respect? How is it that this Lord of the entire universe is fixed upon our cheeks—those of us who are so base? Yet this is a truly unprecedented arrangement:
that while the moon, scattering a mass of rays consisting of liquid nectar, possesses a spot, the jewels on the hoods of venomous serpents are priceless.

When Vittoka encountered a difficult calamity that threatened the destruction of his life, he was so gripped by imminent fear that he no longer perceived his own wealth; he longed only for his life. But once he had emerged from that, he entered yet another calamity for the sake of his riches. This mutual wager between life and wealth is such that each serves as the cause for the other.
I did not act as a cloud over the crop of wealth that was withered by the lack of the water of riches; nor did I act as a hurricane blowing away the mountain ranges of my rival enemies.
Nor did I act as a bee among the stainless lotus-faces of lovely-eyed women; I have merely acted as an axe for the felling of the forest of my mother’s youth.

Those virtuous ones who, out of a commitment to compassion, do not sell their own interests but assist others even at the cost of their lives, are far away from those who, following a trail of hatred, remain harsh and devoid of pity. Close your eyes; restrain the flow of your tears now—for before whom are you weeping? (Bhartṛhari, VidV 42.39)
Mātṛgupta has been surpassed by kings such as Śrī Candragupta and others, and he has been outstripped by various poets such as Abhinanda and the rest.
Now, O Speech, be silent! Why do you prattle in vain? Where is the abundance of offerings, and where is your impetuous joy in the manifestation of your virtues?
The source of nectar for the multitude of eloquent speech, this Lord of the Gaṇas has but one tusk; the Goddess, though divine, has fallen from her station along with the river of the gods.
Where indeed is the enjoyment seen by other virtuous masters who serve the Lord? Why do you distress your mind here in vain?
Go away, shame; desist, O mind, and your fortitude! Why do you mock me here in vain? What is this pride of manhood?
We act only according to that wretchedness which, having destroyed all virtues and amassed an army of faults, now commands us.
Wives are joyless; kinsmen are distressed by calamity; friendship has become like a stranger; attendants are wretched from the loss of wealth;
the mind is discontented; this life is as hard as a thunderbolt; destiny is full of perverse undertakings—and yet, the heart still longs for happiness. (VidSrk 42.43)

We have seen people in our own homes with bodies soiled by the dust of Durvāsas; we have heard words harsh to the ear from those filled with arrogance regarding wealth they had bestowed; and another, having arrived at our residence, departed his desire unfulfilled because of our lack of acquaintance. We are weary, bearing this body that is impotent in performing service for either ourselves or others.
Where is the mud, and where the lotus, sweet with the humming of swarms of bees? Where is the fierce head of the serpent, and where the jewel flashing with great rays?
Where is this wicked Kali age, and where your birth from a treasury of virtues? Truly, truly, Fate is unskilled in matching things together.

Worthy of homage is the wise man who has discerned the course of the three worlds; he is happy even if he appears foolish, for his heart rests in the non-duality of the greatness inherent within himself.
May no one else become such a person, distressed by the doubt of "is it real or unreal" that arises from a meditative absorption whose mind is variegated by a feeble intellect. (VidSrk 42.46)
While we were wandering over this earth, which is bounded by the four oceans, we have not seen any person of distinguished character whose pure virtues were such that,
having conversed for even a moment or half a moment before him about the sorrows or joys long accumulated in our hearts, we could find rest after sighing. (VidSrk 42.47)
On this side a forest fire with its blazing flames; on this side the ground is thick with tangled undergrowth; on this side a hunter runs, his bow bent, following closely behind;
and right here ahead stands a python with its mouth wide open. Where can this young deer go, and what can he do, fallen as he is under the power of fate?
O Śoṇa, by whom was this glory bestowed upon you, who take delight in calamity? I know that you were once charming with water reaching only to the knees;

but now, with forests of trees on your banks falling away in the current, with waves of difficult-to-cross whirlpools, and with turbid waters that breach the banks—to whom are you dear? VidSrk_42.49 (1509)
The waters of Śatānanda’s ocean, which fill the expanse of the sky and the depths of the underworld, indeed provide many means by way of ships for crossing over here;
yet, if by fate this ocean were somehow to become empty, who then would have the leisure to gaze into the hollows of its shoreless caves? (VidSrk 42.50)
Having offered the long-accumulated burden of delusion to Keśaṭa as a divine gift, dwell at ease and in comfort; what is the use of further begging?
Even for the sun that circumambulates Mount Meru, its horses remain seven and never become eight.
No wealth has been accumulated, no knowledge has been acquired, and no austerity has been practiced; yet, my entire life has passed away. (VidSrk 42.52)
Even though it has been with this stalk since birth, the lotus turns its face away;
for such is generally the way of the wealthy toward those who are full of virtues.
Then, by the splendor of the sage’s wrathful gaze, that lotus pond appeared as if licking with its flames; the *kiṃśuka* creeper, though in full bloom, was blown to the ground by the wind;

the plantain trees were no longer above the two lotuses, nor were the lotus stalks with their sprouting tips; the golden jars were not there, nor was the full moon near the fresh clouds. (VidSrk 42.54)
Moonlight was churned for its water; a rock was squeezed for its oil to obtain ghee or honey; a mirage, shimmering with waves, was scrutinized for the purpose of bathing;
and this old she-ass was milked by one who is senseless and greedy for milk. Alas! That a base person was served indeed out of a long-standing thirst for wealth.
O Kamalā, your father is the ocean, the mine of jewels; your brother is the moon, whose essence is the nectar of immortality; and your husband is the Primordial God.
Tell me, by what other person have you been taught these movements, crooked as the horns of a deer?
Then follows the discourse on old age:
"Behold this grey hair upon your head; it is the banner of victory.
Now we have triumphed; your arrows are of no avail. (VidSrk 43.1)
This is unbecoming of Dharmakīrti and contrary to the natural order of men, that here even in old age there should be amorous transformations;
and it is likewise improper that the life or the sexual pleasure of broad-hipped women has not been made to end with the sagging of their breasts.
Vidyā and Kālidāsa do not accept the expiation for their beloved’s breasts, which have fallen [from her body];
for this very reason, the world is lax in its regard for touching them. (VidSrk 43.3)
Fie on old age, which is like a poisonous creeper; and fie likewise on my own insatiable longing for those fair-browed women!
Who here is at fault? It is fate, treacherous and fit to be hewn with an axe, and the flower-weaponed god of love, whose heart is utterly callous.
May there be well-being; for now, let there be only a libation of water for the talk of love.
Even those tremulous-eyed women look upon me, who am advanced in years, with straightforward glances.
In one moment it awakens, and again it is overwhelmed by darkness.
The intellect of the aged is like the flame of a lamp about to go out.
Even when gray hairs are seen, what kind of desire can a man truly have, since women regard him with indifference as if he were a medicine? (VidSrk 43.7)
Even hair, which dwelt within a single womb, was affectionate, and was cherished and worn upon the head with honor—even that becomes discolored by old age; how much more so for women?

With limbs and voice impaired, I have been made a buffoonish actor for the lords by performing flattery; I do not know by what drama this long-lived one will make me act, now that I am wearing the grey paint of old age. (Vidūṣaka 43.9)
The two breasts appeared unseparated and rigid like those of the wealthy, yet they were seen as separated and drooping like those of the wretched and despised. *VidSrk* 43.10 (1527)
Of the merciless one. [End of] the section on old age, verse 43. Next, the section on the cremation ground.

Behold the flock of vultures, having quickly devoured the abundant, half-burnt flesh of a corpse—which was glowing as if on fire—now rushes into the water in haste, its body being scorched from within; the flesh had been pulled from the breast of the funeral pyre, whose fierce flames were dimmed by the impact of their flapping wings, and which they seized with fierce beaks in a frantic scramble. (Vidvatsarvasva 44.1, by Pāṇini)
Look, far away among the trees filled with the dense darkness of night, rows of jackals stand with necks outstretched, their two paws supporting the earth;

they drink the thick, dripping fat-water from the circles of boiling corpses, which are being watched by the flickering light of torches emerging from the caves of their own mouths. (Vidvatsarvasva 44.2, by Pāṇini)

Having repeatedly torn off the skin, and having first devoured the flesh— abundant with large swellings, easily found in parts such as the limbs, buttocks, and back, and already putrid at the surface—
the wretched *preta*, with its sinews, entrails, and eyes plucked out, its teeth bared, calmly eats the raw meat even from within the hollows of the bones in the skeleton lying on its lap.

It is surrounded by [other spirits] running hither and thither, their mouths wide open and terrifying with gaping corners near their ears, blazing with fire, and formidable with the tips of their fangs.
With faces like firebrands, their long bodies withered and barely visible, they possessed masses of hair, eyes, brows, and beards that resembled clusters of lightning. VidSrk_44.4 *(1531) //
Having fashioned auspicious amulets from entrails, wearing visible crests made from the red lotuses of women’s hands, and having suddenly fastened garlands of heart-lotuses,
these delighted female Piśācas, smeared with the saffron-paste of blood-mud, join their lovers to drink the wine of bone-marrow from skull-cups.

This wheel of Pūtanas is seen as a withered skeleton— a dense cage of bones bound together by joints of sinews stretched all around and covered in black skin, with shanks as thick as date-palm trunks— fostering wolves on all sides with half-released breaths and the remains of human flesh, while it shrieks with a crushing roar.

On the far side of the cremation ground flows a river whose banks are terrifying with the weight of the fierce howling of jackals mingled with the hissing of flocks of owls hooting in the bowers of the groves; its current, as it rushes along, strikes the crumbling shores and creates a dreadful gurgling roar as it passes over the gravel of decaying skeletons submerged within.

Here, a ghost from Bhavabhūti’s work, devoid of all hope, having torn off the entire flesh of a corpse with his hard nails— his fingers smeared with brains from the terrible, gaping hollows of his naked sinews—
bites with his lip and, with face contorted, sucks out the marrow from within the cavity of the shank-bone, heated by the funeral pyre and drawn forth with hissing sounds. (VidSrk 44.8)

In this place, where dense darkness is established by vultures whose greed is increased by seizing morsels of flesh half-dropped from their flickering beaks and who have begun to flap their pair of wings, the rows of flame-tips vomited from the mouths of jackals fall with a *chimiti* sound into the stream of blood; there, amidst the stench of the fat that has flowed thickly and incessantly, they shriek. (Jayāditya) 44.9 (1536)
These vultures, having practiced many times from afar in the sky with hundreds of circles formed by their wings— held steady and spread wide at the tips of their upturned tails—
now descend, both sides of their beaks drenched by the moisture of saliva trickling from the caves of their mouths as they greedily crave the flesh of the corpse. (VidSrk 44.10)
One, his tongue lolling, drinks thick blood from another after snatching the cup away; while the other licks what has fallen from his mouth as he drinks.
Then, some drops of blood that have fallen on the ground and congealed, another with neck upraised and a shimmering long tongue tastes them in an instant.

A ghost, his terrifying mouth quivering with thirst, repeatedly snatches a human head drawn from the funeral pyre and impaled on the tip of a reed; having extinguished it with hundreds of his own hissing breaths like powerful gusts of wind, he devours it, yet vomits it back up as the cavity of his mouth begins to burn.
These [are the exploits] of the illustrious Kṣemīśvara, who—

by seizing the wretched spirits afflicted by the calamity of being subject to the inner turmoil of others' greed— caused the cremation ground to appear as if it were another sky for a moment; there, as all [the spirits] rushed forward with cries released while grasping the tips of corpses from which flesh was falling away as they were devoured, their mouths wide open in the pleasure of devouring the glowing embers, they became visible through the radiance of their gaping maws.

This flesh-eating demon dances, his very clear day and night marked by the sequence of Vallana’s closing and opening of his eyes; he fills the sky with the mass of his excellent mane spreading to the ends of the horizon; drinking the streams of clouds released from the cave-like hollows of skulls held in his hands, his ear-cavities are split by the sounds he emits. VidSrk_44.14 (1541)
Thus ends the "Course on the Cremation Ground" (44).
Then follows the "Course on the Heroes" (45):
Having heard [the challenge], the sons of Daśaratha, on the ridge of Mount Suvela, joyfully fill the quarters with the twanging of their bows halfway drawn and polish their swords.
In that very same way, the hands of the Lord of Laṅkā are practicing once more upon a painting board that skillful artistry in the curling of leaf-patterns upon the breasts of Vaidehī.

When his enemy, who was content with even three cities, was a hero whose itching circle of arms had playfully severed and regrown his heads, and who desired a boon, the faces of the gods turned away from the wretchedness of begging and began to quarrel among themselves, saying "You choose! You choose!"—how can that Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa) be described?
Whether you alone, or ten like me, bow down with bows whose twang fills the sky, take up your weapon along with the world-protectors and Lakṣmaṇa; let there be a battle for a moment that befits us.

O old vulture, O great hero, why do you heedlessly become like a moth in this forest fire at such an untimely hour? Can a mere embankment of sand on a river bank hold back the waters of the ocean when it is tossed by the winds at the end of an aeon?
These two [are the sons] of Saṃghaśrī.
When I suddenly began with my sword Candrahāsa to swiftly cut through the forest of his neck-stalk up to his shoulders— while the mass of his veins was being severed—

if even a single face of his remained without a smile, with tears falling and words faltering, and with his eyebrows knit together, then may that Blessed One himself be the witness of my auspicious intent.
Even though that divine Lord, whose crest-jewel is the half-moon, is your preceptor, and even though this entire circle of the earth has been conquered by him twenty-one times;
nevertheless, O young son of Bhṛgu, you must behold him bearing an axe around his neck before the descendant of Pulastya, with palms joined in fresh service as he performs prostrations.

I am that Lord of Laṅkā, whose pastimes included the weighing of Rudra and others, the cutting down of the forest upon his own neck, the housing of Hari in a prison, and the conquest of the Puṣpaka chariot; I, who have as my counselor the invincible Bāhudaṇḍa—what praise is there for me in drawing or breaking a bow that is as decayed as a wood-worm-eaten log?
Victorious is Bhārgava Reṇukā alone, the mother of heroes, who gave birth to you as her son— the ornament of the three worlds—
by whom this Candrahāsa sword, possessing a fierce luster capable of cleaving the temples of Indra’s elephant, was not taken into account by me in battle.

While Rāma stood smiling as he weighed Rudra’s bow against it, the kings remained intent on snapping their finger-guards; they exchanged mutual claps of derision. When he had strung it, they grew faint at the touch of his sprout-like fingers trembling with effort; and when the bow snapped its joints under the strain of his wide-drawn pull, they fainted away once more upon their thrones. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 45.9)

"O Earth, be firm! O Serpent, support her! O King of Tortoises, you must bear this pair! O Elephants of the Quarters, maintain your resolve to uphold that triad! Let Rāma string the bow of Hara! (VidSrk 45.10)
By him, Rājaśekhara,
the sun was encircled with his tail, the moon was pierced through by his crest, the clouds were shaken off by his mane, and the stars were seized by his fangs;
the ocean was crossed by his mere glance, and the cruel fire of the Lord of Laṅkā’s prowess was leaped over in every direction by the waves of his loud laughter.
As each arm of the Ten-faced one was severed by Abhinanda, the remaining arms grew ever more arrogant, having acquired the very prowess of those that were cut;
for if the head of the Ten-faced one had not been severed, its splendor would have transferred to the remaining faces, making their beauty even more extraordinary.

"O Lord, Murāri has been broken; the entire host of monkey warriors has fled, and the troop-leaders have vanished! What is the use of courage now that this Ten-necked one is seen nearby?"—while King Sugrīva was thus speaking with a face agitated by alarm, Rāma repeatedly cast a sidelong glance at him as he slowly straightened his ten arrows.
By the winds of my whirling speed, groves of *śāla* trees lie prostrate; by the tips of my thunderbolt-like claws, mountains with their rocky cores shatter.
And even the python, its mouth crushed by my fist, I turn into a water-basin at the foot of the tree that is my own arm.

He by whom the daughter of the Pāñcāla king was dragged by her hair while she wept, and by whom even her garment was snatched away in the presence of kings and elders—he, for whose sake I vowed to drink the wine of blood from his chest, has now fallen into the cage of my arms; let him be protected, O Kauravas!

Gazing repeatedly at Jānakī’s lotus-face— her cheeks flushed with thrills of passion and smiling with love, while her cheeks steal the luster of the tusks of a young elephant— the Lord of the Raghus, hearing the tumultuous clamor of the night-stalking host, tightens the knot of his matted locks.
Hari, his eyes languid, looked at Bala with pride and fell back asleep;
but his beloved, her fear dispelled by having witnessed her husband’s prowess, continued to watch. (Vidagdhamukhamandana 45.17) [of Meṭha]
Furthermore, in battles, he brought about a gloomy day for his enemies with mere droplets of spray tossed far upward by the multitude of golden javelins;
moreover, he who, though fearless, made even Indra and the Lord of Serpents apprehensive when he suddenly exerted himself with a multitude of boats moving upon the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā).
Is this Maināka obstructing my unimpeded path through the sky? What power could he have? He is terrified even of Mahendra due to the fall of the thunderbolt.
Is that Tārkṣya here with his own lord? He too knows me as Rāvaṇa. Ah, it is known: this is Jaṭāyu, distressed by old age; he desires death.

"You are the son of the Destroyer of Tripura, while I am but his disciple; how can you be equal to him on that account? Moreover, he was initiated by you into the ritual of the bow—this is even more significant for you.
If the emergence of the qualities of the contained depends upon its substratum, then, O Skanda, take up this bow and let the difference between us be determined."

May the daughter of the Earth rest upon the chest of that hero of the world, which—like the Fortune of Valor—is radiant with the knots of healed scars set with fragments of a thunderbolt shattered by a sudden impact; and upon which, when the tusks of an elephant raised to strike, the flood of calamity was broken, as if it were a garland of flowers woven by the goddesses of the Nandana grove for her husband.
[The substitution of] *ceḥ* [occurs].
Thus ends the section on Heroes (Vīravrajyā), the forty-fifth.
Next follows the section on Eulogies (Praśastivrajyā), the forty-sixth.

During the undertakings of his world-conquest, in every direction, the rivers—whose broad banks were filled with schools of large fish—seized him with their laughter-like splashing, while the women of the quarters stood with their thighs trembling in fear.

O water! [We are] startled by the soft, tinkling cries of the peacocks, who are warbling as they are struck by the rolling, tossing waves released from being swallowed into the cavity of the deep navel-pits of amorous women. (VidSrk 46.1)
When the lord of serpents, his circle of hoods smooth with the immersion of his unbaked clay-like body,

sank down, the king of tortoises— resting with difficulty upon the thick, supportless mud at the base of the netherworld which was turbid from being churned by the weight of the great mountain-pilings shaken by the unrestrained sport of his army— bore the earth as it bent down, its stability resting on the pillar of its shell.

In his military expedition, even when his forces set out but once, the solar chariot somehow moves with difficulty along the path of the sky—which is filled with the rising dust that turns it into a mire of mud—amidst the flood of waters from the celestial river Ganges; for its wheels and axles sink deep, and it is slowed by the two or three leaps offered by the cavalry, who are struck by the rays of the sun as they struggle through the sinking wheels.
When Bhavabhūti set out with great eagerness for the conquest of the quarters before the Lord, there, by the weight of his army spreading without restraint,
the Lord of Serpents supports the earth, his life-breath held fast by the tight binding of the jeweled stakes being driven in.

During his expedition for world conquest, proclamations— dense with echoes from the Trikaṭuka peak marking Laṅkā, causing feverish distress to the ears of herds of elephants in the humming bowers of Murāri’s groves, and disturbing the sleep of lions in the caves and caverns of the eastern and western mountains— resounded, filling the quarters with the roar of mighty drums.
"O moon among kings, you have always been a seeker of the fortune of victory; I was never your beloved, even in a dream.
Thus, as if by Fortune herself departing toward her enemies in anger, he struck down the pleasures of his martial sports. (VidSrk 46.6)

In his lineage were born the rulers of Dhārā, possessed of wonderful virtues, whose arms were formidable in their skill at scorching the heat of all other kshatriyas' prowess; they anointed the heavens with the loveliness of waves of fame that rivaled the surging billows of the Mandākinī as it binds the head of the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
For a moment, in the lunar world, there arose a clamor like that of a swarm of Rāhus attacking the moon, caused by the circles of the heads of enemies severed by swords;
moreover, because these [heads] bore the illusion of ten million suns due to their shimmering gems, a great festival of plenty was produced even in the realm of Rāhu.
Thus, by constructing this celestial palace, he has exhausted this entire multitude of mountains, their masses of rock shattered by the series of hammers;
yet, by raining wealth upon supplicants, he has caused that Mount Rohaṇa to flourish once more, its thousands of peaks smiling with rows of newly sprouted jewel-sprouts.
He is the protector of the gods; moreover, his heart is solely devoted to supreme merit. That planet has Jupiter in its proper place and is intent upon the right path.
Its hand bears an exceeding affection for the hundred-peaked [mountain], and it gives away its entire wealth like a blade of grass; thus, he surpasses the Lord of the Gods.

On the battlefield, he performed the summoning of the life-force of his enemies with his bow; the foe became breathless, and the attainment of the target by his arrows occurred within the enemy host. By that means, he acquired fame;

"forgiveness" was released by him and swiftly accepted by the hosts of enemies with their heads. Death remained in the army of his foes, yet that lord of the earth did not reach another state [than victory].
(VidSrk 46.11) By those suppliants, even the unripe fruits of those wish-fulfilling trees—gems such as rubies—are bartered under the guise of emeralds.
In those [trees], the gods, climbing upon the tips of branches bent low by the crushing of ripe fruit, sing day and night of the non-duality of renunciation to the virtuous.
That king, whose two arms bore the stain of being reproached for forcibly seizing the fortune of all rival monarchs under the guise of the calluses from his bowstring,
caused the worlds to read the narrative of his own valor— a tale that, here and there, was enriched by the inclusion of episodes concerning Arjuna as he pursued it.

By that king, who with his hand—encircled by the blade of his sword as if by a *darbha* grass-garland—sportively made the Fortune of the Lord of Utkala his remarried wife during festivals of war, wherein handfuls of parched grain were fashioned from the pearls fallen from the frontal globes of furious scent-elephants, shattered by the flaming tongues of fire flickering from the maces of their tusks; [that king was Śaṅkaragaṇa]. VidSrk_46.14 *(1576) //
[This concludes] the section on Vasukalpa.
Thus ends the section on eulogies (praśastivrajyā). 46. Next is the section on mountains (parvatavrajyā). 47.
This is Mount Krauñcāvata, where the flocks of owls are silenced by the tumultuous resonance of the hollow bamboo thickets, sounding like the hooting of owls in the bowers of humming groves;
here, the serpents, agitated by the cries of the flapping peacocks, coil themselves about the trunks of the ancient Rohaṇa trees.
These mountains, composed of masses of moonstone, roar with rivers of water flowing from every limb as they flash in the moonlight;
on their plateaus where peacocks wake in wild frenzy, the *koyaṣṭi* birds perched upon *nameru* trees utter deep and faltering cries that seem to surpass even the nightingale.
Mount Mandara brings joy through its jewels, which consist of rows of scars from the friction of the multitude of diamond-points on the armlets of the slayer of Danu’s son;
we now know that this mountain is taller than it was before the churning of the ocean, for its broad base has been worn away by rubbing against the back of the supporting tortoise.
How indeed did this Mount Mandara endure such friction from the ropes of the serpent-kings, and how did it bear the agonizing blows of the wounds from the severed wings?
By this very evil-souled mountain, having raised up this wicked Fortune from the ocean, the world has been made to stumble in the confused dealings between the wealthy and the destitute.
This is that Mount Kailāsa, where, though their shadows are swallowed by the blazing nets of rays from its floors of crystal gems, the forms of the trees are nevertheless made manifest there;
and where, even for a lotus held by the rays of the sun as it approaches its edge, the unrestrained beams of the crescent moon upon the head of the Destroyer of Tripura provide a seal of protection.
This is Mount Kailāsa, its rocks marked with the signs of crocodiles, leaf-sprouts, and rows of jewels shimmering from the armlets of the Ten-faced one;
having ascended this mountain, which is beautiful in every part as it consists of crystal, the Yakṣas behold even the activities of the city of the Lord of Serpents.
This crystal mountain, its girdle pressed down by the firm grasp of the circle of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s staff-like arms,
provides for Śiva the pleasures of the balconies within his watery palace.

On the slopes of Mount Kailāsa, the trees—whose mother is the river born from the waters of the moonstones that sprout from the moonlight of the crescent moon adorning Śiva’s matted locks—nourish their offspring;

their bodies have grown through the touch of Gaurī’s hand, and they enjoy the pleasure of playing with the infant Ṣaṇmukha, who is carried along by the brotherly affection felt for his foster-brothers.
I remember this very mountain, its dark caves inhabited by owls terrified by the clamor of crows gathering at night with the brilliance of jewel-rays;
there, when I had pulled aside your bodice, you were angry, and the forest deities, out of curiosity, raised high the branches of trees as they gathered leaves for you to wear as a garment.
O Lakṣmaṇa, these clouds, though laden with spray, produce a pain of love in my eyes; even the winds, accompanied by raindrops, cause me intense torment during my separation from Sītā.
This is that very Mālyavat mountain, where even today the parrots in the forest inspire the sages to transcend the mind with words that have been refined through an ancient lineage of tradition.

These foothills of the Vindhyas terrify with their forest thickets at the edge of the paths, where the tips of tree branches, stripped and chewed by elephants, lie scattered along the reddened tracks; they are further agitated by wild boars startled by the fierce sound of cow-horns blown by a moving army of Śabaras.
(Vidūṣaka’s Verse 47.11, Kamalāyudha)
These are those lands of the Vindhya mountain, dense with bamboo groves green as parrots, where trees are bent by the tusks of elephants restless in play;
from whose vine-bowers, near the river, the breezes blow away the clusters of sweat-drops from the cheeks of Śabara women exhausted by lovemaking.

In some places the slopes of the Daṇḍaka and Vindhya foothills are smooth and dark, while in others they are harsh with terrifying expanses; here and there, the quarters of the sky resound with the splashing of waterfalls.
Interspersed with sacred fords, hermitages, mountains, rivers, ravines, and forests, these familiar terrains come clearly into view.

In some places silent and still, in others resounding with the cries of fierce beasts; where fires are kindled by the breath of deep and terrible serpents sleeping at their own will; whose boundaries consist of narrow ravines and crevices containing but little water, wherein thirsty *pratisūryaka* lizards drink the sweat-fluid of the pythons. (Bhavabhūti, Vidagdhamukhamandana 47.14)
Here, the deep, resonant growls of young bears dwelling in the caves become thick with their own echoes;
and the cold, pungent, and astringent scent of the resinous exudations from the joints of *śallakī* trees, shattered and scattered by elephants, grows heavy in the air.
Here, these mountain streams of Bhavabhūti become cool, clear, and fragrant with the blossoms of cane thickets trodden by flocks of birds;
their many currents are made resonant by stumbling through rose-apple groves darkened by the ripening weight of fruit. (VidSrk 47.16)

These forest regions on the slopes of the snowy mountains, possessing the exceedingly lovely splendor of Śiva and Śivā through their occupation as their dwelling place, nourish a festival for the eyes;

there, the divine trees are glossy with the flow from the sacrificial pits of the celestial rivers, which issue from the hollows created by the fresh blows of the tusks of the pre-eminent elephants of the fleeing enemy forces.
Thus ends the section on the Mountain, the forty-seventh. Next is the section on Peace, the forty-eighth:
This independent wandering, this food obtained without begging, this dwelling together with noble companions, and this sacred learning—the sole fruit of which is the exertion toward tranquility.
My mind moves slowly as I dwell upon it for a long time, reflecting; I do not know whose noble asceticism this is the ripened fruit of. *VidSrk_48.1* (1594)

Whose heart would these auspicious forest lands not fill with joy—lands whose borders are trampled by the feet of deer, which possess lush grassy meadows and waterfalls, where trees are set in motion on all sides by winds variegated with flowers, and which resound with the diverse cries of flocks of joyful birds? (VidSrk 48.2)
Having fulfilled the hopes of those who seek their aid, having acted kindly even toward their enemies,
and having reached the further shore of the flood of sacred learning, the fortunate ones retire to the forest. (VidSrk 48.3)

Those alone are steadfast who are not pierced by the arrows of insults from sharp-tongued wicked men; they alone enjoy the bliss of tranquility who, having cast aside the thicket of the poisonous creepers of women, have settled in penance groves where the fruit is peace.
Bark for clothing, young shoots for a bed, the foot of trees for a dwelling, roots to quell hunger, mountain stream water to assuage thirst,
playful deer as companions, birds as friends, and the moon as a lamp at night— even when such things are available in the forest, it is a marvel that miserable people still beg.

The time has passed, dear friend, when your side-glance—crooked with love for me and moving like a gentle ripple on the Yamunā—held power over me. Now our mental state is as hard as the shell of a tortoise’s belly; so why, O distressed one, do you waste yourself in vain?
O Mother Old Age, even though you bring death so near, we have been thoroughly satisfied by you;
for having removed youth—whose previous stages were fragile due to various pleasures and calamities—it is your appearance [that we welcome]. Fie on that youth!
(VidSrk 48.7) Or rather, let us remain with our minds at ease, having made our beloved wife the object of our affection, while savoring the pleasure of sporting with her own beautiful, full breasts.
Or else, we remain with concentrated minds, meditating upon the state of Brahman on a seat of eight blades of darbha grass upon the sandy banks of the celestial river.
You repeatedly gaze upon the face of Jñānānanta; you do not speak false flatteries to the wealthy, nor do you listen to their arrogant words, nor do you run about again with expectations.
At the proper time you eat young grass and sleep happily when sleep comes. Tell me, O deer, where did you perform such penance?
In one place a musical gathering of lutes; in another, the words of poets sprinkled with nectar; in one place the pain of disease; and in another, even the separation from friends.
Reflecting thus, rejoicing for a moment and then reeling for a moment—alas, I know not whether this worldly existence consists of nectar or of poison.

Oh, how difficult it is that those whose intellects are purified by the discernment of self-knowledge renounce even wealth that provides enjoyment, being entirely free from desire! We, however, are not able to give up those things which we neither obtained in the past nor possess now, nor have any firm certainty of obtaining in the future—things held merely by the grasp of our own longing. (VidSrk 48.11)

If there were song before you, sweet poets at your sides, the tinkling of playful bracelets behind you from the chowrie-bearers, and the sound of their fans—then, O mind, indulge in the pleasures of worldly existence; otherwise, enter into the Supreme Brahman. This is my prayer.

O King, let alone this sovereignty over the earth which is fraught with thorns; I consider even the sovereignty over the three worlds to be but thirst. My heart turns instead toward the mountain forest plateaus, teeming with herds of does sleeping without fear. (VidSrk 48.13)
These sense objects grant pleasure only so long as this delusion throbs within the heart;
but for those who know reality and possess discernment, where are the sense objects, where is the pleasure, and where is the grasping?
It is true that women are captivating; it is true that worldly prosperities are delightful. Yet, life is indeed as flickering as the sidelong glances of an intoxicated woman.

Shame, shame on those whose bodies are no different from worms, who—despite possessing great supernatural powers—have utterly extinguished their peace while dwelling in the prison-cells of asceticism!

We praise that wise man here, for whom there is no distinction in his taste, whether it be the meager vegetables obtained as alms in his cupped hands or the honey from the lotus-face of a charming girl.

Sense-objects are loathsome, the body is most repulsive, life is fleeting, and association with kinsmen—like that of travelers on a road—generally leads to separation; this cycle of existence is a dispersion to be abandoned and not to be cultivated. Such thoughts are indeed on the lips of everyone, yet they reside in the hearts of only some whose souls are virtuous.
When Bhartṛhari was under the influence of ignorance produced by the latent impressions of the darkness of passion, he saw this entire world as consisting solely of women.
But now, for us who apply the salve of keen discernment, our vision has become equalized, and we perceive even the three worlds as Brahman.
O Mother Lakṣmī, resort to someone else; do not be one who longs for me. Those who crave enjoyments are under your sway, but what are you to those who are free from desire?
At present, we seek our livelihood solely through barley-meal obtained by alms, purified by being placed in a vessel made from a freshly sewn cup of palāśa leaves.
O Bhāgīrathī, daughter of Jahnu, wife of the Ocean, crest-wreath of the Lord of Gaurī, banner of the festival of Dharma—I implore you:
my life-breaths depart as I sit upon a stone within your waters, swaying upon your waves, remembering your name, and fixing my gaze upon you.
"Abandoning worldly pleasure—which is as flickering as a garland of lightning and yields blinding darkness upon its cessation—one must instead adopt the faultless bliss of tranquility.
Thus we, with restless speech but empty minds, recite these words like parrots, utterly devoid of shame. (VidSrk 48.21)

The rivers of sense-objects have been crossed, desires have been cast aside at will, the exhaustion from separation from sense-objects has subsided, and the mind’s impurity has departed. Thus, having attained long-lasting happiness, the corpse lying in the cremation ground—its eyes slightly closed and its body well-nourished—reaches a state of supreme contentment.
I would gladly dwell in the forest wearing a patched garment made from a heap of withered *palāśa* leaves, maintaining my life even with water obtained without begging;
yet I cannot bring myself to utter that wretched, contemptible word, "Give!"—a speech accompanied by the exhaustion of the limbs, trembling, fear, and the internal fever of thirst.

Objects of the senses must inevitably depart even after one has dwelt among them for a very long time; what difference is there, then, in their departure whether people abandon them of their own accord?
For when they depart of their own volition, they cause extreme torment to the mind, whereas by abandoning them oneself, they bestow the infinite bliss of tranquility.
Where indeed lies such fortune for us, whose ascetic merit is so slight, that we might become the ornaments of the forest—trees whom the forest fire incessantly consumes;
yet whose kin, these clouds, forming their bodies from masses of smoke, unfeignedly protect the earth’s shores with their waters?

"Here is that face; where is that honey of the lower lip? Where have those sidelong glances gone? Where are those tender conversations? And where is that play of the eyebrows, curved like the bow of Love? Thus, with teeth bared upon the tip of the skull-topped staff and the wind whistling sweetly, this skull—a snare of delusion—is, alas, a loud mockery of those blinded by passion. (VidSrk 48.26)
"In this way, this foolish girl incessantly casts her eye toward me—an eye that steals the luster of the blue lotus petal; what does she intend?
Our delusion has passed, and the feverish flames from the impact of Cupid’s war-arrows have been extinguished; yet even so, this poor creature does not desist."
Experiencing childhood, then youth, and subsequently reaching old age— playing in the dust, traversing the course of sensual pleasures, and finally attaining tranquility—
the meritorious, shining in the lap of lotus-eyed mothers, drink at will from the breast, the lower lip, and the water of the sacred rivers.
Nearby flows the stream of time, bringing all manner of fear, with its banks—the days and nights—constantly crumbling away.
For those falling here, there is no support, nor even a turning back; yet what is this delusion of the great ones that they remain so unperturbed? (VidSrk 48.29)
"‘My wife, my son, all my wealth, and my circle of kinsmen’—
binding him who thus thinks ‘mine, mine,’ Time leads him away like a tethered beast.
The quarters of the sky are his garment, the hollow of his hand his bowl, deer are his friends, meditation is his sleep, the earth is his bed, and roots are his food."
When will this, which is so intensely fierce, become complete and desired by my heart's activity, for the sake of increasing supreme satisfaction? (VidSrk 48.31)
The splendors of youth are as fleeting as the shadows of autumn clouds; sense objects are pleasant at first sight, yet they bring torment in the end.
"O deer, may there be well-being for you at every branch; O forest, may health flow forth; O sandbanks, may there be safety for you; O stones, may there be welfare and prosperity.
Having somehow now emerged from that wretched dwelling, our hearts long for an extended acquaintance with you."
If people find satisfaction through my disparagement, then surely this is a favor bestowed upon me without effort;
for men seeking their own welfare renounce even riches acquired with great hardship for the sake of pleasing others. (VidSrk 48.34)

Devouring a human bone, devoid of flesh, covered with swarms of worms, drenched in saliva, foul-smelling, and loathsome—yet out of a craving for its incomparable taste—a dog regards even the Lord of the Gods standing at its side with suspicion; for a base person does not reckon with the worthlessness of his own possessions. (VidSrk 48.35)

What is that discernment in which compassion does not flow spontaneously? What is that path in which there is no taste for benefiting others? What is that dharma in which the cessation of malice toward others does not manifest? Or what indeed is that learning which does not lead to the state of tranquility? VidSrk_48.36 (1629)
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, having assumed the lotus posture upon a stone of the Snowy Mountain, and having entered the sleep of yoga through the practice of meditating on Brahman—
what could those days of mine not bring forth, wherein old deer might come without fear to relieve the itching of their horns?
This family was formerly embraced with love, then cherished, and protected until this day;
even now, like a wet garment clinging to my body, though I wish to leave it behind, I am unable to let it go. (VidSrk 48.38)

Forgiveness was practiced, yet not out of true forbearance; the comforts of home were abandoned, yet not out of contentment. The unbearable afflictions of cold, wind, and heat were endured, yet no austerity was performed.
Wealth was meditated upon day and night, but never that other eternal reality. Thus, we have performed those very same actions as the sages, yet have been cheated of their respective fruits.
Alms for food, a corner of a temple for a dwelling, the bare earth for a bed, and one's own body as the only retinue—[such is the life of the ascetic].
And as for clothing, it is a ragged quilt patched together from scattered scraps of cloth; alas, alas! even so, the mind does not abandon the objects of the senses.
This physical body, which is the transformation of semen and blood, has become the prey of death, the abode of heavy sorrows, and the resting place of disease;
yet, though he knows this, the man of passion—lacking self-control and devoid of discernment, sinking in the ocean of ignorance—alas, desires sons, desires women, desires fields, and desires wives.
Since this collection of elements had no existence previously and will likewise not exist hereafter, it is but a fleeting acquaintance during its intermediate state;
therefore, when this union is subject to inevitable separation by its very nature, what basis can there be for love, and what foundation can there be for grief?
Jackals and birds, this pack of dogs, and likewise insects and worms all around are devouring you;
since you did not perceive your own prosperity and the benefits conferred upon you by all these living beings, O corpse, you have been deceived. (VidSrk 48.43)
Keśaṭa says:
This man, out of a desire for happiness, was deceived by rogues called the "senses" who induced him to form an intimacy with them so that they might enjoy the objects of sense themselves;
now that they have achieved their purpose, they have adopted an attitude of indifference, while he, subject to the dictates of fate, is bound by other karmas.
Of Daśaratha. Thus ends the section on tranquility, followed by the section on miscellaneous topics. 49.

May the body of the Lord, who possesses both the form of the universe and his own sovereign nature—remaining inseparable from those resembling mountains of snow and mountains of collyrium—delight you; a body that rivals the white half-moon situated within an autumnal cloud and the path of the stars. *Vidvatsaṃvādasamvāda* 49.1 (1638).

I bow to that single form which bears matted locks tied upward and a crown of bones; which possesses both the splendor and the garland of the moon and the emerald-like Mandara mountain, radiant with jasmine and sapphire; which is formidable through the contact of the skull-topped staff and the discus; and which is marked by the various signs of Nandin, the Great Bull, and Tārkṣya, belonging to Śrīkaṇṭha and Vaikuṇṭha.
"Do not harbor pride, thinking, 'This cluster of blossoms, written by my beloved’s own hand upon the surface of my cheek, belongs to me alone.
O friend, would another woman not also be a worthy recipient of such things, were it not for the obstacle of internal trembling caused by a rival?"

O heart, abandon your despondency and immediately take hold of composure; for that beloved has arrived, the healing medicine for protecting you from the wounds of Love’s arrows—the tinkling of whose bangles, as she waves her hands in play to ward off the swarms of bees falling toward the fragrance of her breath, repeatedly causes [your pain] to faint away.
"O friend, while we were somehow passing much time with stories of various lands, my beloved arrived; by then, half the night had already passed.
Then, as soon as I became feigning anger out of playful affection, this eastern quarter turned crimson, like a rival wife provoked to great wrath."
O King, though your friend is full of affection and his hands are outstretched, you always keep your treasury sealed;
thus your conduct does not evoke the laughter of the night-lotus, which is ignorant of what is fitting.
O Lord, [your palace] has a vast vessel of gold and all your attendants are adorned.
At present, our residence is alike, dense with sporting female elephants.
(VidSrk 49.7) Even one's sense of discernment wanes, the mind falters, and wisdom perishes;
a man’s fortitude falls away when his mind reels from the poison of the sensory objects. (VidSrk 49.8)
In the presence of the king amidst a circle of scholars, during a union of excellent lovers,
even a man eloquent in speech becomes timid when his heart is defiled by trepidation.
What can a hungry parrot do with a *kiṃśuka* tree, even if it is laden with fruit?
Even if a non-giver prospers, what can his dependents do?
Though I remain here, I am yours; though you dwell there, you are mine. O Noble One, a true union is one of the heart alone; a union of the body is not a true union.
This is merely the toil of the astrologers who watch the heavens for auspicious moments, calculate the lunar phases, and gather their shadows, while their fingers grow weary.
Blessed is that night, fortunate is that day, and holy is that very moment when a beloved, long unknown, finally comes within the range of one's eyes.
"You are the treasury of their offenses; she too is intolerant and haughty with pride. Therefore, you are being forbidden from going to her house.
But if you go anyway, I think you will stay there for a long time—firmly restrained by her girdle, struck by her ear-lotuses, and cast down at her feet, seeking refuge in her alone."
I know that she possesses great pride, yet when I stand before her, there will arise within her a certain surge of trepidation that dispels her anger;

for in that state, with limbs bristling with horripilation and trembling unsteadily, where is the ear-lotus, where is herself, and where is the girdle? Thus, her stubbornness of pride almost surely slips away.

As soon as he was born, King Bhoja of the Turuṣkas beheld his sweet splendor of form; and for that amorous man, amidst the throng of brides who had arrived for the great festival of the son's birth, the heart burned with longing, thinking: "Alas, my life has not attained even a single moment of union with him, whose youth is so lovely, and who bears the dark beauty of a young woman’s face! VidSrk_49.15 (1652)
"It teaches Vallaṇa the whistling sound, it wounds the lower lip, and it spreads horripilation—is it that a city-dweller has met her? No, no, friend, it is the winter wind. (VidSrk 49.16)

The bashful half-glance shared by both, the sending of a female messenger with the thought that "the union will take place today or tomorrow," the joy and delight born of affection, and the impulsive kisses and embraces once the union has been attained—this alone is the fruit of desire and true sexual union; everything else is like the mating of beasts.

Behold, with his body bent upward and downward, occupying both the hind and front halves [of his frame], his mind fixed upon his stiffly arched and upturned back, bearing a tail whose tip is slightly curved;
with the cavity of his mouth made formidable by the tips of his tusks, raising his mane, and pricking up his ears, the lion of cruel form paces toward the lord of elephants.
These currents of water, lovers of the Mekala maiden, reaching down to the very base of the underworld and splitting the Vindhya mountains, cause terror before me;
for they sportively uproot, dance, strike, turn back, propel, abandon, seize, hide, move, and toss aside the trees upon their banks.
Having brought the world to a state of bliss with breezes that are kin to the spray, with the cries of swans pleasing to the ear, and with blooming lotuses and pure waters,
the lotus-pond later beheld its own external condition of diminished wealth and, under the guise of lotus stalks, gave its bones— white as the new moon— to those who sought them.
Indeed, there exists no means whatsoever that can satisfy all the world;
one must act for one's own welfare in every way—what will people, with their much talk, do?
The supreme excellence of the bow's two ends shines forth, since even arrows devoid of string obtain their targets. (VidSrk 49.22)
Even after performing the ordeal of drinking from the vessel, the young bee still longs for the *bakula* bud right before the lotus; O dark bee, where is there truth in you?
(VidSrk 49.23) In this village, no lodging is given to travelers now; a young traveler fell asleep last night on the floor of the wedding pavilion here.
When the clouds thundered with a harsh roar, he sang aloud; because of what he did then while remembering his beloved, people even today remain apprehensive of the falling of a thunderbolt.

In the heat of the sun, the bird separated from its mate for the night could not endure even the rays of the moon with its patient wife; for when the mind is afflicted by grief, everything becomes unbearable.

If the Ganges of our well-spoken verses were to flow into the unfathomable ocean of your heart—a sea made difficult to fathom by those various priceless qualities that have unveiled the weight of universal wonder—then [our purpose would be fulfilled].
The confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, with its dense flow of liquid essence from the Viśvaśvitramataṅginī river and its resonant roar, unfolds once more as if it were something unprecedented.

Alas! This herd of elephants, whose bellies are dark from the ripening *tinduka* fruits and whose flanks are pale, appears fit for the touch of the hands of beautiful Pulinda hunters. O daughter of the lord of that forest, this herd—miserable in its plea for the gift of life—entreats you; do not cover your pair of breasts with the silken garments of leaves.
Out of shame, she lowers her face when she realizes, "He knows me," and upon seeing the conversation between the two, she steers the talk toward herself.
When her friends smile, she displays even greater embarrassment; for the most part, the beloved remains distressed with anxiety hidden within her heart.
Whether an action be virtuous or devoid of virtue, a wise person performing a multitude of deeds must carefully consider its ultimate consequence.
For the ripening of actions performed with excessive haste becomes like a piercing thorn, causing a burning in the heart until their final resolution. (VidSrk 49.29)
The rains are the cause of mud; autumn is the root of daily distress; in the early winter there is numbness, and likewise in the late winter one is afflicted by the wind;
the spring season brings madness to the mind, and summer has scorching heat. "It is time! It is time!"—thus people rejoice, yet what beauty is there in time? VidSrk_49.30 (1667)
The darkness born of youth, which obstructs the vision of young men,
cannot be dispelled by the light of jewels and cannot be warded off even by the rays of the sun.

O you who delight only in the momentary taste [of beauty], why do you wish to sow the seed of the lotus in the pond? This world is the Kali age; O ignorant one, it will destroy the splendor of your very face by remaining there.
He who remains dear even while doing what is unpleasant is indeed truly dear;
for who would show disregard for fire, even when the essence of its house has been consumed? (VidSrk 49.33)

"This one is blind, this Śukra has uneven feet, this son of the Sun has mangled limbs, this Rāhu has diminished majesty, and this cool-rayed moon is incomplete"—ignorant even of their own fixed karma and its fruits, people prattle thus, thinking, "We are seized by the host of planets. (VidSrk 49.34)
If a gem fit for a collection of golden ornaments is fastened to tin, it neither cries out nor does it flee; rather, the blame falls upon the one who joined them. (VidSrk 49.35)

We pay homage to the gods; yet surely even they are subject to the Ordainer. That Ordainer is to be revered; yet even he bestows only the fruits of specifically determined actions. If the fruit depends on action, what is the use of others, and what need is there for an Ordainer? Homage to those noble actions, before which even the Ordainer has no power!
When he quarrels, he destroys his reputation; when he practices friendliness, his virtues are corrupted.
Observing both sides with equanimity, the discerning man treats the common person as one who is ruined by contempt.
O Goddess Tṛṣṇā, homage to you; you have now accomplished your purpose, for that form which is called "Infinite" has been made small by you. (VidSrk 49.38)

In the past some have departed; others have set out after them, and still others follow. What cause for despair is there for us? For we too shall go there. Yet, why this mental anguish? How is it that our friends, having failed to establish a signal on this great road, will not come within the range of our vision?
A man remains on the path of virtue only so long, he masters his senses only so long, he maintains his modesty only so long, and he upholds his discipline only so long,

as these arrows of the glances of playful women— drawn and released from the bow of their brows, with dark lashes reaching the path of the ears— do not fall upon his heart and steal away his fortitude.

"If his wife, distressed by separation and remembering her husband, should give up her life while he is on his journey, whose great sin would that be?"—while the traveler was thus reflecting in his heart, a cuckoo perched atop a tree repeatedly cried out loudly, "Yours! Yours! many times over.
That lord of the earth beheld the garden, which— with the sky obscured by the foul weather of pollen falling from creepers bent low under the weight of unopened buds—
was the assembly hall of the King Spring, the abode of the god who dwells in the heart, and an unsurpassed shelter-house for bees and a single pavilion for travelers.
To dispel the fever of love, now constantly employ these two remedies:
drinking the honey from the young girl’s lip, and the practice of pressing her breasts with your fist. What can even one who knows the rules of medical treatment do if he is destitute?
Like one mounted on the head of a rutting elephant without a goad.
Whose name is not known here? For even while looking at him, this world remains as if mute toward me; yet every person suffers on my account.
It is impossible to show this body by splitting it in two like a betel nut; truly, friend, I have surely seen the moon on the fourth day.
[The bull] strikes travelers daily with the blows of his hooves and his horns; he is renowned throughout the entire city for his great skill in utterly destroying the crops.
He does not carry the yoke upon his shoulders at all, but rather walks firmly upon the earth; it would be better to have an empty stall than this wicked bull.
When a tank is under pressure from a flood, the remedy is an overflow channel;
and when the heart is agitated by grief, it is steadied by lamentations. (VidSrk 49.47)
Fie on sandalwood! What is the wretched nectar of immortality? And what has been lost by the moon through its lotus-roots?
I do not know of any object in this world that could serve as a worthy comparison for the dust from the limbs of my daughter. (VidSrk 49.48)
Having reflected that youth is fleeting, the body is perishable, and wealth is transitory,
the discerning person does not perform even an action that appears pleasant in this life, if its bitter ripening must be experienced in another birth.
For one who looks further and further down, how could greatness not arise?
But those who look higher and higher, everyone indeed becomes impoverished.
This is a film of darkness coming from the orb of the moon; this is a foul odor from the interior of a lotus;
for that which is uttered as false speech by one born of noble lineage is truly contemptible.
He who was nourished in childhood with handfuls of wild rice and tips of grass, and by whom the water remaining from oblations was drunk from the hollow of a lotus leaf—*VidSrk_49.51*(1688)*.
Standing at a distance, the ascetic gazes slowly and with longing yet fear upon that elephant, its cheeks quivering as it is intoxicated by drinking the wine of rut-fluid.

With their hair disheveled from the tossing of their hands and their beauty marred by sweat, those long-lashed women have left some impression upon our minds through the mere fragments of their forms; yet, bearing the mark of repetition due to their variety, these lines of characters in their letters convey a sense of distraction through broken sentences.
That this palm leaf is not harsh, that the impression upon it is formed from thick sandalwood paste from her breasts,
and that the binding consists of thin fibers of lotus stalks— this is the love-letter of some woman, its seal having faded away.
"This is a lotus stalk that she has fashioned into a bracelet;
this indeed is the sprout from her own ear-ornament; and this is her garment of plantain leaves, upon which the fever of love seems to have been transferred."—These verses are by Rājaśekhara.

The month is sweet, the forest is secluded, you are a young woman in the bloom of youth when the onset of passion is manifest, and we too have our duties to fulfill. Let my mother go, O charming girl; stay here for a moment, or rather, this has already become a clear subject for the words of backbiters.
If not even a single drop of the speech of Vallaṇa— the moon among sages— which is the supreme flood of spreading nectar, somehow enters the vessel of this mind’s anxiety,
how could the unbearable onset of the burning pain of separation from a beloved ever be endured, even by one dwelling within the heart of the Snowy Mountain?
Indeed, that which Dharmakīrti holds himself in high esteem is the greatest among all the thousands of illusions of Viṣṇu.

Emaciated, one-eyed, lame, deaf, tailless, wasted by hunger, decrepit, with a neck bound by the shards of a broken pot, his body covered with wounds oozing pus and swarming with clusters of worms—a dog approaches a female dog; yet even such a dog, though struck down, still kills her. So too does the god of love. (VidSrk 49.59)
Many are seen here crossing this deep lake, causing a hundred wonders in the hearts of these two sisters;
yet he who, having entered, discerns and extracts some hidden thing within after holding his breath for a long time—he indeed is rare among them.
[The work] of Paṇḍita Jñānaśrī.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous topics,
followed by the section on the praise of poets.
We have devotion for Subandhu; who here does not delight in the author of the *Raghuvamśa*? Our steadfastness is captivated by the son of Dākṣī; Haricandra also steals our heart.
Śūra possesses pure expression, and the words of Bhāravi are naturally beautiful; nevertheless, Bhavabhūti spreads an indescribable inner joy.
My father alone has here brought to perfection a creation concerning subjects never before seen; Vāgūra is an expert in the path of poetic discourse followed by the great elephant among poets.

Yogeśvara knows how to cause his words to sprout forth upon subjects that are mostly things dispatched by the *jhañjhā* winds from the women of the Pulinda tribes in the Revā, the Vindhya, and the Pāmaras.

O brother, if you have the curiosity to drink the nectar for the ears, to compose words esteemed by the virtuous, to attain supreme proficiency, to find the ultimate limit of the stream of aesthetic flavor, and to enjoy the sweet fruit of the tree of life, then listen to the well-spoken words of the poet Rājaśekhara, which distill the essence of ambrosia. *Vidvatsaṃvādasamuccaya* 50.3. (1700)

Many indeed revere the Goddess of Speech as the patroness of Śaṅkaravarman; however, this poet Murāri, who has undergone the hardships of living in the house of his teacher, knows the true essence of Sarasvatī most thoroughly.
The ocean was indeed crossed by the monkey warriors, but only Mount Mandara—its massive body fixed deep within the underworld—knows its profound depth.

These words of the poet Murāri possess the splendor of falling into the nectar-well of Vālmīki’s speech— words that are profound and captivating, filled with the fragrance of the glorious panegyric of the radiant lineage of Kakutstha.
Fie, fie on those doctrines of Murāri!
Fie on those tiresome and painful scriptures! Fie on those fruitless words in which these [verses] do not appear—these verses which are the delight of the nectar extracted by the virtues of Vallaṇa;

which are the dance-floors for the hairs of the body, the rising of the moon for the ocean of the flood of tears from the eyes, and the cause of the action that dissolves the exhaustion of pride in rival poets. VidSrk_50.6 *(1703)
How can the poetic art of poets—who have established the reality of the entire universe within every single word—be grasped by the ears of the young who are deceived by shallow chatter?

Where can the ocean of beauty be fathomed by those who perform the wonder of plunging into the ditches of the streets; for within it, the great mountains sink while sporting with the leaping fish that are the goddesses of fortune?
The essence of the meaning of words, though not explicitly proclaimed by sounds, delights through its manifestation as a vivid rasa; it does not delight when its rasa is laid bare.
Just as the swelling breasts of women captivate when partially veiled by silk garments fluttering in the breeze, but not so when their form is fully uncovered. (VidSrk 50.8)
Now that the sun of Bhāravi has set through the power of time, and the moon of Kālidāsa has been eclipsed by the darkness,
this world— its lamp of Bāṇa extinguished— is no longer illuminated today by the jewel of Vallaṇa.
While the lineage of Raghu stands before him, only a poet such as Kumāradāsa— or perhaps Rāvaṇa himself— is capable of composing the *Jānakīharaṇa*.
Those words which do not dwell upon the path of the world’s intellects are not such [words]; nor is that essence of meaning which does not hasten along the royal road of speech.
Yet there exists another, a union of word and meaning cooled by its own arrangement, by which these poets—who have mastered themselves—churn the hearts of us all.
Victorious is the illustrious author of the *Raghuvaṃśa*, the ornament of the poets' throats, in the field of knowable objects;
for when that field has been harvested by the sickle of his intellect, other poets merely gather grains like gleaners.
Surely the pride of poets vanished because of the *Vāsavadattā*.
As if by her own power, she went within the range of Karna's vision for the sake of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The fame of Pravarasena, radiant as a flower,
has reached the far shore of the ocean by means of his poetry, just as a monkey army crossed by way of a bridge.
In every house there are countless breeders like dogs,
but poets who produce [true poetry] are not many, like śarabha deer.
These poets of Bāṇa’s, such as Kālidāsa and others, and we here are also poets;
for both possess the nature of reality (vastutva), whether in a mountain or in an atom.

O root of the sprout of kindness, the entire essence of beautiful stories, the mantra that attracts the hearts of women, the wave upon the river of Love, the beloved of speech, the sole abode of good fortune, the repository of elegant words, the ocean of fortitude, the tree upon the mountain of Dharma—O crest-jewel among kings, my friend, you have been seen; we must now depart.
This nectar, consisting of the interplay between word and meaning, bathes the minds of the sensitive with streams of joy;
this is poetry. But that reality which flashes forth herein—the subtle, supreme essence—is clearly manifest within the intellects of the wise, yet remains beyond the reach of words.

O Lord of Poets, your speech— adorned with golden ornaments, skilled in manifesting the flavor of embrace, possessing the radiant expression of the Vaidarbha style, moving with a graceful progression of word-arrangement, gleaming with abundant sentiment, and though soft, having a body fit for the pressure of friction— captivates the heart like a deer-eyed woman.
That mother Sarasvatī, who possesses sons, bestows her aesthetic flavors upon him through various forms of flattery; yet he, unrestrained, has toyed with her through his sports.
Seeing those wicked sons who cause afflictions and diseases through the vices of their tongues, she buries her own wealth here and there, making herself appear destitute.
Even if its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the eye, even before its fragrance has been perceived. (VidSrk 50.21)
In ancient times there was the poet Subandhu, born from an anthill; after him, Bhartṛmeṇṭha attained fame upon the earth;
and now, he who once again stood forth by the stroke of destiny as Bhavabhūti exists as Rājaśekhara.
When an arrow remains lodged in the heart, not even a breath can escape;
how much less so the speech of one whose poetic composition is characterized by grand and elaborate flourishes?
That which does not cause the heads of men to shake again and again within their hearts—is that even the poetry of a poet? Or is it the arrow of archers? (VidSrk 50.24) [The lotus].
In some way, through much time, I have, as it were, plunged into the deep and smooth-flowing current of Kālidāsa’s eloquence. (VidSrk 50.25)
One is capable of composing speech, while another is merely able to hear it; thus your auspicious intellect brings us wonder from both sides.
For the collection of excellences does not reside in one place: one [stone] produces gold, while another is capable of testing it.
Of Kālidāsa.
Note: Ingalls points out that the attribution to Kālidāsa is based on a misunderstanding of the remarks with which Rājaśekhara prefaces his citation of the verse in the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*.

If one considers our opinion regarding the mastery of technical application, the explanation of the specific meanings of individual words, clarity, profundity, the infusion of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the composition of sentence-meanings,
and the transformation of both sense and expression in a direction inaccessible to others— then the poet Amarasiṃha is victorious.
