This cow of Śālika is unrestrained; for how is it that, though bound tightly by you, she does not touch anything other than Vaidarbha?

And how is it that, despite being easily accessible, she is known on earth as fruitful and yet inaccessible to the bulls among poets? Or how is it that she flows with abundant nectar, even when milked by many?

Vālmīki bound the ocean of words with mountains brought by monkeys, and Vyāsa likewise [bound it] with the arrows of Pārtha; yet even so, no charge of exaggeration is leveled against them. Word and meaning are like two things held on a scale; nevertheless, this world finds fault with the compositions in this [work]. O you who have spread out your mouth [in criticism], salutations to your two feet! *Vidagdha-śrīkaṇṭha-carita* 50.29 (1726)
Alas, what a tragedy! The illustrious King Utpalarāja, the beloved of the bride that is Learning, was not seen by the skillful Dharmakīrti—the crest-jewel of the circle of poets.

Thus, the fortune of this skillful man, who was a unique Rohaṇa mountain for those seeking his favor, became in vain, since the ear-ornaments of his beautiful verses were never placed upon [the king’s] ears. (VidSrk 50.30)
Whatever one’s understanding may be, Dakṣa, such is the true disposition of one’s heart here;
it blossoms both in the words of the preeminent sage and in the Ancient Puruṣa.
No one precedes me, nor does anyone follow behind; the path, freshly trodden by my feet, is not yet worn. How is it that I am all alone?
It is now understood: the broad, crooked path that was previously cleared has now become a wasteland; indeed, it was clearly and forcefully chosen by me.

Fie upon that man who applies the title "human" to himself, if he has not wedded the learned consort of Dharmakīrti’s words— worthy of his lineage like a praiseworthy daughter— and if, having failed to produce from her the Fortune [of eloquence], he does not bestow her upon a seeker with affectionate courtesy. (VidSrk 50.33)
Those who spread contempt for us here, whoever they may be—Bhartṛhari says: "They know nothing at all; this effort is not for them.
But someone of similar nature will surely arise; for time is infinite and fortune is vast. (VidSrk 50.34)

A treasury of sciences, a family home of boundless fame, a pure mirror-surface for the stories of the good conduct of kings, and a celestial tree for the creepers of the jewels of artistic perfection—a poet, profound by nature and celebrated in this world, reigns supreme. (VidSrk 50.35)
That path which was formerly led by Bhavabhūti every day when Bāṇa had departed; which was trodden for a long time by Kamalāyudha, by whom Keśaṭa reached [eminence];
and which has long been purified by contact with the dust of the feet of the illustrious Vākpatirāja—by good fortune, that path of a certain man of praiseworthy virtues is now being opened up.

When this world, tossed upon the ocean of existence, becomes the abode of the most wondrous aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), there arises a certain profound depth that, being stilled by its share of that flavor, brings rest. — By Vallana. (VidSrk 50.37)
As if being pulled by the tongue within the mouth by the undertakings of wealthy kings—even when merely remembered while remaining in the heart—one does not venture forth into poetry. (VidSrk 50.38)

The poetry of Bāṇa and Vālmīki is merely a bud; what respect can there be for the words of Vyāsa? The speech of Bhāravi is nothing but a mockery. If a poem has attained the status of an ornament upon the ears of Dharmāyaṇa, then why say more of that blessed lord, the master of the Vaidarbha style?

As long as the left side of Dharmāśoka’s body remains adorned with the clusters of his broad breasts; as long as the Lord of Bhavānī (Śiva) retains his addiction to forcibly seizing the neck of Lakṣmī; as long as Hari (Viṣṇu) remains the remover of faults;

and as long as Brahmā’s hands remain occupied with the ritual of drawing back his bowstring—so long shall the well-spoken verses of the virtuous remain to be licked like honey by the ears of the learned.

Vidyākara composed this treasury of rare and beautiful verses for the adornment of the throats of virtuous poets—those true bards who, like the gods descended to the mortal world, have attained residence in the third heaven through their fame. (VidSrk 50.41)
Thus ends the section on the description of excellent poets.
Thus ends this *Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa*.
[The work] of the scholar, the illustrious Bhīmārjunasoma.
